Draft to enacted text

What changed from the 2023 draft to PP 33/2026

The draft of 31 August 2023 ran to 245 articles in 10 chapters. The enacted text has 225 in 12. Below are 112 differences found by comparing the two clause by clause, each quoted from both texts, with 72 of them marked as changing an obligation. Statutory text is Indonesian and untranslated.

01
Indonesia · Personal data protection

The implementing regulation brings legally significant changes from the 2023 draft

PP 33/2026 takes effect on 16 January 2027. Comparing the 2023 draft with the enacted text clause by clause turns up 112 verified differences, 72 of which change what a controller actually has to do. Every one is quoted from both texts.

Why this matters now

Six months to comply and the rules still unwritten

16 Jan 2027
the regulation takes effect, six months after promulgation
36
provisions carrying administrative sanctions, Pasal 184(1)
34

72
of the changes below shift an obligation materially
The through-line

Almost every enforcement mechanism in the regulation is routed to a Peraturan Lembaga that has not been issued. Pasal 223 requires processing to conform to this regulation until the Peraturan Lembaga on processing is issued, which is what keeps compliance possible in the meantime.

The same differences, sorted by compliance domain rather than by chapter, on the ten domain framework the gap assessment working paper uses. One bucket, the regime, holds what shapes the programme without sitting inside it.

Accountability and Governance

Audit becomes mandatory the checklist goes

mixed 7 changes, 7 material
What a practitioner needs to know

PP 33/2026 Pasal 138(2) turns accountability into a floor introduced by paling sedikit harus: technical and organisational measures, documentation of every processing activity, responses to the Lembaga, proof of compliance, and both an internal and an external protection audit, where draft Pasal 154(3) had said only that a controller dapat audit.

Pasal 169(2) adds kepada Lembaga as the addressee for the accountability documents behind a transfer safeguard, and Pasal 69(3) to (8) makes a data quality standard, periodic or ad hoc verification and a record of the results standing controls, after draft Pasal 82(3)(d) let a controller conclude that verification was not needed.

What thinned is the scaffolding around all that: draft Pasal 10 to Pasal 15 hung a duty checklist on each lifecycle stage and enacted Pasal 8 lists the stages with nothing attached, the seven-part public body instrument at draft Pasal 67 shrinks to two headings at Pasal 50 with no publication and no filing, and the data-room access gate at draft Pasal 152 survives only as a duty to prepare terms at Pasal 133(6).

Why that direction

The controller now owes two audits, a maintained verification regime and documents producible to the regulator, while the lifecycle checklist, the public body instrument and the transaction access gate that used to carry the programme have gone.

Do now
  • Book an internal and an external protection audit for this cycle under Pasal 138(2)(e), name the external provider, and set a retention rule for both reports so they stand as accountability evidence.
Still open

Pasal 169(2) states no trigger, form or deadline for producing accountability documents to the Lembaga, and the Peraturan Lembaga on the policy document promised by Pasal 50(3) has not been issued, so whether filing is proactive or on request is still open.

Every change in this domain
Data Protection Officer

More officers appointed with weaker protection

mixed 4 changes, 4 material
Inside this domain
What a practitioner needs to know

The dan/atau at PP 33/2026 Pasal 142(1) follows the Constitutional Court. Putusan 151/PUU-XXII/2024, pronounced 30 July 2025 and granted in full, declared the dan in UU 27/2022 Pasal 53(1) huruf b conditionally unconstitutional sepanjang tidak dimaknai dan/atau, so the three appointment triggers are alternative, not cumulative.

Draft RPP Pasal 165(1) is dated 31 August 2023, predates the ruling, and joined the triggers with dan; that cumulative reading would have failed it. Any one trigger now pulls a controller into the duty, where the draft required all three at once.

The officer's own position moved the other way: RPP Pasal 168(1)(c) barred dismissal or punishment for doing the job and enacted Pasal 146(1)(c) asks only that the officer operate objectively and independently and free from interference, while the direct report to the Lembaga PDP at RPP Pasal 169(2)(c) becomes a report to internal leadership at Pasal 147(2)(c).

On dissolution the duty to appoint a surviving contact point at RPP Pasal 147(3) is now discretionary under Pasal 136(2), with no period attached.

Constitutional CourtPutusan No. 151/PUU-XXII/2024 UU 27/2022 Pasal 53 ayat (1) huruf b, pronounced 30 July 2025, the petition is granted in full
Why that direction

Many more controllers now have to appoint an officer, but the officer they appoint has lost the tenure guarantee and the route to the regulator that the draft gave them.

Do now
  • Re-run the appointment test against each limb of Pasal 142(1) on its own, and record which limb catches which entity, because processing for public services alone is now enough.
  • Add a no dismissal and no penalty for performing the role term to the officer's engagement contract and job description, since Pasal 146(1)(c) no longer supplies it.
  • Open a dated escalation log for the officer's findings and recommendations, with the internal recipient named, because that record is the only trace once escalation stays inside the organisation.
  • Add a named post-dissolution contact and a period to winding up and merger templates, rather than relying on Pasal 136(2).
Still open

Pasal 142(2) leaves the detail of the officer's duty to a Peraturan Lembaga that has not been issued, so the qualification standard, whether a group may share one officer, and whether contact details must reach the Lembaga are all still open.

What a practitioner needs to know

Both texts list the same three triggers: processing for public services, core activities involving regular and systematic large-scale monitoring, and core activities built on large-scale processing of specific or crime-related data. The difference sits in one connector. RPP Pasal 165(1) closes limb b with dan, so a controller had to satisfy all three at once. PP 33/2026 Pasal 142(1) closes it with dan/atau, so any one limb is enough.

The connector is the Court's wording. Putusan 151/PUU-XXII/2024, pronounced 30 July 2025, declared the dan in UU 27/2022 Pasal 53(1) huruf b conditionally unconstitutional sepanjang tidak dimaknai dan/atau. The draft is dated 31 August 2023 and predates the ruling; the enacted text writes what the Court required. Public bodies processing for public services now fall within the duty on that ground alone, as does a controller running large-scale systematic monitoring.

Two smaller moves sit beside it. Inside limb b the draft's sifat, ruang lingkup, dan/atau tujuan becomes sifat, ruang lingkup, atau tujuan. The appointment standard at RPP Pasal 165(2), professionalism, knowledge of the law and of protection practice, and capacity for the tasks, becomes its own article at PP Pasal 143, and both the duty and the standard now wait on a Peraturan Lembaga for their detail.

Constitutional CourtPutusan No. 151/PUU-XXII/2024 UU 27/2022 Pasal 53 ayat (1) huruf b, pronounced 30 July 2025, the petition is granted in full

Consent and Privacy Notice

Notice template gone consent test added

mixed 18 changes, 12 material
Inside this domain
What a practitioner needs to know

The sixteen item content schedule at draft Pasal 76(2) did not survive: enacted Pasal 62 fixes only seven headings, a notice channel that stays available throughout processing and delivery before processing begins, with the content detail parked in Pasal 66 for a Peraturan Lembaga that has not issued. Consent moved the other way.

Pasal 32(2) now requires it to be free, conscious, specific and unambiguous, and the draft escape at Pasal 104(2), which let a controller keep processing on another basis after a withdrawal, is gone, so Pasal 92 runs verification, cessation and a confirmation back to the subject. Deadlines shifted quietly as well, since Pasal 64 gives thirty Hari for the indirect collection notice and Pasal 1 defines Hari as a working day.

Why that direction

The controller lost the drafting specification it could audit its notice against but gained a validity test for consent and lost the ability to switch basis once consent is withdrawn.

Do now
  • Freeze the draft Pasal 76(2) sixteen item list as the internal notice template, map every item to a field in the live notice, and note that Pasal 62(3) requires the notice to stay reachable for as long as processing continues.
Still open

Pasal 66 sends the content of the privacy notice to a Peraturan Lembaga that has not issued, so until it does nothing in force states what a notice must actually say beyond the seven headings in Pasal 62(1).

Every change in this domain
Consent and Privacy Notice

Seven headings survive the sixteen items do not

7 changes
What a practitioner needs to know

The sixteen item content list at draft Pasal 76(2) was the specification a controller could audit a notice against: identity, officer contact, basis, the use, storage and destruction periods, the withdrawal, access and objection mechanisms, the security measures.

Enacted Pasal 62(1) keeps seven headings, Pasal 62(3) adds a channel that must stay reachable throughout processing, and Pasal 66 parks the content detail in a Peraturan Lembaga that has not issued, so keep drafting to the draft list. Timing moved twice.

Pasal 62(4) starts the duty before processing where draft Pasal 77(1) said before collection, and a controller that treats collection as a prior step has an argument the chapter never closes, so serve the notice at collection anyway.

The indirect collection notice at Pasal 64 now runs 30 Hari, a working day term under Pasal 1, roughly six calendar weeks, and its trigger widens to data obtained as well as collected. The specific notices thinned. The vital interest notice at Pasal 47(1) loses wajib, its parent and guardian addressees and any fixed time, while the public task notice moves to the start of processing with any deferral recorded under Pasal 51(3).

Pasal 65 then re-scopes the exoneration ban to the notice itself, tidak dapat where the draft said dilarang, so a liability disclaimer sitting in terms of service falls outside it on its face.

The findings on this slide
Consent and Privacy Notice

Consent gains a test and loses its exit

5 changes
What a practitioner needs to know

Pasal 32(2) adds the test the draft never had: consent must be obtained freely, consciously, specifically and unambiguously. The draft regulated the mechanism, the prior information and the proof, so a flow could pass every rule while bundling purposes or relying on a pre-ticked box.

Now it fails on validity, and the proof duty at Pasal 36 means the controller must evidence which design feature delivers each of the four qualities. The exit closed. Draft Pasal 104(2) let a controller answer a withdrawal by switching to another basis and carrying on; Pasal 92 keeps the duty to stop, adds verification and a confirmation of cessation, and carries no exception, so the basis is fixed at collection.

The mechanism, withdrawal and non-discrimination duties drop from wajib to harus, but neither instrument's sanction list ever reached them, so rank remediation by the Pasal 184(1) list. Two scope lines moved. The marketing disclosure duty at Pasal 35(2) now applies only where the processing rests on explicit consent, so direct marketing run on legitimate interests escapes it, and Pasal 62 does not require recipients or an offer specific withdrawal route.

And the duty to identify service users is no longer keyed to services children can reach: Pasal 38(1) calibrates it to the purpose of processing, though parental consent at Pasal 38(2) keeps wajib.

The findings on this slide
Consent and Privacy Notice

The bases beyond consent are redrawn

5 changes
What a practitioner needs to know

The contract basis carries new weight. Pasal 43(1) swaps the draft's specific security guarantee for a general compliance guarantee, adds the subject's rights and the controller's duties, and drops the disclosure of other bases used beyond the contract purpose, the one contractual transparency device against basis stacking.

And where the draft voided a non compliant contract, Pasal 43(2) instead disqualifies it as a basis, triggered by any of the nine items rather than the consent limb alone. Public task narrowed and legitimate interest opened. Pasal 49(2) keeps only the statutory mandate limb, so processing the draft grounded on a directly threatened public interest must now find a statute that commands the action or fall back on vital interests.

Pasal 55 then hands public bodies the basis the draft flatly denied them, confined to purposes outside the public task, which is exactly the space GDPR Article 6(1)(f) leaves open. Underneath the bases the fairness standard slipped.

Honest and good faith processing was a free-standing wajib at draft Pasal 79(2); Pasal 60(2) restates it as a harus riding on transparency, so the general hook against conduct that is disclosed but substantively misleading is gone, and a fairness argument now has to run through the three transparency requirements Pasal 60(1) sets out.

The findings on this slide
Third Party and Vendor Risk

Vendor oversight now rests on contracts

weaker 9 changes, 3 material
What a practitioner needs to know

The supervision chapter lost its working parts. RPP Pasal 135 took the pre engagement vetting of a processor and the internal, external and exit audit programme with it, and RPP Pasal 137 took the eleven minimum contract terms and the Bahasa Indonesia requirement, leaving PP 33/2026 Pasal 127 with three bare headings and Pasal 128 pointing at a Peraturan Lembaga that has not been issued.

The appointment side still stands and is where the work now sits: PP Pasal 14 carries the eleven item clause list intact including the audit and inspection mechanism, Pasal 15(2) keeps written controller approval before a processor engages another, and the new Pasal 141(2) gives the processor its own four duties of documenting, answering the Lembaga, showing compliance and auditing.

Around that the floor drops, because sub processor assurance falls to harus at Pasal 15(3) and outside the Pasal 184(1) sanction list, an instruction under Pasal 139(2) need only be documented rather than written, Pasal 126(2) recasts affiliates as Pengendali Data Pribadi lain instead of supervised parties, and Pasal 10 no longer deems a party that requests personal data a controller.

Why that direction

The enacted text deletes the only mandated diligence and audit programme over processors and softens the assurance and instruction duties, so almost everything the controller does here it now does because its own contract and policy say so.

Do now
  • Rebuild the data processing agreement template on PP Pasal 14 and write back the four RPP Pasal 137 clauses no enacted article now requires: return or deletion of data at termination, protection standard parity with the controller, notice of any change to the processor's security policy, and an incident procedure. Name the documented instruction channel in the same agreement so Pasal 139(2) is satisfied by something you control, and keep executing bilingually because UU 24/2009 Pasal 31 still bites even though the language clause went.
  • Keep the RPP Pasal 135 diligence and audit calendar as internal vendor policy: legality, compliance history, breach record, technical readiness and references checked before onboarding, then periodic and exit audits. Map the processor's reporting obligations to the four items at Pasal 141(2), since those are what the Lembaga will ask a processor to produce.
  • Re paper intra group data flows, which are no longer supervised by default: characterise each as joint control under Pasal 1 angka 20 or as controller to controller, and allocate controller status expressly in every data sharing agreement. Add a counterparty check on any claimed defence or security exemption, asking which body issued the surat keterangan under Pasal 150(d) and which requirements it disapplies, because one body can now sign it and the letter need not say.
Still open

The Peraturan Lembaga promised at Pasal 128, which is meant to carry the supervision detail, the minimum agreement content and the audit cadence, and which does not yet exist even though the underlying duty at Pasal 126(1) keeps wajib and sits in the Pasal 184(1) sanction list.

Every change in this domain
Record of Processing Activity

Register template fixed production duty widened

mixed 6 changes, 4 material
Inside this domain
What a practitioner needs to know

PP 33/2026 Pasal 74(2) fixes thirteen minimum fields for the controller register and Pasal 74(5) a four-field list for the processor, updated under Pasal 74(7) whenever the information changes. RPP Pasal 87(8) put a wajib on the controller alone to hand records to the authority; Pasal 74(9) recasts the duty as harus, extends it to the processor, and the new Pasal 74(10) makes records a standing requirement for audit and supervision.

The minimisation entry changed shape too. RPP Pasal 74(2) asked for processing seminimal mungkin, an open standard with nothing to document against. Enacted Pasal 59(2) replaces it with three named factors: the relationship between the data and the purpose, whether the data is sufficient for the purpose, and whether it exceeds what is needed. The register can now carry an answer per field instead of an assertion.

Why that direction

The register itself is heavier to build and must now be produced by the processor and kept audit-ready, while the entries recorded against several lawful bases became easier to justify.

Do now
  • Rebuild the inventory template against the thirteen fields in Pasal 74(2), add a separate processor sheet carrying the four fields in Pasal 74(5), and set a change trigger so the record updates under Pasal 74(7) rather than at an annual review.
Still open

Whether harus in Pasal 74(9) and (10) carries the same sanction exposure as wajib under UU PDP Pasal 57, which no Peraturan Lembaga has yet settled.

What a practitioner needs to know

Both texts open the same way: a wajib on the controller to record every processing activity, a minimum field list, a shorter list for its processor, and an update whenever the information changes. The list itself grew from twelve fields to thirteen, because Pasal 74(2)(m) adds transfer details to the controller register, and the new Pasal 74(4) states that the processor's own record does not discharge the controller's duty.

Storage loosened. Draft Pasal 87(5) and 87(7) put a wajib on the controller to keep the record in written form; Pasal 74(6) and 74(8) say the record is stored and managed by the controller and/or the processor, with no deontic marker at all. The sharper movement sits at the end. RPP Pasal 87(8) placed a wajib on the controller alone to hand the record over when the authority asked.

Pasal 74(9) recasts that as harus and extends it to the processor, and Pasal 74(10) adds a standing duty to keep the record available for audit and supervision. Whether harus carries the sanction exposure of wajib under UU PDP Pasal 57 is unresolved; the wider reach is the reliable half of the change.

The findings on this slide
Record of Processing Activity

Dasar pemrosesan between draft and enactment

4 changes
What a practitioner needs to know

Three bases got easier to invoke. Draft Pasal 65 barred the public interest basis wherever the processing carried a commercial benefit for the controller; no enacted provision replaces it, so the only remaining filter is whether legislation mandates the action.

Pasal 45(2) opens the legal obligation list with termasuk where the draft closed it, and Pasal 46 cuts the vital interests conditions from three to two and widens the protected class from third parties to any other party. One moved the other way.

Pasal 42(1)(a) requires a pre contract request to be written or recorded, so an oral enquiry no longer triggers the basis unless the controller captures it; the draft's agreement to sign gives way to the easier intention to be bound. Each shift changes what the controller documents: record the instrument grounding a legal obligation, log inbound enquiries at the point of contact, and disclose any commercial upside in the Pasal 50 policy document.

Data Protection Impact Assessment

Assessment stays wajib mitigation does not

weaker 3 changes, 2 material
Inside this domain
What a practitioner needs to know

PP 33/2026 Pasal 120(1) keeps the wajib on running an impact assessment for the seven high risk categories, but Pasal 121(3) and (4) state the implementation of the identified protective measures and the documentation of the assessment in the plain indicative, where RPP Pasal 128(5) and (6) said wajib, and Pasal 121(2)(a) drops secara sistematis from the description of processing.

Prior consultation under Pasal 122(1) is still only dapat, though the draft's cumulative dan at RPP Pasal 129 became dan/atau, so either ground now opens the door and the Lembaga still owes no answer. The legitimate interest balancing analysis required by Pasal 53 is now only documented under Pasal 54 and explained on request under Pasal 56, where RPP Pasal 71 made the controller send it to the subject unprompted.

Why that direction

The controller must still produce the assessment but is no longer compelled by a wajib to act on it, to document it, or to be methodical in describing the processing, and the balancing analysis no longer has to reach the person it concerns.

Do now
  • Add a closure register to the DPIA template: every measure recorded under Pasal 121(2)(d) gets a named owner, a go live date and an internal sign off, and make that sign off a policy gate for the processing to start, since the enacted text no longer supplies one.
Still open

Pasal 122(2) sends the rest of the impact assessment regime to a Peraturan Lembaga, so the required format, any published list of processing that always needs an assessment, and whether the Lembaga responds to a consultation at all are unwritten.

The transfer assessment

The transfer risk assessment lives in Data Transfer and Sharing, where enacted Pasal 163 now binds the controller alone with harus, in place of the draft's wajib on controller dan/atau processor.

Every change in this domain
Data Protection Impact Assessment

Running the assessment stays wajib and acting on it does not

2 changes
What a practitioner needs to know

PP 33/2026 Pasal 120(1) keeps the wajib on running the impact assessment. Pasal 121(3) and (4) then state the implementation of the identified protective measures and the documentation of the assessment in the plain indicative, where RPP Pasal 128(5) and (6) said wajib, and Pasal 121(2)(a) drops secara sistematis from the description of processing. A controller can satisfy the surviving wajib by producing an assessment it never implements.

Consultation with the Lembaga widened by one conjunction. RPP Pasal 129 joined its two grounds with dan; PP Pasal 122(1) joins them with dan/atau, so either ground alone now opens the door. The verb stays dapat, the Lembaga owes no stated answer, and Pasal 122(2) sends the rest of the impact assessment regime to a Peraturan Lembaga. Track mitigations to closure internally and do not plan around consultation.

The findings on this slide
Data Protection Impact Assessment

A balancing test the subject must ask to see

1 change
What a practitioner needs to know

RPP Pasal 71 made the controller document the legitimate interest balancing analysis and hand it to the subject as a matter of course. PP Pasal 54 keeps only the duty to document the Pasal 53 analysis, and Pasal 56 makes disclosure contingent on the subject asking for an explanation.

The burden shifts from a controller who must tell to a subject who must know to ask, which in practice means the assessment is read by regulators and litigants rather than by the people it concerns. Write it for an outside reader; it stays private until the moment it does not.

The findings on this slide
Data Subject Rights and Complaints

Refusal tests go the clocks soften

weaker 17 changes, 9 material
Inside this domain
What a practitioner needs to know

The rights themselves survive but the tests around refusing them are gone. Draft Pasal 83(5) obliged a controller to refuse a correction request on three closed grounds, and enacted Pasal 71(5) gives a bare discretion with only a duty to state reasons at Pasal 71(7). Those three grounds survive at Pasal 77(4) for access to change data alone.

Draft Pasal 107(1) made the controller prove there was no significant impact before refusing an objection and Pasal 95(1) now asserts it as fact, while draft Pasal 70, which stopped legitimate interest processing on objection, has no counterpart, so Pasal 93 leaves objection to solely automated decisions.

Intake runs the other way, with Pasal 20 making a recorded request the route rather than one option, Pasal 22 fixing the moment of receipt, and Pasal 21(3) requiring the answer to come back through the channel the subject used.

Why that direction

Almost every hard edge on rights handling came off, the closed refusal grounds, the controller's burden of proof on objections, the objection stop for legitimate interests and the 3 x 24 hour answer to a compensation claim at draft Pasal 118(5)(d), while the new duties are procedural.

Do now
  • Rewrite the refusal step of the rights procedure: adopt the Pasal 77(4) grounds as the internal test for correction and rectification refusals, require written reasons on every one under Pasal 71(7), and file the accuracy and mitigation evidence behind an objection refusal in the Pasal 120 impact assessment, which is where a supervisor will look for it.
Still open

Portability is the open item: Pasal 113 defers the mechanism to a Peraturan Lembaga and the draft's five eligibility criteria at Pasal 122 are gone, so nothing yet says whether observed and inferred data must be exported or only what the subject supplied.

Every change in this domain
Data Subject Rights and Complaints

Two clocks slow and one disappears

timeline3 changes
Counted in hours
Confirming a request for a copy of the data RPP Pasal 90(2), then PP Pasal 78(2)
Draft

Draft

Enacted
30 Hari, working days

The scale is calendar time. Pasal 1 angka 19 defines Hari as a working day, so the same numeral now runs about six weeks on the calendar instead of one month.

What a practitioner needs to know

None of these three deadlines keeps the meaning it had in the draft. The copy request confirmation reads the same, 3 x 24 jam in both texts, but the draft ran the clock from permohonan diterima and enacted Pasal 78(2) runs it from permohonan diterima dan terverifikasi.

Verification now sits in front of the window, and no article caps how long it may take, so the three days begin whenever the controller is satisfied of identity. The compensation answer went further. Draft Pasal 118(5)(d) required the compensation policy to state that a claim would be answered or refused within 3 x 24 hours.

Enacted Pasal 107 asks only for a mechanism and a policy and sets no deadline, so there is no point at which delay itself becomes a breach, and a subject facing silence is left with the court route under Pasal 108(3). The quietest change is the widest.

The indirect collection notice keeps its numeral, 30 in both texts, but the draft wrote hari and the enacted text writes Hari, which Pasal 1 angka 19 defines as a working day. The same figure now runs about 42 calendar days once weekends and public holidays are counted, and the definition attaches to the capital letter, so it stretches every deadline in the regulation written that way.

The findings on this slide
Data Protection

Fewer hard rules more internal policy

mixed 8 changes, 5 material
Inside this domain
What a practitioner needs to know

Privacy by default kept its content and lost its own article. Draft Pasal 130(3) stated it as a standalone wajib. Enacted Pasal 124(2)(b) folds the same requirement into the technical measures a controller prepares under Pasal 123(1)(a). The position matters because Pasal 123(1), not Pasal 124, is on the sanction list at Pasal 184(1). The security choices also widened. Draft Pasal 131(2)(a) required pseudonymisation and encryption together.

Pasal 123(2)(a) now treats them as alternatives and admits any other technical measure that can prevent or mitigate the risk of a protection failure. Pasal 123(5) drops the wajib from the conformity assessment, so the adequacy of the chosen control rests on the controller's own written reasoning. Retention was reorganised rather than cut.

The definition of Masa Retensi moved to Pasal 1 angka 23, so it now reaches the whole regulation. The policy document sits at Pasal 75, stated in the indicative where the draft used harus, with one new item: huruf j asks for the legal basis of any period that rests on a statutory obligation. Erasure of unlawfully obtained data got easier to trigger.

Draft Pasal 95(2) made the duty wait for a court ruling. Pasal 82(2) now supplies three routes: unlawfulness under the legislation itself, an erasure sanction from the Lembaga, or a final judgment. A controller that concludes its own acquisition was unlawful must erase. Two deletion duties went the other way. Draft Pasal 179 told investigators, prosecutors and judges to erase case data within the statutory period.

Pasal 158(1) instead labels them controllers, so retention runs through the general controller chapter. Draft Pasal 146(3) made destruction of transferred data a wajib. Pasal 133(3)(g) keeps only a statement in the transfer notice that destruction will happen, so enforcement attaches to the notice, not to the holding.

Why that direction

The security design window and the erasure triggers both widen, while the camera siting bans, the mandatory conformity assessment and the standalone destruction duty on transferred data all fall away.

Do now
  • Fold the default minimisation evidence into the Pasal 123 technical and organisational security file, and put the risk evaluation on a dated cycle that starts at the planning stage, which is where Pasal 124(1) now begins and Pasal 124(2)(c) requires it to run consistently.
  • Write the camera policy the regulation stopped supplying: keep an internal prohibition on placement in areas of private expectation, and audit the public facing estate so every deployment maps to a Pasal 17(1)(a) purpose with identification features disabled.
  • Add a legal basis column to the retention schedule for each period that rests on a statutory obligation, per the new Pasal 75 huruf j, diary the destruction of transferred data against the representation made in the Pasal 133(3)(g) notice, and put retention questions to law enforcement holders under Pasal 158(1), which now designates them as controllers.
Still open

Nothing yet fixes the standard a technical measure must meet under Pasal 123(2)(a) once the conformity assessment at Pasal 123(5) is optional, and the Lembaga has issued no rule on that or on how it will impose the erasure sanction at Pasal 82(2)(b).

Pengendali Data Pribadi dan/atau Prosesor Data Pribadi harus menempatkan alat pemroses atau pengolah data visual di area publik atau tempat umum serta memastikan perekaman dilakukan secara konsisten dan memastikan Pelindungan Data Pribadi.

PP Pasal 17

  1. a.
    untuk tujuan keamanan, pencegahan bencana, dan/atau penyelenggaraan lalu lintas atau pengumpulan, analisis, dan pengaturan Informasi lalu lintas;
  2. b.
    harus menampilkan Informasi pada area yang telah dipasang alat pemroses atau pengolah data visual; dan

(2)
Ketentuan sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1) huruf b dan huruf c dikecualikan untuk pencegahan tindak pidana dan proses penegakan hukum sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang undangan.
(3)

(4)

PP Pasal 18
(1)

(2)
Pengendali Data Pribadi dan/atau Prosesor Data Pribadi hanya dapat menempatkan dan menggunakan alat pemroses atau pengolah data visual sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1) untuk memantau area yang dituju sesuai dengan tujuan pemantauan.
What a practitioner needs to know

The draft set two hard limits on siting. Pasal 34(4) banned placement in areas where a person has an expectation of privacy, and Pasal 34(3) required the operator to prevent or minimise recording beyond the monitoring purpose. Both are gone, and the word ekspektasi appears nowhere in the enacted text. What survives at Pasal 18(2) limits where the device points, not where it sits.

Public places got two controls the draft never had. Pasal 17(1) closes the permitted purposes to security, disaster prevention and traffic management, and forbids using the device to identify a person. The signage duty is older, carried over from draft Pasal 35 into Pasal 19. Pasal 17(2) exempts crime prevention and law enforcement from signage and the identification ban but leaves the purpose limit standing.

Facial recognition run commercially in a public place therefore has no permitted purpose. Keep an internal ban on cameras in private areas, and map every public deployment to a Pasal 17(1)(a) purpose with identification features off.

The findings on this slide
Breach Management

More incidents notifiable with thinner notices

mixed 5 changes, 3 material
Inside this domain
What a practitioner needs to know

PP 33/2026 Pasal 114 keeps the 3 x 24 jam clock to both the subject and the Lembaga and carries no exception, so the draft off-ramp at RPP Pasal 124(5) for failures that disclosed nothing is gone and encryption-only ransomware, accidental destruction and a botched migration are all now notifiable.

The notice itself got shorter: Pasal 114(3)(c) keeps handling and recovery but deletes dampak, which the draft required, and impact now survives only in the internal documentation at Pasal 116(1)(c) that goes to the authority rather than to the person.

Pasal 115(1) limits public notice to disruption of public service and serious harm to the public interest and drops the RPP Pasal 124(4)(c) trigger for subjects the controller cannot reach, while Pasal 116 and Pasal 117 both lost wajib and Pasal 116 is absent from the sanction list at Pasal 184(1).

Why that direction

The set of incidents that must be reported got wider under Pasal 114, while the mandatory content of the notice, the public notice trigger and the documentation duty all got thinner.

Do now
  • Rewrite the breach triage rule so that any Kegagalan Pelindungan Data Pribadi as defined in Pasal 1 starts the 3 x 24 jam clock, not only incidents involving disclosure, and re-test last year's incident log against the new threshold to see how many would now have been reportable.
Still open

The Lembaga has issued no rule on the notification channel or form, and nothing fixes when the 3 x 24 jam clock starts: Pasal 114(1) counts from the failure rather than from the controller becoming aware of it, so a team that spends two days confirming an incident cannot tell from the text whether it is early or already late.

Breach Management

The breach regime compared

comparative table5 changes
AspectDraft · 31 August 2023 Enacted · PP 33/2026
Notification trigger and its exceptionAny protection failure, but exempt where the failure disclosed no personal data (Pasal 124(5))Any Kegagalan Pelindungan Data Pribadi; Pasal 114 carries no exception clause
The clockWritten notice within 3 x 24 jam of the failure being known with certainty (Pasal 124(1) and (2))Unchanged: 3 x 24 jam from the same starting point (Pasal 114(1) and (2))
Who is notifiedThe subject and the Lembaga PDP, both in writing (Pasal 124(1))Unchanged: the subject and the Lembaga, both in writing (Pasal 114(1))
Notice contentData exposed, when and how, impact plus handling and recovery, contact point (Pasal 124(3))Impact deleted; data exposed, when and how, handling and recovery, PPDP or contact point (Pasal 114(3) and (4))
Public notice triggerPublic service disruption, serious public interest impact, or subjects the controller cannot reach (Pasal 124(4))First two triggers kept; the unreachable subjects trigger is deleted (Pasal 115(1))
Breach prevention policyWajib to adopt and implement a prevention and handling policy (Pasal 126)Wajib dropped; policy scoped to the controller's own organisation; four minimum contents kept (Pasal 117)

What a practitioner needs to know

The clock and the recipients did not move: written notice within 3 x 24 jam to the subject and the Lembaga, in draft and enacted alike. Everything around them did. The draft's exemption for failures that disclosed nothing is gone, so more incidents notify. The notice lost its impact statement, the public notice lost its unreachable subjects trigger, and the prevention policy and documentation duties both lost wajib.

The findings on this slide
Data Transfer and Sharing

Transfer gates move onto the controller

mixed 19 changes, 13 material
What a practitioner needs to know

The Pasal 165 cascade survives, but the checks that used to sit elsewhere now sit with you: Pasal 163 puts the transfer risk assessment on the controller alone and drops the draft delegation at RPP Pasal 194(2), and Pasal 165(1) measures equivalence against UU 27/2022 rather than the whole body of PDP legislation.

On domestic sharing the draft's gates are gone, with no counterpart to the attachment rule at RPP Pasal 177(4), the requester-identity limb at RPP Pasal 173(d) and Pasal 175(d), or the camera-footage gateway at RPP Article 36, so Pasal 155, Pasal 151 to Pasal 153 and Pasal 30(3) leave the testing to you.

Two transfer routes closed as well: the inter-state agreement at RPP Pasal 186 is now a public-body instrument at Pasal 169(1)(a), and the foreign court order clause at RPP Pasal 191 has no replacement, while the new Pasal 166 sends outbound law enforcement exchange through the cascade.

Why that direction

Several transfer duties dropped from wajib to harus and the clause-tailoring test at Pasal 170(3) loosened, but the controller now carries the risk assessment alone, evidences equivalence without a list, and verifies every disclosure demand on its own judgment.

Do now
  • Rewrite the processing agreement so the processor must supply the inputs for the Pasal 163 assessment, and write the Pasal 165 cascade into the onward-transfer clause by contract, because Pasal 160(4) states the duty and specifies nothing the onward recipient must satisfy.
Still open

The Lembaga has issued neither the adequacy list it must now establish under Pasal 168(2) nor the assessment method deferred by Pasal 168(4), so every equivalence call stays yours to evidence, with the consent-route detail also deferred to a Peraturan Lembaga under Pasal 174.

Every change in this domain
The regime

Later start longer clocks wider discretion

mixed 16 changes, 10 material
What a practitioner needs to know

PP 33/2026 was promulgated on 16 July 2026 and binds on 16 January 2027 under Pasal 225, where draft Pasal 245 would have applied on promulgation, and the new Pasal 223 makes the enacted text itself the interim standard for processing until the Peraturan Lembaga on processing is issued, with Pasal 224 saving existing personal data rules that do not conflict with it.

Pasal 1(19) defines Hari as a working day and the defined term is used throughout, so a sanctioned party now has 30 working days at Pasal 195(5) where draft Pasal 220 gave seven calendar days, objections run 14 working days at Pasal 197 and mediation 30 at Pasal 218.

The 2 per cent ceiling holds at Pasal 185(1), but Pasal 185(2)(i) prices your compliance record into the calculation and Pasal 185(3) allows a fine of zero, while draft Pasal 119(2), Pasal 120, Pasal 211 and Pasal 222 are gone, so a refused compensation claim goes to court under Pasal 108(3), the authority cannot sue for subject compensation, and ignoring a decision draws a fresh proceeding under Pasal 188 rather than an accruing penalty.

Why that direction

The controller gets a six month runway, working day clocks and no arrears penalty, but also a supervision order that carries a fixed period, an action plan and progress reports under Pasal 181, a fine calculation that now reads its compliance file, and a specific data category any sectoral ministry can extend under Pasal 6(2) with the draft criteria deleted.

Do now
  • Rebuild the programme calendar on working days against the Indonesian public holiday list, covering the Pasal 197 objection window at 14, the Pasal 195(5) sanction compliance window at 30 and the Pasal 211(2) first mediation meeting at 10, and reset any internal service level that was set against calendar days.
  • Assemble the compliance evidence pack that Pasal 185(2)(i) now values, meaning dated board approvals, training and awareness records, DPIA sign offs and remediation logs held in a form you can hand over on the day an order is served, together with a standing argument on the Pasal 181(5) complexity ground.
  • Back plan from 16 January 2027 by mapping current processing against the enacted articles under Pasal 223 instead of waiting for the delegated rules, and add sectoral regulators to the watch list alongside the Lembaga because Pasal 6(2) lets them extend the specific personal data category.
Still open

The Peraturan Lembaga are all still outstanding, and four of them decide how this domain actually bites: the residual fine variable at Pasal 185(2)(j), the pertimbangan tertentu behind a zero fine at Pasal 185(3), mediator competence at Pasal 222 and mediation fees at Pasal 210. Nothing yet defines the conflict test that Pasal 223 and Pasal 224 both turn on.

  5. e.

  7. g.

(5)

(6)
Pengendali Data Pribadi lama menyiapkan syarat dan ketentuan pengaksesan Data Pribadi oleh pihak lain yang terlibat dalam penggabungan, pemisahan, pengambilalihan, peleburan, atau pembubaran badan hukum.
What changed

RPP Pasal 152 defined the pihak lain in a transaction, required it to accept the controller's access terms before receiving any access, fixed a minimum content for those terms, and prohibited access where they were not accepted. PP 33/2026 keeps only the preparation of the terms, at Pasal 133(6).

Analysis

The draft gated adviser and data-room access; the enacted text merely asks for terms to exist. RPP Pasal 152(3) to (5) made acceptance a condition precedent and fixed access duration and return or deletion as minimum content, whereas PP 33/2026 Pasal 133(6) requires only that the old controller prepare access terms for the parties involved.

Nothing in the enacted text prohibits access by a party that has not accepted them, and the deemed-processor rule at RPP Pasal 152(2) disappears with it. Diligence platforms and advisers now sit under the general appointment rules in Pasal 13 to Pasal 15 or under nothing at all.

What to do about it

Make acceptance of access terms a contractual condition of data-room entry.

Against Indonesia. The GDPR reaches the notification limb through two general duties rather than a dedicated one.

(1)

What changed

RPP Pasal 146(3) imposed a free standing obligation on the old controller to destroy personal data it had transferred to the new controller. PP 33/2026 keeps that content only inside Pasal 133(3)(g), as a statement the old controller must include in its transfer notification to subjects.

Analysis

The draft made destruction an obligation; the enacted text makes it a disclosure. RPP Pasal 146(3) used wajib and stood alone, whereas the surviving text at PP 33/2026 Pasal 133(3)(g) requires only that the notification contain a pernyataan that the old controller will destroy the transferred data when the transaction ends.

Enforcement therefore attaches to the notification rather than to the retention, since Pasal 133 ayat (1) is listed for administrative sanction at Pasal 184(1) while the promise itself founds no separate duty. Holding by the old controller after closing falls back on the general triggers in Pasal 84(1), which run off the retention period, a subject request or unlawful processing, none of which is keyed to the transfer.

What to do about it

Treat the notice statement as a binding representation and schedule the destruction against it.

Cross-border transfer

Equivalence is now measured against the UU alone

narrowedchanges an obligation

(2)
Dalam hal ketentuan sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1) tidak terpenuhi, Pengendali Data Pribadi wajib memastikan terdapat Pelindungan Data Pribadi yang memadai dan bersifat mengikat.
(3)

Enacted · PP 33/2026
PP Pasal 165
PP Pasal 165
(1)
Dalam melakukan transfer Data Pribadi sebagaimana dimaksud dalam Pasal 160, Pengendali Data Pribadi wajib memastikan negara tempat kedudukan Pengendali Data Pribadi dan/atau Prosesor Data Pribadi yang menerima transfer Data Pribadi memiliki tingkat Pelindungan Data Pribadi yang setara atau lebih tinggi dari yang diatur dalam Undang-Undang mengenai Pelindungan Data Pribadi.
(2)
Dalam hal ketentuan sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1) tidak terpenuhi, Pengendali Data Pribadi wajib memastikan terdapat Pelindungan Data Pribadi yang memadai dan bersifat mengikat.
(3)

(4)
Lembaga berwenang melakukan penilaian pemenuhan persyaratan transfer Data Pribadi sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1), ayat (2), dan ayat (3).
What changed

The draft measured the recipient country's protection against the peraturan perundang-undangan di bidang Pelindungan Data Pribadi, meaning the whole body of PDP legislation and implementing rules. Pasal 165(1) measures it against the Undang-Undang mengenai Pelindungan Data Pribadi alone. The three-step order of equivalence, adequate binding protection and consent is otherwise preserved intact.

Analysis

Narrowing the comparator to UU 27/2022 excludes PP 33/2026 itself and every Peraturan Lembaga still to come, so a destination can be adequate while offering nothing that matches the enacted regulation's own operational duties. The same instrument keeps the wider comparator for binding corporate rules in Pasal 171(1)(a), where the recipient must match the peraturan perundang-undangan di bidang Pelindungan Data Pribadi, so two routes to the same destination are benchmarked differently.

That asymmetry rewards the adequacy route and penalises the group-internal one, which is the opposite of the incentive a controller-led safeguard regime needs.

What to do about it

Benchmark adequacy analyses to UU 27/2022 and reserve the wider corpus benchmark for binding corporate rules drafting.

2/2018 02/2024 C-311/18 C-362/14
04
Cross-border transfer

Foreign court orders lost their treaty precondition

deletedchanges an obligation
Draft · 31 August 2023
RPP Pasal 191
RPP Pasal 191

Transfer Data Pribadi yang diperintahkan oleh putusan pengadilan, tribunal, atau putusan otoritas administrasi negara ketiga, hanya diakui dan dapat dilaksanakan apabila terdapat perjanjian internasional yang mendasarinya dengan negara yang meminta transfer Data Pribadi.

Enacted · PP 33/2026
no counterpart

The enacted text carries nothing in its place.

What changed

The draft recognised a transfer ordered by a third-country court, tribunal or administrative authority only where an international agreement underpinned it. The enacted text has no such provision; the words tribunal and otoritas administrasi appear nowhere in it.

Analysis

This was the draft's analogue of GDPR Article 48, which stops a foreign judgment or administrative order operating on its own as a ground for export. Its deletion removes the one clause in the draft that spoke to compelled disclosure to a foreign authority, and it is the exposure that an adequacy assessment is least able to price. Pasal 160 to 174 contain no replacement.

The nearest provision, Pasal 166, routes law enforcement exchange out of Indonesia back to the same transfer rules and says nothing about an order arriving from abroad.

What to do about it

A foreign order is no longer addressed by the transfer chapter. Handle it in contract, because the regulation now says nothing.

Where Europe stands

This finding cites no article of the enacted text, so there is no implementing provision to carry a comparison. The subject is treated in the reading pages.

PP Pasal 172

Ketentuan lebih lanjut mengenai pelaksanaan Pelindungan Data Pribadi yang memadai dan bersifat mengikat diatur dalam Peraturan Lembaga.

What changed

Draft Pasal 185(2)(a) put an agreement between the transferor's and the recipient's home states first among the forms of adequate and binding protection, and Pasal 186 gave that route a dedicated article with its own delegation to the Lembaga PDP. Enacted Pasal 169(1)(a) substitutes a legally binding and enforceable instrument for agencies or authorities acting on statutory powers, and Pasal 186 has no counterpart.

Analysis

The draft's first limb was a state-to-state treaty that no private controller could procure. PP 33/2026 Pasal 169(1)(a) replaces it with an instrument binding and enforceable on agencies or authorities acting on statutory powers, which is the construction GDPR Article 46(2)(a) uses for public bodies.

The first safeguard therefore moves out of treaty practice and into administrative practice, and private controllers are left with the three limbs at Pasal 169(1)(b) to (d) rather than four. Draft Pasal 186, which gave the treaty route its own article and its own delegation to the Lembaga PDP, has no counterpart, so the content of the new limb now rests on the general delegation at Pasal 172 and is not fixed in the regulation itself.

What to do about it

Private controllers should plan on standard contractual clauses or binding corporate rules; the first limb is now a public-sector route.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Articles 44, 45, 46, 48, 49

The provision. Chapter V builds a three-step cascade.

Against Indonesia. The three rungs sit in Chapter V's order, ayat (2) against Article 45, ayat (3) against Article 46 and ayat (4) against Article 49(1)(a), but only the first two rungs do the same work.

What changed

The draft named an inter-state agreement as its own form of adequate binding protection. That phrase appears nowhere in the enacted text, which uses a general legally binding and enforceable instrument instead.

Analysis

Perjanjian antarnegara was a distinct safeguard route in RPP Pasal 185(2)(a) and was elaborated at Pasal 186. PP Pasal 169(1)(a) replaces it with an instrument that is legally binding and enforceable for agencies or authorities, so the treaty case survives only where the instrument binds a public body, and a private controller is left with the standard contractual clauses at Pasal 169(1)(b) or the binding corporate rules at Pasal 169(1)(c).

The international agreement does not disappear from the chapter, but it is demoted: under Pasal 168(1)(c) it now appears as one of three criteria feeding the adequacy assessment rather than as a basis for transfer in its own right.

What to do about it

A bilateral arrangement no longer has a named slot for a private controller. It survives only where the instrument binds a public body, and otherwise counts as evidence of adequacy rather than a substitute for it.

(2)

  1. a.

  2. b.
    pemberian akses Data Pribadi Pengendali Data Pribadi lama kepada Pengendali Data Pribadi baru diberikan sepanjang transaksi berlangsung;
  3. c.
    penggunaan akses terhadap Data Pribadi tersebut kepada Pengendali Data Pribadi baru hanya untuk keperluan penentuan apakah akan melanjutkan transaksi ini atau tidak;
  4. d.

(4)
Perjanjian sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1) tetap wajib tun duk pada ketentuan perjanjian yang harus disusun dan dilakukan oleh Pengendali Data Pribadi Bersama sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan.
Enacted · PP 33/2026
PP Pasal 134
PP Pasal 134
(1)
Pengalihan Data Pribadi dalam penggabungan, pemisahan, pengambilalihan, atau peleburan badan hukum, Pengendali Data Pribadi lama dan Pengendali Data Pribadi baru harus membuat perjanjian mengenai Pelindungan Data Pribadi.
(2)
Perjanjian sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1) paling sedikit memuat:
  1. a.
    dasar pemrosesan Data Pribadi masing-masing Pengendali Data Pribadi;
  2. b.
    pemenuhan prinsip Pelindungan Data Pribadi;
  3. c.
    pemenuhan hak Subjek Data Pribadi; dan
  4. d.
    pembagian kewajiban dan tanggung jawab Pengendali Data Pribadi lama, Pengendali Data Pribadi baru, dan pihak yang terlibat dalam pemrosesan Data Pribadi.
(3)
Perjanjian sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1) dapat menjadi bagian dari perjanjian yang melandasi terjadinya penggabungan, pemisahan, pengambilalihan, atau peleburan badan hukum.
(4)
Perjanjian sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1) tetap wajib tunduk pada ketentuan perjanjian yang harus disusun dan dilakukan oleh Pengendali Data Pribadi Bersama sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan.
What changed

RPP Pasal 144 ayat (2) put the deal mechanics in the agreement itself. Huruf b limited the new controller's access to the duration of the transaction, huruf c limited the use of that access to the decision whether to proceed, huruf d bound the new controller to destroy or return everything if the transaction failed, and huruf e bound the old controller to destroy what it had transferred.

PP 33/2026 Pasal 134 ayat (2) carries none of the four. Only huruf a survives, as PP Pasal 134 ayat (2) huruf d. The old controller's destruction undertaking reappears outside the agreement, at PP Pasal 133 ayat (3) huruf g, as mandatory content of its notification to data subjects.

Analysis

The old controller's destruction undertaking changed instrument and changed form. RPP Pasal 144 ayat (2) huruf e made it a required term of the agreement between the old and the new controller. PP Pasal 133 ayat (3) huruf g makes it a pernyataan in the old controller's notification to the data subject, and fixes the stated moment of destruction at the close of the penggabungan, pemisahan, pengambilalihan, peleburan or pembubaran badan hukum.

The undertaking is now addressed to the subject rather than to the counterparty, and the agreement under PP Pasal 134 ayat (2) needs only each controller's processing basis, the principles, the rights of the subject and the division of responsibility between the old controller, the new controller and the other parties involved.

Huruf b, huruf c and huruf d of RPP Pasal 144 ayat (2) do not reappear in PP Pasal 133 or PP Pasal 134. PP Pasal 133 ayat (6) leaves the old controller to set the terms of access for the other parties involved, and imposes no purpose limit and no duration limit of its own.

Nothing says what happens to the data if the transaction collapses, so an agreement can satisfy PP Pasal 134 in full and leave the failed deal unaddressed.

What to do about it

Time the destruction to the close of the corporate action, which is what PP Pasal 133 ayat (3) huruf g makes the old controller state to subjects. Keep the access duration limit, the purpose limit and the failed transaction return in the deal documents, because PP Pasal 134 no longer supplies them.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Articles 6, 14

The provision. The GDPR has no article on mergers, demergers, acquisitions, consolidations or dissolution.

Against Indonesia. The GDPR reaches the notification limb through two general duties rather than a dedicated one.

(2)

  1. a.

What changed

Draft Pasal 195(1) required the Pengendali Data Pribadi dan/atau Prosesor Data Pribadi to inform the subject before the transfer, using wajib. Enacted Pasal 164 requires only the Pengendali Data Pribadi, using harus. The four minimum contents and the deferral for vital interests survive unchanged.

Analysis

The information package is preserved in full, including the fourth item, disclosure of the transfer risks and the mitigation the controller has adopted, which is the most demanding of the four and the one that presupposes a completed Pasal 163 assessment. What moved is who owes it: a processor transferring under instruction has no independent notice duty, so the subject's only route to the information runs through the controller.

The vital interests deferral remains the single exception and postpones rather than removes the notice.

What to do about it

Build the four-item transfer notice into the controller's privacy notice and treat processor notice as a contractual pass-through.

What changed

The draft said the authority may publish a list of adequate countries. The enacted text says it must.

Analysis

A discretion became a duty. Under RPP Pasal 184(2) the adequacy list was something the authority could produce if it chose; PP Pasal 168(2) obliges the Lembaga to establish it.

The assessment itself was never the controller's task in either instrument, since RPP Pasal 183(2) and PP Pasal 167 both reserve the penilaian to the authority, so what the list changes is the controller's position under the standing wajib in PP Pasal 165(1) to ensure the receiving country offers equivalent protection.

PP Pasal 168(3) lets a controller transfer to a listed country subject only to compliance with prevailing law, while Pasal 168(4) leaves the method of assessment to a Peraturan Lembaga. Both the list and the method wait on the same body, and until either arrives the controller satisfies Pasal 165(1) on its own evidence or falls back to the binding safeguards in Pasal 165(2) or consent in Pasal 165(3).

What to do about it

Watch for the first published adequacy list. Until it appears you must evidence equivalence under Pasal 165(1) yourself, or fall back to Pasal 165(2) or (3).

    menerapkan langkah -langkah prosedural yang dapat ditempuh jika akan menggunakan instrumen pelengkap; dan
  7. g.
    mengevaluasi ulang secara berkala dalam kurun waktu yang memadai.
(2)
Ketentuan mengenai pelaksanaan transfer Data Pribadi sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1) diatur lebih lanjut dalam Peraturan Lembaga PDP.
Enacted · PP 33/2026
PP Pasal 161
PP Pasal 161

Dalam melaksanakan transfer Data Pribadi sebagaimana dimaksud dalam Pasal 160, Pengendali Data Pribadi dan/atau Prosesor Data Pribadi harus:

  1. a.
    melakukan perekaman dan pemetaan siklus transfer Data Pribadi dan implikasinya;
  2. b.
    memastikan bahwa Data Pribadi yang ditransfer cukup, relevan, dan terbatas sesuai dengan tujuan transfer Data Pribadi;
  3. c.
    mengidentifikasi instrumen hukum yang digunakan sebagai rujukan untuk proses transfer Data Pribadi sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan;
  4. d.
    melakukan penilaian efektivitas instrumen hukum yang digunakan untuk proses transfer Data Pribadi yang akan dilakukan sebelum melakukan transfer Data Pribadi;
  5. e.
    menggunakan instrumen pelengkap apabila dibutuhkan, baik berupa instrumen kontraktual, teknis, dan/atau organisasional;
  6. f.
    menerapkan langkah prosedural yang dapat ditempuh jika akan menggunakan instrumen pelengkap; dan
  7. g.
    mengevaluasi ulang secara berkala dalam kurun waktu yang memadai.
What changed

Draft Pasal 192(1) imposed the seven execution duties, opening with recording and mapping the transfer cycle, using wajib. Enacted Pasal 161 imposes the same seven using harus, and moves them ahead of the consent provisions into Bagian Kesatu of BAB V, immediately after the general transfer article at Pasal 160.

Analysis

The list survives item for item, but wajib is the verb Indonesian drafting reserves for a sanctioned obligation and harus for a normative requirement, and Pasal 184(1) confirms the distinction by naming only Pasal 160(2) and Pasal 165(1) to (3) as administratively sanctionable in the transfer chapter.

Draft Pasal 213(1) drew that same perimeter through draft Pasal 181(2) and Pasal 182(1) to (3), so the exposure is unchanged in substance; what changed is the label, and with it the argument that these are enforceable obligations in their own right.

The relocation is the compensating gain, since Pasal 161 now cross-refers to Pasal 160 and sits in Bagian Kesatu ahead of the three tier rule at Pasal 165, where draft Pasal 192 trailed the consent provisions at draft Pasal 189 and Pasal 190.

What to do about it

Keep the transfer cycle map, but expect the Lembaga to reach it through Pasal 165 compliance rather than by sanctioning Pasal 161 directly.

PP Pasal 163
PP Pasal 163

Pengendali Data Pribadi harus melakukan penilaian atas kebutuhan transfer Data Pribadi dan dampak transfer Data Pribadi terhadap hak Subjek Data Pribadi melalui penilaian atas risiko transfer Data Pribadi.

What changed

Draft Pasal 194(1) placed the transfer necessity and impact assessment on the Pengendali Data Pribadi dan/atau Prosesor Data Pribadi with the verb wajib. Enacted Pasal 163 places it on the Pengendali Data Pribadi alone with the verb harus, and drops the draft's ayat (2) delegation.

Analysis

Removing the processor concentrates the assessment burden on the controller, including for transfers a processor initiates under instruction, and leaves onward transfers governed only by the single sentence in Pasal 160(4), which asks both roles to comply with the prevailing legislation.

Dropping the draft's delegation at Pasal 194(2) also removes the promised Peraturan Lembaga on how the risk assessment is to be run, so its content is left to the controller. Read against Pasal 161, which still binds Pengendali dan/atau Prosesor to record and map the transfer cycle, the enacted chapter splits the assessment duties between controller and processor without saying how the two interlock.

What to do about it

Controllers cannot delegate the transfer risk assessment to a processor; write the input obligation into the processing contract instead.

Analysis

The test moves from positive conformity with the whole body of PDP legislation to mere non-contradiction with UU 27/2022, mirroring the change of comparator in Pasal 165(1) and loosening the constraint in the same direction. Enacted · PP 33/2026
PP Pasal 171
PP Pasal 171
(1)
Peraturan korporasi yang mengikat suatu grup korporasi sebagaimana dimaksud dalam Pasal 169 ayat (1) huruf c paling sedikit memuat:
  1. a.
    kewajiban Pengendali Data Pribadi dan/atau Prosesor Data Pribadi yang menerima transfer Data Pribadi untuk memberikan Pelindungan Data Pribadi yang setara atau lebih tinggi dari yang diatur dalam peraturan perundang-undangan di bidang Pelindungan Data Pribadi;
  2. b.

  3. c.

  4. d.

(2)
Peraturan korporasi yang mengikat hanya dapat digunakan oleh:
  1. a.
    Pengendali Data Pribadi penerima mengendalikan atau dikendalikan Pengendali Data Pribadi pengirim; dan
  2. b.
    Pengendali Data Pribadi penerima dan Pengendali Data Pribadi pengirim berada di bawah kendali pihak yang sama.
(3)

What changed

RPP Pasal 188 ayat (1) said the rules wajib memuat persyaratan paling sedikit the four listed items. PP Pasal 171 ayat (1) says they paling sedikit memuat those items, dropping wajib and dropping persyaratan, and renames peraturan perusahaan as peraturan korporasi. The chapeau re-anchors the rules, from RPP Pasal 185 ayat (2) huruf c to PP Pasal 169 ayat (1) huruf c.

The draft delegation at RPP Pasal 188 ayat (4) has no counterpart in the enacted article, which ends at ayat (3).

Analysis

The four minimum contents are identical: an undertaking by the recipient to give equal or higher protection, the parties bound, the destination countries and territories, and the division of roles, rights and obligations. What changed is the deontic framing.

Dropping wajib removes the ground for treating an incomplete set of rules as a breach in its own right, and leaves ayat (1) reading as a description of what such rules contain. The same drop runs through ayat (3). RPP Pasal 188 ayat (3) said the Pengendali Data Pribadi wajib mendapatkan persetujuan dari Lembaga PDP before transferring.

PP Pasal 171 ayat (3) states only that use of the rules follows setelah mendapatkan persetujuan dari Lembaga, with no verb of obligation. Item (a) keeps its comparator, peraturan perundang-undangan di bidang Pelindungan Data Pribadi, word for word from the draft. The delegation does not survive on the face of the article.

RPP Pasal 188 ayat (4) sent the detail of binding corporate rules to a Peraturan Lembaga PDP, and PP Pasal 171 stops at ayat (3). The nearest enacted delegation, PP Pasal 172, runs to pelaksanaan Pelindungan Data Pribadi yang memadai dan bersifat mengikat, a route rather than an instrument. Whether it reaches binding corporate rules turns on PP Pasal 169 ayat (1), the provision the enacted chapeau now points to and the one this finding does not carry.

What to do about it

Draft binding corporate rules to the four contents in PP Pasal 171 ayat (1), and to the comparator in huruf a, peraturan perundang-undangan di bidang Pelindungan Data Pribadi. Do not read the enacted article as delegating the operating detail. PP Pasal 171 ends at ayat (3), and PP Pasal 172 delegates the route, not the instrument.

PP Pasal 174

Ketentuan lebih lanjut mengenai pelaksanaan persetujuan untuk transfer Data Pribadi ke luar wilayah hukum Negara Republik Indonesia diatur dalam Peraturan Lembaga.

What changed

RPP Pasal 190 ayat (1) said that on a consent-based transfer the controller wajib melaksanakan kewajiban sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan. PP Pasal 173 ayat (1) says the controller tetap melaksanakan those obligations, and it attaches the duty to dalam mendapatkan persetujuan rather than to the transfer itself, with the cross-reference now running to PP Pasal 165 ayat (3) where the draft pointed to RPP Pasal 189.

The draft delegation at RPP Pasal 190 ayat (3) reappears as a standalone article at PP Pasal 174, rewritten to name pelaksanaan persetujuan untuk transfer Data Pribadi ke luar wilayah hukum Negara Republik Indonesia.

Analysis

Tetap melaksanakan is descriptive where wajib melaksanakan was prescriptive, so the clause records that the other duties continue rather than imposing them afresh. That holds because the kewajiban arise sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan and bind independently of this article.

The five cumulative conditions in PP Pasal 173 ayat (2) carry over in substance: a non-repetitive transfer, a limited number of subjects, necessity that does not override the subject's interests, a completed risk assessment with protective measures, and notification of both the Lembaga and the subject. The wording was tidied rather than reopened, with Data Pribadi spelled out through each huruf and Lembaga PDP renamed Lembaga.

The delegation survives the move as well. RPP Pasal 190 ayat (3) sent the consent route to a Peraturan Lembaga PDP, and PP Pasal 174 defers pelaksanaan persetujuan untuk transfer Data Pribadi ke luar wilayah hukum Negara Republik Indonesia to a Peraturan Lembaga, so the operating detail of the narrowest limb is deferred rather than settled in the PP. Consent remains the narrowest of the three limbs rather than the general fallback controllers tend to treat it as.

What to do about it

Do not treat consent as a workaround. The five conditions in PP Pasal 173 ayat (2) rule out routine or bulk transfers, and the operating detail is deferred to a Peraturan Lembaga under PP Pasal 174.

PP Pasal 160
PP Pasal 160
(1)
Pengendali Data Pribadi dapat melakukan transfer Data Pribadi kepada Pengendali Data Pribadi dan/atau Prosesor Data Pribadi di luar wilayah hukum Negara Republik Indonesia sesuai dengan Undang-Undang mengenai Pelindungan Data Pribadi.
(2)
Dalam melakukan transfer Data Pribadi sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1) Pengendali Data Pribadi yang melakukan transfer Data Pribadi dan yang menerima transfer Data Pribadi wajib melakukan Pelindungan Data Pribadi sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan di bidang Pelindungan Data Pribadi.
(3)

  1. a.
    dilakukan oleh Pengendali Data Pribadi sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan;
  2. b.
    Pengendali Data Pribadi membuat Data Pribadi tersedia untuk Pengendali Data Pribadi dan/atau Prosesor Data Pribadi yang menerima Data Pribadi; dan
  3. c.

What changed

Draft Pasal 181(4) said that on an onward transfer the controller or processor wajib tunduk to the applicable legislation. Enacted Pasal 160(4) says harus tunduk. Pasal 160(1) also narrows the authorising reference from peraturan perundang-undangan to the Undang-Undang mengenai Pelindungan Data Pribadi.

Analysis

Onward transfer is the point at which Indonesian control over the data is weakest, and both texts dispose of it in a single sentence. Both verbs are imperative, so the duty itself survives; what falls away is the stronger label, and the sanction position is unchanged, since Pasal 184(1) reaches Pasal 160 ayat (2) only and RPP Pasal 213(1) reached Pasal 181 ayat (2) only.

A defective onward transfer must therefore be reached through the transferring controller's own protection duty rather than directly. Neither text specifies what the onward recipient must satisfy, leaving the Pasal 165 cascade to be applied by analogy or by contract.

What to do about it

Contract for the cascade to apply to onward transfers expressly; the regulation does not do it for you.

Sanctions and enforcement

Authority loses standing to sue for damages in the public interest

deletedchanges an obligation
Draft · 31 August 2023
RPP Pasal 211
RPP Pasal 211
(1)
Lembaga PDP berwenang mengajukan gugatan atas nama kepentingan umum untuk memperoleh ganti kerugian akibat pelanggaran peraturan perundang - undangan di bidang Pelindungan Data Pribadi.

no counterpart

The enacted text carries nothing in its place.

What changed

Draft Pasal 211(1) gave the authority standing to bring a claim in the name of the public interest for compensation, with Pasal 212 allowing it to ask the prosecution service to conduct that claim. Neither provision has a counterpart in the enacted text.

Analysis

The draft built a public enforcer for collective redress and gave it prosecutorial support; the enacted text keeps prosecution assistance only for enforcing a sanction decision under Pasal 198 and for dispute resolution under Pasal 221. Compensation for a mass breach therefore has no public claimant.

A data subject is left with an individual civil claim under Pasal 108(3) or mediation under Bab X, which ends in a Kesepakatan Perdamaian binding on the parties under Pasal 220(4) and enforceable against a defaulting party only if they take it back to court for an akta perdamaian under Pasal 220(5).

The regulatory response to a large breach is now confined to an administrative fine capped at 2 per cent of annual revenue under Pasal 185(1), which Pasal 185(4) routes through the non-tax state revenue rules rather than to the affected subjects. Collective redress is left unbuilt on the regulatory side of the instrument.

What to do about it

Advise on breach exposure on the basis that the authority cannot sue for subject compensation, and model civil claims separately.

Where Europe stands

This finding cites no article of the enacted text, so there is no implementing provision to carry a comparison. The subject is treated in the reading pages.

Sanctions and enforcement

Cross-border law enforcement exchange now runs the transfer cascade

newchanges an obligation
Draft · 31 August 2023
no counterpart

The draft had no such provision.

Enacted · PP 33/2026
PP Pasal 166
PP Pasal 166

Dalam hal pertukaran Data Pribadi antar penegak hukum dilaksanakan ke luar wilayah hukum Negara Republik Indonesia, pertukaran Data Pribadi dilaksanakan sesuai dengan ketentuan transfer Data Pribadi dalam Peraturan Pemerintah ini.

What changed

PP 33/2026 adds Pasal 166, subjecting the exchange of personal data between law enforcement agencies to the transfer rules of this regulation whenever it leaves Indonesian jurisdiction. The draft dealt with inter-agency exchange only at Pasal 180, which set no condition for the cross-border case.

Analysis

Draft Pasal 180 let law enforcement bodies exchange personal data through agreed inter-agency mechanisms without engaging the transfer cascade at all, and enacted Pasal 159 keeps that mechanism for the handling of criminal cases under the data protection law.

Pasal 166 closes the route at the border by directing outbound inter-agency exchange to the transfer rules of the regulation, including the Pasal 165 cascade, so an outbound exchange now requires equivalence, an adequate and binding protection, or the consent of the subject.

Draft Pasal 191, which recognised a transfer ordered by a foreign court, tribunal or third state administrative authority only where an international agreement supported it, has no enacted counterpart, so the regulation now governs outbound state exchange while saying nothing about inbound foreign compulsion.

What to do about it

Agencies and regulated entities answering foreign agency requests must run the Pasal 165 cascade before releasing data.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Articles 44, 45, 46, 48, 49

The provision. Chapter V builds a three-step cascade.

Against Indonesia. The three rungs sit in Chapter V's order, ayat (2) against Article 45, ayat (3) against Article 46 and ayat (4) against Article 49(1)(a), but only the first two rungs do the same work.

What changed

The draft mixed plain hari with hari kerja across the enforcement and mediation timetable. The enacted text defines Hari as hari kerja at Pasal 1 number 19 and uses the defined term throughout, so every period the draft expressed in calendar days is now counted in working days at the same numeral.

Analysis

The clearest instance is the first mediation meeting: draft Pasal 234(2) gave 10 calendar days, enacted Pasal 211(2) gives 10 working days. The same conversion silently lengthens the mediation period in Pasal 218(1) from 30 calendar to 30 working days, the objection window in Pasal 197(1) from 14 calendar to 14 working days and the extension notice in Pasal 218(3) from 7 calendar to 7 working days.

Periods the draft already expressed as hari kerja, such as the 3 day document check and the 14 and 60 day examination periods, are unchanged in substance. The net effect is roughly a 40 per cent lengthening wherever the draft counted calendar days, and no period anywhere in the enacted text is calendar.

What to do about it

Recompute every diary entry in working days and check Indonesian public holidays before relying on any deadline.

Against Indonesia. Both instruments leave procedure to be filled in, but they leave different things and at different levels. Also compared at UU Pasal 64.

What changed

PP 33/2026 Article 1 point 19 defines Hari as a working day, a term the draft did not define at all. The capitalised term then governs the periods in Articles 64, 190, 192, 195, 197, 211, 213 and 218, where the draft used hari kerja only in its sanctions and mediation chapters.

Analysis

The enacted text converts every period it sets into working days by a single definitional move. Article 1 point 19 defines Hari as a working day, and because the capitalised term is then used throughout, periods the draft would have counted in calendar days now exclude weekends and public holidays. A period of 14 Hari runs for roughly three calendar weeks.

Every internal service level built against the draft understates the time available, and every deadline the Lembaga sets against a controller is correspondingly longer than it reads.

What to do about it

Recompute every deadline in the Regulation on working days before setting internal service levels.

What changed

Both texts cap the fine at 2% of annual revenue. The enacted text adds compliance as a calculation variable, hands the residual variable to the Lembaga to determine, and creates an express power to set the fine at zero.

Analysis

The headline number did not move, which makes the change easy to miss. What moved is everything beneath it. PP Pasal 185(2)(i) adds the compliance of the controller or processor to the variables used to calculate the fine, and item (j) converts the draft's konsideran lain yang relevan at RPP Pasal 225(2)(i) into a variabel lain yang relevan yang ditetapkan oleh Lembaga, so the residual limb is now the regulator's to fill rather than an open consideration.

Pasal 185(3) then permits a fine of Rp0,00 on unspecified pertimbangan tertentu, which the draft nowhere contemplated. Against GDPR Article 83, which structures severity through two fixed tiers, the enacted text concentrates a wide and largely unstructured discretion in a regulator whose own implementing rules are not yet made.

What to do about it

Compliance now carries a monetary value in the fine calculation. Document it before you need it.

What changed

Seven calendar days became thirty Hari, and PP Pasal 1(19) defines Hari as a working day.

Analysis

The draft gave a sanctioned controller a week to comply. The enacted text gives thirty working days, which is at least six weeks once weekends and public holidays are counted. What changed

The draft mentioned public participation only as something the authority could involve when supervising, at Pasal 203(2). The enacted text creates a standalone chapter, Bab VII, whose Pasal 179 lets the public act directly or indirectly through education, training, advocacy, socialisation and oversight, with the detail delegated to a Peraturan Lembaga under Pasal 179(3).

Analysis

Pasal 179 gives civil society a textual foothold that the draft confined to the authority's discretion, and the inclusion of pengawasan in the list means public oversight is contemplated alongside the authority's own supervision under Pasal 180. The verb is dapat berperan, so nothing here creates a right of access to documents or a right to be heard in a proceeding, and the complaint route remains Pasal 189(2).

The practical consequence is a broader pool of complainants, since Pasal 189(3) does not require the complainant to be the affected data subject. What the chapter does not do is give the public any standing once a proceeding starts.

What to do about it

Expect complaints from advocacy organisations as well as data subjects and prepare a single response protocol for both.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Articles 35, 57, 80

The provision. The GDPR gives the public no role in supervision.

Against Indonesia. UU Pasal 63 has no close GDPR counterpart, but the GDPR does address civil society, so this is a divergence rather than a subject the Regulation ignores.

(7)

(8)
