(9)
Pengajuan keberatan dianggap dikabulkan sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (8) dapat diajukan ke pengadilan tata usaha negara untuk diputus sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan.
(10)
Dalam hal Pengendali Data Pribadi dan/atau Prosesor Data Pribadi menolak keputusan keberatan sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (4) huruf b, Pengendali Data Pribadi dan/atau Prosesor Data Pribadi dapat mengajukan gugatan ke pengadilan tata usaha negara sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan.
(11)
Kepala Lembaga PDP dapat mendelegasikan kewenangan sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1) dan ayat (6) kepada pejabat Lembaga PDP.
Enacted · PP 33/2026
PP Pasal 197
PP Pasal 197
(1)
Pengendali Data Pribadi dan/atau Prosesor Data Pribadi yang dikenai sanksi administratif dapat mengajukan keberatan secara tertulis kepada pimpinan Lembaga paling lambat 14 (empat belas) Hari sejak menerima pemberitahuan keputusan tersebut.
(2)
Pengajuan keberatan sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1) tidak menunda pelaksanaan sanksi administratif.
(3)
Berdasarkan pengajuan sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1), pimpinan Lembaga menetapkan keputusan keberatan paling lambat 14 (empat belas) Hari sejak pengajuan keberatan diterima.
(4)
Keputusan keberatan sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (3) berupa:
  1. a.
    menerima keberatan sebagian atau seluruhnya; atau
  2. b.
    menolak keberatan disertai dengan alasan penolakan.
(5)
Keputusan keberatan disampaikan kepada Pengendali Data Pribadi dan/atau Prosesor Data Pribadi paling lambat 7 (tujuh) Hari sejak keputusan tersebut ditetapkan.
(6)
Apabila pimpinan Lembaga tidak memberikan keputusan keberatan dalam jangka waktu sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (3), pengajuan keberatan dianggap dikabulkan.
(7)
Pengajuan keberatan dianggap dikabulkan sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (6) dilaksanakan sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan.
(8)
Dalam hal keberatan ditolak, Pengendali Data Pribadi dan/atau Prosesor Data Pribadi yang bersangkutan dapat mengajukan gugatan ke pengadilan tata usaha negara sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan.
(9)
Pimpinan Lembaga dapat mendelegasikan kewenangan sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (3) kepada pejabat Lembaga.
What changed

The draft gave the head of the authority a binary choice at Pasal 223(4), accept or reject with reasons. Enacted Pasal 197(4) allows acceptance in part or in whole. The draft's statement that acceptance may revoke or annul the sanction, at Pasal 223(7), is dropped, and a deemed grant on silence can no longer be taken to the administrative court for a ruling as draft Pasal 223(9) permitted, it is simply implemented under general legislation per Pasal 197(7).

Analysis

Partial acceptance changes how an objection should be pleaded, because a controller can now attack the quantum or one limb of a multiple sanction without having to defeat the decision entirely. What the enacted text does not say is what a partial grant does to the sanction, since the draft's revocation and annulment language went with Pasal 223(7).

The deemed grant on the authority's silence within 14 Hari under Pasal 197(6) is likewise left without a mechanism for giving it effect, where the draft at least pointed to the administrative court. The route to the administrative court survives only for a rejected objection under Pasal 197(8).

What to do about it

Plead the objection limb by limb with a fallback quantum position and record the Pasal 197(3) deadline for a deemed grant.

Parties lose the right to put experts and fact witnesses

RPP Pasal 242
(1)

(2)
Atas persetujuan Para Pihak yang Bersengketa dan/atau kuasa hukumnya, Mediator dapat menghadirkan seorang atau lebih ahli dan/atau tokoh masyarakat.
(3)
Sebelum Mediator menghadirkan ahli dan/atau tokoh masyarakat, Para Pihak yang Bersengketa harus terlebih dahulu mencapai kesepakatan tentang kekuatan mengikat atau tidak mengikat dari penjelasan dan/atau penilaian ahli dan/atau tokoh masyarakat.
Enacted · PP 33/2026
PP Pasal 219
PP Pasal 219
(1)
Atas persetujuan Para Pihak yang Bersengketa dan/atau kuasa hukumnya, Mediator dapat menghadirkan seorang atau lebih ahli, pihak ketiga, dan/atau tokoh masyarakat.
(2)
Sebelum Mediator menghadirkan ahli, pihak ketiga, dan/atau tokoh masyarakat, Para Pihak yang Bersengketa harus terlebih dahulu mencapai kesepakatan tentang kekuatan mengikat atau tidak mengikat dari penjelasan dan/atau penilaian ahli, pihak ketiga, dan/atau tokoh masyarakat.
What changed

Draft Pasal 242(1) gave the disputing parties a right, berhak, to submit one or more experts and fact witnesses, separately from the mediator's own power at Pasal 242(2). The enacted Pasal 219 keeps only the mediator's route, and saksi fakta disappears from the chapter altogether.

Analysis

Under the draft a party could bring evidence into the mediation on its own initiative; under Pasal 219(1) evidence reaches the table only if the mediator elects to call it and both sides consent. Pasal 219(2) then requires the parties to agree in advance whether the expert's assessment binds them, so a reluctant respondent can block expert input twice over.

In a data protection dispute, where the technical facts of a breach usually sit with the controller, this asymmetry falls on the data subject. The mediation is correspondingly less capable of resolving contested facts.

What to do about it

Secure written agreement on expert evidence before the first mediation meeting, since Pasal 219 gives no unilateral route.

Against Indonesia. Both instruments leave procedure to be filled in, but they leave different things and at different levels. Also compared at UU Pasal 64.

PP Pasal 208
(1)
Dalam hal Para Pihak yang Bersengketa tidak mencapai kesepakatan dalam penunjukan Mediator, Para Pihak yang Bersengketa menyerahkan penunjukan Mediator kepada pimpinan Lembaga untuk menunjuk Mediator dari daftar Mediator sebagaimana dimaksud dalam Pasal 207 ayat (2).
(2)
Pimpinan Lembaga menerbitkan penetapan yang memuat perintah untuk melakukan Mediasi dan penunjukan Mediator.
(3)
Pimpinan Lembaga dapat mendelegasikan kewenangan sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1) sampai dengan ayat (2) kepada pejabat Lembaga.
What changed

Where the authority has no mediator available, draft Pasal 231(2) let the head of the authority appoint one from a registered professional mediation institution. Enacted Pasal 207(4) transfers that appointment to the parties, and the qualifier Profesional is dropped from the institution's description at Pasal 207(2)(b).

Analysis

The appointment power moves from the authority to the disputants at precisely the point where the authority is least able to help, namely before any register of mediators exists. Draft Pasal 231(2) let the head of the authority reach outside its own register, whereas enacted Pasal 207(4) leaves the parties to find an institution themselves.

Cost gives no relief either, because draft Pasal 233(1) put the fees of a Lembaga PDP mediator on the state while enacted Pasal 210 says only that the Lembaga will regulate the fees of both kinds of mediator, so who pays is now unstated.

Dropping Profesional lowers the threshold for what counts as a qualifying institution, with competence left to a Peraturan Lembaga under Pasal 222, and the authority's residual appointment power survives only where the parties fail to agree, at Pasal 208(1).

What to do about it

Identify a registered mediation institution before filing a dispute report, because Pasal 207(4) leaves that choice to the parties.

Sanctions and enforcement

Publication of supervision results becomes a power not a duty

duty changed
Draft · 31 August 2023
RPP Pasal 205
RPP Pasal 205
(1)
Lembaga PDP melakukan publikasi hasil pelaksanaan pengawasan Pelindungan Data Pribadi sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan.
(2)
Pelaksanaan publikasi dilakukan melalui pengumuman terbuka atau pengumuman yang dapat diakses oleh publik.
Enacted · PP 33/2026
PP Pasal 183
PP Pasal 183
(1)
Lembaga berwenang melakukan publikasi hasil pelaksanaan pengawasan Pelindungan Data Pribadi sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan.
(2)
Pelaksanaan publikasi dilakukan melalui pengumuman terbuka dan dapat diakses oleh publik.
What changed

The draft stated flatly that the authority publishes supervision results. The enacted Pasal 183(1) recasts publication as a power the authority is empowered to exercise, and Pasal 183(2) changes the mode from an open announcement or a publicly accessible one to an open announcement that is also publicly accessible.

Analysis

The shift from melakukan to berwenang melakukan converts an operational statement into a discretionary competence, so a controller cannot assume that supervision outcomes reach the public record. The change in Pasal 183(2) from the draft's disjunctive to a conjunctive requirement means that when the authority does publish, the result must be both openly announced and publicly retrievable, which raises the reputational stakes of the decision to publish.

Sanction decisions travel a different route under Pasal 195(2), on the authority's official media and coordinated with the relevant ministry under Pasal 195(3). Whether a supervision file becomes public is now a matter of authority judgement rather than rule.

What to do about it

Plan reputational response for supervision outcomes on the assumption publication is discretionary and unannounced.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Articles 58, 84

The provision. GDPR Article 58 splits the authority's powers into three sets.

Against Indonesia. The lettered list in UU Pasal 60 reaches many of the same places by a route of its own: huruf j to huruf n answer most of GDPR Article 58(1), huruf c and huruf g answer part of GDPR Article 58(2), and huruf f, read with PP Pasal 170 and PP Pasal 171 ayat (3), answers the authorisation powers at GDPR Article 58(3)(g) to (j) rather than any corrective power. (3)

  2. b.

  3. c.
    memanggil dan menghadirkan ahli yang diperlukan dalam pemeriksaan dan penelusuran terkait dugaan pelanggaran Pelindungan Data Pribadi;
  4. d.
    melakukan pemeriksaan dan penelusuran terhadap sistem elektronik, sarana, ruang, dan/atau tempat yang digunakan Pengendali Data Pribadi dan/atau Prosesor Data Pribadi, termasuk memperoleh akses terhadap data dan/atau menunjuk pihak ketiga; dan/atau
  5. e.
    melakukan tindakan dalam rangka menjalankan kewenangan sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan.
(4)
Dalam melakukan pemeriksaan dan penelusuran terhadap Pengendali Data Pribadi dan/atau Prosesor Data Pribadi sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (2), Lembaga dapat memanggil Pengendali Data Pribadi dan/atau Prosesor Data Pribadi.
(5)
Pemanggilan Pengendali Data Pribadi dan/atau Prosesor Data Pribadi sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (4) dilakukan secara tertulis paling lambat 3 (tiga) Hari sebelum tanggal pemeriksaan dan penelusuran terhadap Pengendali Data Pribadi dan/atau Prosesor Data Pribadi.
(6)
Pemanggilan terhadap Setiap Orang dan/atau Badan Publik yang terkait dengan dugaan pelanggaran Pelindungan Data Pribadi sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (3) huruf a dan/atau ahli yang diperlukan dalam pemeriksaan dan penelusuran terkait dugaan pelanggaran Pelindungan Data Pribadi sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (3) huruf c dilakukan secara tertulis paling lambat 3 (tiga) Hari sebelum tanggal pemeriksaan dan penelusuran terhadap Setiap Orang, Badan Publik, dan/atau ahli.
(7)
Pemeriksaan dan penelusuran terhadap sistem elektronik, sarana, ruang, dan/atau tempat yang digunakan Pengendali Data Pribadi dan/atau Prosesor Data Pribadi sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (3) huruf d harus dilakukan secara proporsional dengan melampirkan dokumen yang paling sedikit memuat Informasi:
  1. a.
    dasar hukum;
  2. b.
    tujuan dan ruang lingkup;
  3. c.
    daftar sistem elektronik, sarana, ruang, dan/atau tempat yang digunakan; dan
  4. d.
    relevansi antara sistem elektronik, sarana, ruang, dan/atau tempat yang digunakan dan dugaan terjadinya pelanggaran Pelindungan Data Pribadi oleh Pengendali Data Pribadi dan/atau Prosesor Data Pribadi.
(8)
Dalam hal Lembaga meminta kepada Pengendali Data Pribadi dan/atau Prosesor Data Pribadi untuk memperoleh akses terhadap data sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (3) huruf d, permintaan akses dilakukan dengan menyampaikan Informasi paling sedikit mengenai:
  1. a.
    dasar hukum;
  2. b.
    tujuan dan ruang lingkup;
  3. c.
    deskripsi mengenai jenis Data Pribadi yang dimintakan akses;
  4. d.
    deskripsi mengenai cara akses terhadap Data Pribadi; dan
  5. e.
    jangka waktu pemberian akses terhadap Data Pribadi.
(9)
Dalam hal Lembaga menunjuk pihak ketiga dalam melakukan pemeriksaan dan penelusuran terhadap sistem elektronik, sarana, ruang, dan/atau tempat yang digunakan Pengendali Data Pribadi dan/atau Prosesor Data Pribadi sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (3) huruf d, penunjukan harus disertai dengan surat penugasan dari Lembaga.
(10)
Pemeriksaan dan penelusuran terhadap dugaan terjadinya pelanggaran Pelindungan Data Pribadi diselesaikan paling lambat 14 (empat belas) Hari terhitung sejak pemeriksaan dan penelusuran dimulai.
(11)
Apabila diperlukan, jangka waktu pemeriksaan dan penelusuran terhadap dugaan terjadinya pelanggaran Pelindungan Data Pribadi sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (10) dapat diperpanjang paling lama 60 (enam puluh) Hari.
What changed

Draft Pasal 204 listed six things the authority could order but attached no period for compliance and no form requirement. The enacted Pasal 181 requires the order in writing at ayat (2), requires the authority to fix a compliance period calibrated to supervisory need and complexity at ayat (4) and (5), and lets it demand an action plan and progress reports at ayat (6).

Analysis

The draft order was an instruction with no clock, which made non-compliance difficult to establish. Pasal 181(4) supplies the clock and Pasal 181(6) converts the order into a supervised remediation programme with its own reporting duty on the controller or processor.

Because the period is set case by case rather than in the regulation, its length is a matter for negotiation at the point the order is issued, and Pasal 181(5) supplies the two grounds on which to argue for more time. Pasal 182 adds a further constraint where the addressee is a public body, requiring the authority to weigh the legislation governing that body's functions.

What to do about it

Argue the Pasal 181(5) complexity ground when the order is served rather than after the period has run.

PP Pasal 127, 128
PP Pasal 127

Dalam melakukan kewajiban pengawasan sebagaimana dimaksud dalam Pasal 126 ayat (1), Pengendali Data Pribadi harus memiliki:

  1. a.
    kebijakan terkait pemrosesan Data Pribadi;
  2. b.
    perjanjian pemrosesan Data Pribadi yang mengatur kewajiban dan tanggung jawab Pelindungan Data Pribadi; dan
  3. c.
    kanal komunikasi pelaporan bagi masyarakat.
PP Pasal 128

Ketentuan lebih lanjut mengenai pengawasan oleh Pengendali Data Pribadi sebagaimana dimaksud dalam Pasal 126 dan Pasal 127 diatur dalam Peraturan Lembaga.

What changed

RPP Pasal 137(1) prescribed eleven minimum terms for the controller to processor agreement inside the supervision chapter, covering audit rights, adherence to instructions, written approval for sub-processing, notification of security policy changes, equivalence of protection standards, return or deletion on termination, liability and incident procedure. PP 33/2026 Pasal 127(b) requires only that an agreement exist and regulate obligations and responsibilities, with Pasal 128 delegating the detail to a Peraturan Lembaga.

The draft's other contract provision, RPP Pasal 21, survives intact as PP Pasal 14 with the same eleven items.

Analysis

The enacted text keeps the draft's appointment agreement and drops its supervision chapter counterpart. PP Pasal 14 reproduces RPP Pasal 21 item for item, including the mekanisme pengawasan, pendokumentasian, audit, dan inspeksi at huruf h, and PP Pasal 15(2) keeps the processor's duty to obtain the controller's written approval before engaging another processor, so the audit mechanism and the control over sub-processing both survive.

What goes is the RPP Pasal 137(1) list: PP Pasal 127(b) reduces it to a single clause about kewajiban dan tanggung jawab and Pasal 128 sends the detail to a Peraturan Lembaga that has not been made. No enacted provision now requires the contract to address return or deletion of data when the engagement ends, equivalence between the processor's protection standard and the controller's, notification of a change in the processor's security policy, or an incident procedure.

Those four controls survive only where a contract already states them.

What to do about it

Keep the RPP Pasal 137 clauses on return or deletion, security parity and incident handling, since Pasal 14 and Pasal 15 already carry audit and sub-processing.

PP Pasal 127, 128
PP Pasal 127

Dalam melakukan kewajiban pengawasan sebagaimana dimaksud dalam Pasal 126 ayat (1), Pengendali Data Pribadi harus memiliki:

  1. a.
    kebijakan terkait pemrosesan Data Pribadi;
  2. b.
    perjanjian pemrosesan Data Pribadi yang mengatur kewajiban dan tanggung jawab Pelindungan Data Pribadi; dan
  3. c.
    kanal komunikasi pelaporan bagi masyarakat.
PP Pasal 128

Ketentuan lebih lanjut mengenai pengawasan oleh Pengendali Data Pribadi sebagaimana dimaksud dalam Pasal 126 dan Pasal 127 diatur dalam Peraturan Lembaga.

What changed

RPP Pasal 134 and PP 33/2026 Pasal 127 list the same three supervision instruments in the same order, a processing policy, a protection agreement and a public reporting channel, with the draft's wajib menyiapkan becoming harus memiliki.

What goes is RPP Pasal 135, which filled those headings out over four ayat, including the internal and external audit policy at Pasal 135(1)(b), pre engagement vetting of a processor, periodic and ad hoc audits, exit audits, audit follow up and publication of results to management, the public and the authority. PP 33/2026 Pasal 128 sends the whole of that detail to a future Peraturan Lembaga.

Analysis

The most detailed accountability machinery in the draft chapter was removed in a single stroke. RPP Pasal 135(4)(e) obliged a controller to check a processor's legality, experience, compliance history, breach record, technical readiness and references before instructing it, and Pasal 135(4)(f) made that assessment the basis for selection.

PP 33/2026 requires no pre engagement audit of a processor; the nearest survivor is Pasal 125(2), which asks only that the controller ensure an appointed processor can support the confidentiality duty.

Pasal 127 keeps the three headings without their contents and Pasal 128 places the audit regime in a Peraturan Lembaga that does not yet exist, so controller supervision of processors is the least operationalised duty in the chapter even though Pasal 126(1) keeps wajib and appears in the sanction list at Pasal 184(1).

What to do about it

Run the RPP Pasal 135 due diligence and audit programme as internal policy and watch for the Peraturan Lembaga.

RPP Pasal 222
RPP Pasal 222
(1)
Setiap Pengendali Data Pribadi atau Prosesor Data Pribadi yang tidak melaksanakan keputusan Lembaga PDP dapat dikenai denda atas keterlambatan pelaksanaan keputusan.
(2)
Denda atas keterlambatan sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1) merupakan penerimaan negara bukan pajak yang wajib disetorkan ke kas negara sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang -undangan tentang penerimaan negara bukan pajak.
Enacted · PP 33/2026
no counterpart

The enacted text carries nothing in its place.

What changed

Draft Pasal 222 exposed a controller or processor that failed to carry out an authority decision to a separate fine for delay, payable to the state as non-tax revenue. The word keterlambatan appears nowhere in the enacted text.

Analysis

The draft paired a short compliance window in Pasal 220(4) with an arrears penalty in Pasal 222, so delay had its own price. The enacted text sets a longer window of 30 Hari in Pasal 195(5) and removes the penalty, leaving the Lembaga with a discretionary request for prosecutorial assistance under Pasal 198 and the debt recovery route in Pasal 186(2), which presupposes a fine already final and binding.

A controller that simply ignores an order to delete data or to suspend processing therefore faces no automatic escalation within the sanctions chapter, only a fresh proceeding through the stages set out in Pasal 188. Non-monetary sanctions are left without any arrears mechanism at all.

What to do about it

Expect enforcement of an ignored decision to come as a new proceeding rather than an accruing penalty.

Where Europe stands

This finding cites no article of the enacted text, so there is no implementing provision to carry a comparison. The subject is treated in the reading pages.

    instruksi pemrosesan dari Pengendali Data Pribadi kepada Prosesor Data Pribadi;
  4. d.
    kewajiban bagi Prosesor Data Pribadi untuk meminta persetujuan Pengendali Data Pribadi secara tertulis dalam hal melakukan sub - processing;
  5. e.
    kewajiban Pr osesor Data Pribadi menginformasikan Pengendali Data Pribadi ketika terjadi perubahan kebijakan keamanan dan/atau Pelindungan Data Pribadi Prosesor Data Pribadi;
  6. f.
    kewajiban Pengendali Data Pribadi menginformasikan Prosesor Data Pribadi ketika terjadi perubahan kebijakan keamanan dan/atau Pelindungan Data Pribadi Prosesor Data Pribadi;
  7. g.
    pernyataan bahwa Prosesor Data Pribadi akan menerapkan standar Pelindungan Data Pribadi yang sama dengan standar Pengendali Data Pribadi;
  8. h.
    larangan bagi Prosesor Data Pribadi me mbuat kebijakan dan tindakan yang mengurangi pelindungan terhadap keamanan Data Pribadi;
  9. i.
    mekanisme pengembalian atau penghapusan Data Pribadi oleh Prosesor Data Pribadi dalam hal berakhirnya pemberian perintah pemrosesan dari Pengendali Data Pribadi terhadap Prosesor Data Pribadi;
  10. j.
    tanggung jawab Prosesor Data Pribadi dalam kegiatan pemrosesan; dan
  11. k.
    prosedur Prosesor Data Pribadi dalam hal terjadi insiden keamanan.
(2)
Perjanjian antara Pengendali Data Pribadi dan Prosesor Data Pribadi wajib menggunakan Bahasa Indonesia.
(3)
Perjanjian antara Pengendali Data Pribadi dan Prosesor Data Pribadi wajib dibuat sesuai dengan peraturan perundang-undangan.
Enacted · PP 33/2026
no counterpart

The enacted text carries nothing in its place.

What changed

RPP Pasal 137(2) required the controller to processor agreement to be in Bahasa Indonesia. PP 33/2026 contains no language requirement for that agreement anywhere in Bagian Kedelapan Belas.

Analysis

The language rule disappeared with the rest of RPP Pasal 137, and no minimum content list for the controller to processor agreement survives anywhere in the enacted text. Its deletion does not make English-only data processing agreements safe, because UU 24/2009 Pasal 31 independently requires Indonesian for agreements involving Indonesian parties.

What changes is the forum: the point is no longer a data protection compliance item the Lembaga can raise, and becomes a contract validity risk argued in the civil courts. Cross-border groups that standardise on English master agreements should not read the deletion as a relaxation.

What to do about it

Keep executing processor agreements bilingually; UU 24/2009 Pasal 31 still applies.

Where Europe stands

This finding cites no article of the enacted text, so there is no implementing provision to carry a comparison. The subject is treated in the reading pages.

(1)

(2)

What changed

RPP Pasal 133(2) listed four categories under controller supervision: processors, internal units, majority-owned or otherwise controlled legal entities, and a catch-all covering any other party involved in processing. PP 33/2026 Pasal 126(2) lists three, replacing the affiliate limb and the catch-all with Pengendali Data Pribadi lain.

Analysis

Group companies moved from supervised subordinates to independent controllers. RPP Pasal 133(2)(c) captured majority-owned entities as parties under the controller's kendali, which brought intra-group data flows inside the supervision duty and inside the RPP Pasal 138 agreement requirement; PP 33/2026 Pasal 126(2)(c) substitutes Pengendali Data Pribadi lain, a category that by definition determines its own purposes.

The deletion of the draft's catch-all at huruf d removes the residual limb that would otherwise have caught arrangements fitting none of the named categories. Intra-group processing must now be characterised as joint control under Pasal 1 angka 20 or as a controller to controller transfer, each carrying a different documentation set.

What to do about it

Recharacterise intra-group flows; affiliates are no longer supervised parties by default.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Articles 24, 28

The provision. The GDPR imposes no free-standing duty of supervision.

Against Indonesia. GDPR Article 28 attaches to a moment and to an instrument.

What changed

Draft Pasal 185(3) required the controller to demonstrate accountability for the adequate and binding safeguard in written or recorded form. Enacted Pasal 169(2) adds kepada Lembaga as the addressee and changes wajib to harus.

Analysis

The draft required the controller to demonstrate the accountability in written or recorded form without naming anyone to demonstrate it to; the enacted duty runs to the Lembaga, which converts a documentation obligation into a production obligation without stating a trigger, a form or a deadline. Pasal 169(3) then preserves the regulator's power to assess compliance notwithstanding the documents, so production settles nothing on its own.

Nothing in the chapter says whether production is on request or on adoption of the safeguard, which is the first question a controller relying on standard contractual clauses needs answered.

What to do about it

Keep the safeguard file in a form that can be handed to the Lembaga on demand and seek clarification on whether filing is proactive.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Articles 44, 45, 46, 48, 49

The provision. Chapter V builds a three-step cascade.

Against Indonesia. The three rungs sit in Chapter V's order, ayat (2) against Article 45, ayat (3) against Article 46 and ayat (4) against Article 49(1)(a), but only the first two rungs do the same work.

RPP Pasal 147(3) obliged a dissolving controller to appoint a contact person or data protection officer to answer subject queries for a defined period. PP 33/2026 Pasal 136(2) makes that appointment discretionary and drops the duration.

The draft guaranteed a surviving point of contact; the enacted text leaves it to the entity being wound up. RPP Pasal 147(3) used wajib menunjuk and sepanjang waktu tertentu, whereas PP 33/2026 Pasal 136(2) reads dapat menunjuk with no period attached.

The notification content at Pasal 136(1)(c) still names a narahubung or PPDP as the route for subject queries, so the enacted text compels disclosure of a contact that need never be appointed. Subjects of a dissolved controller may be left with a named right and no addressee.

What changed

RPP Article 34(3) required prevention or minimisation of recordings of persons and property beyond the monitoring purpose, and Article 34(4) prohibited placement in areas where an individual has an expectation of privacy. PP 33/2026 Article 18(2) retains only the requirement that placement and use serve the intended monitoring purpose.

Analysis

The two hard limits the draft placed on camera siting are gone. The word ekspektasi appears nowhere in PP 33/2026, so the prohibition on placement in private areas has no successor, and the minimisation duty in RPP Article 34(3) disappears with it. What survives at Article 18(2) constrains the direction of monitoring, not the location of the device.

Placement in workplaces, fitting rooms and similar areas is now governed only by the general processing bases in Article 30(3), and the visual device provisions are absent from the sanctions list in Article 184(1), as they were from RPP Article 213(1).

What to do about it

Keep an internal prohibition on cameras in private areas because the Regulation no longer supplies one.

Analysis

The draft closed the financial supervision exception to three named authorities; the enacted text leaves the class open. RPP Pasal 175(d) named Bank Indonesia, OJK and LPS exhaustively, whereas PP 33/2026 Pasal 153 ends at the safeguards limb.

The deletion is systematic rather than sector specific, because Pasal 151 and Pasal 152 drop the same requester limb that RPP Pasal 173(d) and Pasal 174(d) carried for law enforcement and for the public interest. Any body able to characterise its work as pengawasan sektor jasa keuangan, moneter, sistem pembayaran, dan stabilitas sistem keuangan in the conduct of the state can now engage the criteria, subject only to Pasal 149(2), which confines every exception to the implementation of a statute.

For a bank or payment institution the question shifts from who is asking to whether the requester's own statute supports the request.

What to do about it

Test each financial supervision request against the requester's own statutory basis rather than a fixed list of three.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Article 23

Against Indonesia. GDPR Article 23 assumes two instruments: the Regulation, and a later national law that does the restricting under the GDPR Article 23(2) checklist. Also compared at UU Pasal 50.

PP Pasal 17
(1)

  1. a.
    untuk tujuan keamanan, pencegahan bencana, dan/atau penyelenggaraan lalu lintas atau pengumpulan, analisis, dan pengaturan Informasi lalu lintas;

What changed

PP 33/2026 Article 17(1) permits installation in public places and public service facilities only for security, disaster prevention or traffic purposes, and forbids use of the device to identify a person. The draft set no list of permitted purposes and contained no non-identification rule, tying use only to the operator's own monitoring purpose at RPP Article 34(2). The signage duty is not new, since RPP Article 35 already imposed it and enacted Article 19 carries it over.

Analysis

The enacted text introduces two controls the draft never contained. Article 17(1)(a) closes the permitted purposes to security, disaster prevention and traffic management, where RPP Article 34(2) had asked only that the operator consider its own monitoring purpose, and Article 17(1)(c) forbids use of the device to identify a person, a restriction with no draft analogue.

Article 17(2) exempts crime prevention and law enforcement from the information and non-identification limbs while leaving the purpose limitation intact. Facial recognition deployed in a public place for a commercial purpose therefore has no permitted purpose under Article 17(1), which is the sharpest new constraint in this chapter for retail, venue and transport operators.

What to do about it

Audit any public facing camera estate for identification features and map each deployment to Article 17(1)(a).

What changed

RPP Pasal 155(2) required the controller's instruction to be delivered secara tertulis dan terdokumentasi. PP 33/2026 Pasal 139(2) requires only that the instruction be terdokumentasi and executed in line with the controller and processor agreement.

Analysis

The draft required both a written form and a record; the enacted text keeps only the record. RPP Pasal 155(2) coupled tertulis to terdokumentasi as a free-standing rule, whereas PP 33/2026 Pasal 139(2) drops the written form and recasts the clause as an attribute of the kewajiban in ayat (1).

A ticket entry or call log can now satisfy Pasal 139(2), which weakens the position of a processor later asked to prove that it acted on instruction, and matters directly under the new liability rule in ayat (3). The evidential burden shifts to whatever documentation system the parties happen to operate.

What to do about it

Keep instructions in writing anyway and name the documented channel in the Pasal 14 agreement.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Article 28

The provision. GDPR Article 28(1) lets a controller use only processors that provide sufficient guarantees of appropriate technical and organisational measures.

Against Indonesia. UU Pasal 51 reaches the same allocation of responsibility, then parts company with Article 28 on two mechanisms. Also compared at UU Pasal 52.

  2. b.

  3. c.

  4. d.

(5)

(6)

What changed

RPP Pasal 128(5) and (6) used wajib for implementing the identified mitigation measures and for documenting the assessment. PP 33/2026 Pasal 121(3) and (4) state both in the plain indicative, and Pasal 121(2)(a) also drops secara sistematis from the description requirement.

Analysis

The obligation to conduct the assessment survived; the obligation to act on it did not. PP 33/2026 Pasal 120(1) keeps wajib for carrying out the penilaian dampak, while Pasal 121(3) removes wajib from the step that gives the assessment effect, namely implementing the protective measures identified at ayat (2) huruf d. A controller can therefore satisfy the surviving wajib by producing an assessment it never implements.

The deletion of secara sistematis from Pasal 121(2)(a) compounds this, since the description of processing no longer has to be methodical, leaving the enacted DPIA weaker on both rigour and follow-through than RPP Pasal 128.

What to do about it

Track DPIA mitigations to closure internally; the enacted text no longer compels implementation.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Articles 35, 36

The provision. GDPR Article 35(1) requires a data protection impact assessment before processing likely to result in a high risk to rights and freedoms, in particular where new technologies are used.

Against Indonesia. The seven triggers at UU Pasal 34 ayat (2) do not track GDPR Article 35(3), which names three.

What changed

RPP Pasal 165(1) joined the three appointment triggers with dan, requiring all three to be met at once. PP 33/2026 Pasal 142(1) joins them with dan/atau, so any single trigger suffices.

Analysis

The draft's conjunction made the appointment duty nearly unreachable, and it tracked UU 27/2022 Pasal 53(1), which also closes limb b with dan, so the enacted text departs from the statute it implements. RPP Pasal 165(1) huruf b closed with dan, meaning public service processing, large-scale systematic monitoring and large-scale specific or criminal data all had to coincide, whereas PP 33/2026 Pasal 142(1) huruf b closes with dan/atau.

Public bodies processing for public services now fall within the duty on that ground alone, as does a controller running large-scale systematic monitoring. The population of controllers required to appoint a PPDP expands sharply against the draft, and Pasal 142(2) leaves the detail of the duty to a Peraturan Lembaga.

What to do about it

Re-run the appointment test on each limb separately because the cumulative reading no longer holds.

Where Europe stands ported from the GDPR GDPR Article 37

The provision. GDPR Article 37(1) requires a controller or processor to designate a data protection officer in three cases.

Against Indonesia. The tracking is limb for limb: UU Pasal 53 ayat (1) huruf b carries the Article 37(1)(b) formula intact, with kegiatan inti and sifat, ruang lingkup, dan/atau tujuan sitting where core activities and nature, scope and/or purposes sit, huruf c carries Article 37(1)(c) down to the criminal offence category, ayat (2) follows Article 37(5) in the same order and ayat (3) is Article 37(6).

What changed

RPP Pasal 169(2)(c) allowed the officer to report the performance of the unit responsible for processing security to the board and/or to the Lembaga PDP. PP 33/2026 Pasal 147(2)(c) directs that report to internal leadership only.

Analysis

The draft gave the officer an external escalation route; the enacted text closes it. RPP Pasal 169(2)(c) read direksi dan/atau Lembaga PDP, whereas PP 33/2026 Pasal 147(2)(c) reads pemimpin di internal Pengendali Data Pribadi. Combined with the loss of the dismissal protection at Pasal 146(1)(c), an officer who finds security measures inadequate must escalate inside the organisation that employs them, with no channel of their own to the regulator.

Inadequate security now reaches the Lembaga only through the controller's own breach and documentation duties under Pasal 114 and Pasal 116.

What to do about it

Log escalations internally with dates because the internal record is now the only trace.

Where Europe stands ported from the GDPR GDPR Articles 38, 39

The provision. GDPR Article 39(1) gives the officer at least five tasks: informing and advising the controller, processor and staff who process; monitoring compliance with the GDPR and with internal policies, including allocation of responsibilities, awareness raising, training and audits; advising on a data protection impact assessment and monitoring its performance under Article 35; cooperating with the supervisory authority; and acting as its contact point, including for prior consultation under Article 36.

Against Indonesia. UU Pasal 54 ayat (1) is Article 39(1) in the same order with the last two limbs folded into one: huruf a is Article 39(1)(a), huruf b is Article 39(1)(b), huruf c sits where Article 39(1)(c) sits, and huruf d merges cooperation with the authority and the contact point role from Article 39(1)(d) and (e), with paling sedikit doing the work of at least in the chapeau.

What changed

RPP Pasal 168(1)(c) required the controller to ensure the officer was not dismissed or punished for carrying out the role. PP 33/2026 Pasal 146(1)(c) requires instead that the officer operate objectively, free from intervention and independently.

Analysis

The draft protected the officer's tenure; the enacted text protects the officer's conduct. RPP Pasal 168(1)(c) named diberhentikan atau dihukum, a concrete employment consequence, whereas PP 33/2026 Pasal 146(1)(c) substitutes tidak diintervensi dan independen, which speaks to interference in the task rather than to retaliation for completing it.

Dismissal following an unwelcome recommendation is no longer expressly prohibited, so the officer's remedy sits in employment law rather than in the data protection instrument. The independence guarantee is genuine but far harder to evidence than a tenure rule.

What to do about it

Write the no-dismissal-for-performing-the-role term into the officer's engagement contract.

  1. a.
    Kepala Kepolisian Negara Republik Indonesia, kepala kepolisian daerah, kepala kepolisian resor, atau pejabat yang ditunjuk dalam hal permintaan diajukan oleh penyidik dari Kepolisian Negara Republik Indonesia;
  2. b.
    pimpinan instansi atau lembaga, atau penjabat yang ditunjuk dalam hal permintaan diajukan oleh penyidik selain penyidik Kepolisian Negara Republik Indonesia;
  3. c.
    Jaksa Agung, kepala kejaksaan tinggi, kepala kejaksaan negeri, kepala cabang kejaksaan negeri, atau pejabat yang ditunjuk dalam hal permintaan diajukan oleh jaksa dan/atau penuntut umum; atau
  4. d.

What changed

RPP Pasal 177(5) confined signature to the national or provincial police chief, the head of the requesting agency, the Attorney General or a high prosecution office head, and the presiding judge of the panel. PP 33/2026 Pasal 155(4) adds the district police chief, the district and branch prosecution heads, and in every limb a pejabat yang ditunjuk, while moving the judicial signature from the presiding judge to the Supreme Court, high court or district court chair.

Analysis

The draft reserved the police and prosecution demand to a small set of senior offices; the enacted text pushes it down to district level and to any designated official. RPP Pasal 177(5)(a) stopped at kepala kepolisian daerah, whereas PP 33/2026 Pasal 155(4)(a) adds kepala kepolisian resor and the open ended atau pejabat yang ditunjuk, with the same designation clause repeated for other investigating agencies at ayat (4)(b) and for prosecutors at ayat (4)(c).

The volume of validly signed demands a controller may receive rises accordingly. Two changes cut the other way and neither closes the gap. Pasal 155(1) drops penyelidik from the officers who may ask, and Pasal 155(2)(g) requires the demand to state the basis of the authority relied on, which partly replaces the police report and warrants that RPP Pasal 177(4) required and the enacted text no longer does.

The copy to the pimpinan Lembaga under Pasal 155(5) remains the only external check.

What to do about it

Build a verification workflow for district-level demands and treat the Pasal 155(5) copy as the audit trail.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Article 23

The provision. GDPR Article 23(1) lets Union or Member State law restrict the rights in Articles 12 to 22 and Article 34, and the Article 5 principles so far as they correspond, but only by a legislative measure that respects the essence of the right and is necessary and proportionate in a democratic society, and only for one of ten listed objectives.

Against Indonesia. GDPR Article 23 assumes two instruments: the Regulation, and a later national law that does the restricting under the GDPR Article 23(2) checklist. Also compared at UU Pasal 50.

Compared at UU Pasal 15, where the full comparison sits.

no counterpart

The enacted text carries nothing in its place.

What changed

RPP Pasal 153(4) required the appointed officer or external contact to explain the basis of a refusal where a subject right could not be honoured because the controller had been legally dissolved. PP 33/2026 Pasal 137 carries no equivalent.

Analysis

The draft closed the loop on rights that die with the entity; the enacted text leaves it open. RPP Pasal 153(4) attached an explanation duty to the officer or external contact, whereas PP 33/2026 Pasal 137(2) stops at naming the two controllers to whom a request may be addressed.

Read with the discretionary appointment at Pasal 136(2), a subject facing a dissolved controller has neither a guaranteed addressee nor a right to reasons. This is the sharpest gap the corporate-actions bagian now leaves.

What to do about it

Record refusal reasons in the winding-up file regardless; a complaint to the Lembaga will still ask for them.

Where Europe stands

This finding cites no article of the enacted text, so there is no implementing provision to carry a comparison. The subject is treated in the reading pages.

(2)

Enacted · PP 33/2026
PP Pasal 157
PP Pasal 157
(1)
Untuk kepentingan penanganan dalam perkara tindak pidana Pelindungan Data Pribadi, Pengendali Data Pribadi dan/atau Prosesor Data Pribadi memberikan Data Pribadi yang diproses atas permintaan Data Pribadi dari penyidik, penuntut umum, atau hakim sebagaimana dimaksud dalam Pasal 155.
(2)

What changed

RPP Pasal 178(1) obliged the controller or processor to hand over data wajib and only on a permintaan yang sah. PP 33/2026 Pasal 157(1) states that the controller or processor memberikan the data on a request under Pasal 155, with neither the mandatory verb nor the lawfulness qualifier.

Analysis

The draft framed disclosure as a duty owed on a lawful request; the enacted text states it as a description of what happens. RPP Pasal 178(1) used wajib memberikan and permintaan yang sah, whereas PP 33/2026 Pasal 157(1) reads memberikan atas permintaan Data Pribadi and cross-refers to Pasal 155 as a whole.

Losing yang sah removes the express hook for refusing a defective demand, and losing wajib leaves the disclosure in the indicative, though the sanction position is unchanged, since RPP Pasal 213(1) omitted Pasal 178 and PP Pasal 184(1) omits Pasal 157. The enacted text also drops penyelidik from the officers who may demand, so compliance turns entirely on whether a demand from a penyidik, penuntut umum or hakim meets the Pasal 155 formalities.

What to do about it

Test every demand against each limb of Pasal 155 because Pasal 157 no longer states a lawfulness condition.

PP Pasal 150

Penerapan pengecualian hak Subjek Data Pribadi untuk kepentingan pertahanan dan keamanan nasional sebagaimana dimaksud dalam Pasal 148 ayat (1) huruf a dan pengecualian kewajiban Pengendali Data Pribadi untuk kepentingan pertahanan dan keamanan nasional sebagaimana dimaksud dalam Pasal 149 ayat (1) huruf a harus memenuhi kriteria:

  2. b.

  4. d.

  5. e.

What changed

RPP Pasal 172(d) required a letter from both the Lembaga PDP and the defence ministry, stating that the controller was exempt from identified processing requirements. PP 33/2026 Pasal 150(d) accepts a letter from the Lembaga or the relevant ministry or agency and drops the content requirement.

Analysis

The draft made the data protection authority a co-signatory to every defence exception; the enacted text makes it optional. RPP Pasal 172(d) used dan and specified what the letter had to state, whereas PP 33/2026 Pasal 150(d) uses atau twice and is silent on content.

A defence or security body can therefore certify the exception without the Lembaga seeing the case, and the certificate need not identify which requirements are disapplied. The authority's structural check on the widest exception in the instrument is removed at the point where it would have operated.

What to do about it

Ask which body issued the surat keterangan and what it disapplies before relying on a counterparty's exception claim.

(2)

PP Pasal 158
PP Pasal 158
(1)

(2)

What changed

RPP Pasal 179 imposed three duties on investigators, prosecutors and judges: specific and proportionate processing that guarantees subject rights, protection and security of the data, and destruction or erasure within the statutory period. PP 33/2026 Pasal 158 replaces all three with a designation of those officers as controllers of the data they process.

Analysis

The draft regulated the criminal justice recipient directly; the enacted text regulates it by classification. RPP Pasal 179(1) to (3) used wajib three times, including an express pemusnahan dan/atau penghapusan duty, whereas PP 33/2026 Pasal 158(1) declares the officers to be Pengendali Data Pribadi and Pasal 158(2) says the processing follows this regulation.

The controller duty set does reach retention through the Masa Retensi rules, so the substance is not wholly lost, but the article-level deletion duty for case data is. A subject must now locate the obligation inside the general controller chapter rather than in a single provision addressed to prosecutors.

What to do about it

Cite Pasal 158(1) when asking a law enforcement recipient about retention because it is a controller on the enacted text.

  2. b.

  3. c.

  4. d.

(6)

(7)

What changed

RPP Pasal 82(3)(d) listed the need for periodic verification as something the controller assessed, expressly including the option not to verify periodically through the words atau tidak. PP 33/2026 Pasal 69(4) makes periodic or ad hoc verification a standing requirement and Pasal 69(5)(d) drops atau tidak from the same item.

Analysis

The draft let a controller conclude that periodic verification was unnecessary; the enacted text removes that conclusion from its reach. PP 33/2026 Pasal 69(4) states that verification is carried out secara berkala dan/atau sewaktu-waktu, and Pasal 69(3) adds a prior step of fixing a data quality mechanism or standard, with Pasal 69(8) requiring the results to be documented.

Accuracy has therefore moved from a one-off gate at intake to a maintained control with an evidential trail. A controller with no verification schedule and no recorded quality standard is now non-compliant on the face of Pasal 69 rather than merely unpersuasive.

What to do about it

Publish a data quality standard and a verification schedule and keep the verification records.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Articles 5, 16

The provision. GDPR Article 5(1)(d) requires personal data to be accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date.

Against Indonesia. Article 5(1)(d) is purpose relative, so the reasonable steps to erase or rectify are measured against what the data is used for.

(1)

(2)

  3. c.
    uraian singkat tindak pidana yang disangkakan atau didakwakan;
  4. d.
    jenis Data Pribadi yang diminta dan relevansinya dengan penanganan dalam perkara tindak pidana Pelindungan Data Pribadi;
  5. e.
    jangka waktu pemrosesan Data Pribadi;
  6. f.
    pernyataan telah memiliki dan menerapkan mekanisme pelindungan dan pengamanan yang layak dan memadai dalam memproses Data Pribadi sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan di bidang Pelindungan Data Pribadi; dan

(4)
Surat permintaan Data Pribadi sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (2) harus ditandatangani oleh:
  1. a.
    Kepala Kepolisian Negara Republik Indonesia, kepala kepolisian daerah, kepala kepolisian resor, atau pejabat yang ditunjuk dalam hal permintaan diajukan oleh penyidik dari Kepolisian Negara Republik Indonesia;
  2. b.
    pimpinan instansi atau lembaga, atau penjabat yang ditunjuk dalam hal permintaan diajukan oleh penyidik selain penyidik Kepolisian Negara Republik Indonesia;
  3. c.
    Jaksa Agung, kepala kejaksaan tinggi, kepala kejaksaan negeri, kepala cabang kejaksaan negeri, atau pejabat yang ditunjuk dalam hal permintaan diajukan oleh jaksa dan/atau penuntut umum; atau
  4. d.
    Ketua Mahkamah Agung, ketua pengadilan tinggi, atau ketua pengadilan negeri yang memeriksa perkara yang bersangkutan dalam hal permintaan diajukan oleh hakim.
(5)
Surat permintaan sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (4) ditembuskan kepada pimpinan Lembaga.
What changed

RPP Pasal 177(4) required a demand to be accompanied by a police report and investigation order, a prosecutor's appointment letter or a panel determination. PP 33/2026 Pasal 155 imposes no attachment requirement and instead adds a self-stated basis of authority at ayat (2)(g).

Analysis

The draft required documentary proof of authority; the enacted text accepts an assertion of it. RPP Pasal 177(4) used wajib disertai and named the instrument for each class of requester, whereas PP 33/2026 Pasal 155(2)(g) asks only that the dasar kewenangan be stated in the request letter itself.

The controller loses the independent artefact against which a demand could be tested and retains only the signature rule at Pasal 155(4) and the copy to the Lembaga at Pasal 155(5). That residue is thinner than it looks, because Pasal 155(4) extends signing authority down to a kepala kepolisian resor, a kepala kejaksaan negeri and a pejabat yang ditunjuk, where draft Pasal 177(5) stopped at national and provincial heads and at the presiding judge.

What to do about it

Request the underlying order regardless and record it if the requester declines to produce one.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Article 23

The provision. GDPR Article 23(1) lets Union or Member State law restrict the rights in Articles 12 to 22 and Article 34, and the Article 5 principles so far as they correspond, but only by a legislative measure that respects the essence of the right and is necessary and proportionate in a democratic society, and only for one of ten listed objectives.

Against Indonesia. GDPR Article 23 assumes two instruments: the Regulation, and a later national law that does the restricting under the GDPR Article 23(2) checklist. Also compared at UU Pasal 50.

Compared at UU Pasal 15, where the full comparison sits.

What changed

RPP Pasal 177(1) empowered penyelidik, penyidik, penuntut umum and hakim to demand personal data from a controller or processor. PP 33/2026 Pasal 155(1) removes penyelidik and conditions the power on the prevailing legislation.

Analysis

The draft reached the preliminary inquiry stage; the enacted text starts at formal investigation. RPP Pasal 177(1) listed penyelidik first, whereas PP 33/2026 Pasal 155(1) begins at penyidik and adds sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan, with the signature list at Pasal 155(4)(a) likewise naming only penyidik. A controller served with a demand issued in a penyelidikan therefore has a textual basis to refuse.

The framing also moves from pemeriksaan to penanganan of a personal data protection offence, which covers the case as a whole rather than the examination stage.

What to do about it

Check the stage of the case because a penyelidik demand has no basis under Pasal 155.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Article 23

GDPR Article 23(1) lets Union or Member State law restrict the rights in Articles 12 to 22 and Article 34, and the Article 5 principles so far as they correspond, but only by a legislative measure that respects the essence of the right and is necessary and proportionate in a democratic society, and only for one of ten listed objectives.

Against Indonesia. GDPR Article 23 assumes two instruments: the Regulation, and a later national law that does the restricting under the GDPR Article 23(2) checklist. Also compared at UU Pasal 50.

RPP Pasal 130

(2)
Dalam menerapkan langkah sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1), Peng endali Data Pribadi harus mempertimbangkan teknologi, biaya implementasi, sifat, ruang lingkup, konteks dan tujuan pemrosesan serta risiko yang ditimbulkan oleh pemrosesan.
(3)
Pengendali Data Pribadi wajib menerapkan langkah organisasi dan teknis untuk memastikan bahwa secara default Data Pribadi yang diproses terbatas hanya pada data yang diperlukan untuk tujuan pemrosesan.
(4)
Pengendali Data Pribadi wajib melakukan evaluasi risiko dan mengimplementasikan tindakan pencegahan yang diperlukan untuk melindungi Data Pribadi dalam melaksanakan kewajiban sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1) dan ayat (3).
Enacted · PP 33/2026
PP Pasal 124
PP Pasal 124
(1)
Penyusunan dan penerapan langkah teknis operasional untuk melindungi Data Pribadi sebagaimana dimaksud dalam Pasal 123 ayat (1) huruf a dimulai dari tahapan perencanaan sistem pemrosesan Data Pribadi sampai dengan penyelenggaraan pemrosesan Data Pribadi.
(2)
Dalam melaksanakan penyusunan dan penerapan langkah sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1), Pengendali Data Pribadi harus:
  1. a.
    mempertimbangkan teknologi, biaya implementasi, sifat, ruang lingkup, konteks, dan tujuan pemrosesan Data Pribadi serta risiko yang ditimbulkan oleh pemrosesan Data Pribadi;
  2. b.
    memastikan secara baku (default) Data Pribadi yang diproses terbatas hanya pada Data Pribadi yang diperlukan untuk tujuan pemrosesan Data Pribadi; dan
  3. c.
    melakukan evaluasi risiko dan tindakan pencegahan yang diperlukan untuk melindungi Data Pribadi secara berkala dan konsisten.
What changed

RPP Pasal 130(3) stated privacy by default as its own wajib, a free standing duty to implement organisational and technical measures ensuring default minimisation. PP 33/2026 Pasal 124(2)(b) restates the same requirement as one of three things a controller harus do when preparing the technical operational measures required by Pasal 123(1)(a).

Analysis

Default minimisation survives in substance and changes its enforcement route. Pasal 124(2)(b) still requires the controller to ensure by default that the data processed is limited to what the purpose needs, but it now hangs off Pasal 123(1)(a), and it is Pasal 123 ayat (1), not Pasal 124, that appears in the administrative sanction list at Pasal 184(1).

Pasal 124(1) extends the design window, running the measures dari tahapan perencanaan rather than the draft's tahap pengembangan, and huruf c requires risk evaluation and preventive action secara berkala dan konsisten. The draft was no better placed on enforcement, since RPP Pasal 130 was itself absent from the draft sanction list at Pasal 213(1), so the shift is one of drafting position rather than of whether the duty exists.

What to do about it

Evidence default minimisation inside the Pasal 123 security file, because that is the provision the sanction list reaches.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Article 32

The provision. GDPR Article 32(1) requires the controller and the processor to implement technical and organisational measures appropriate to the risk, judged against the state of the art, the cost of implementation, and the nature, scope, context and purposes of the processing.

Against Indonesia. Both texts calibrate security to risk and UU Pasal 35 huruf b does the work of GDPR Article 32(2), but the calibration inputs and the addressee both differ.

Compared at UU Pasal 35, where the full comparison sits.

Enacted · PP 33/2026
PP Pasal 138
PP Pasal 138
(1)
Pengendali Data Pribadi wajib bertanggung jawab atas pemrosesan Data Pribadi dan menunjukkan pertanggungjawaban dalam pemenuhan kewajiban pelaksanaan prinsip Pelindungan Data Pribadi.
(2)
Dalam melaksanakan pertanggungjawaban sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1), Pengendali Data Pribadi paling sedikit harus:
  1. a.
    menetapkan dan menerapkan langkah teknis dan organisasi yang sesuai untuk memenuhi persyaratan akuntabilitas atau pertanggungjawaban;
  2. b.
    mendokumentasikan seluruh kegiatan pemrosesan Data Pribadi;
  3. c.
    merespons permintaan Informasi dari Lembaga;
  4. d.
    menunjukkan pemenuhan kepatuhan dan bukti dokumentasi seluruh kegiatan pemrosesan Data Pribadi; dan
  5. e.
    melakukan audit Pelindungan Data Pribadi secara internal dan eksternal.
What changed

RPP Pasal 154(3) said a controller dapat conduct an internal or external protection audit. PP 33/2026 Pasal 138(2)(e) lists internal and external audit among the things a controller paling sedikit harus do, and Pasal 138(2)(a) adds appropriate technical and organisational measures for accountability.

Analysis

The draft made auditing a permission; the enacted text makes it a floor. RPP Pasal 154(3) used dapat and kept audit outside the accountability list, whereas PP 33/2026 Pasal 138(2) folds it into a five-item minimum introduced by paling sedikit harus and joins internal and external with dan rather than the draft's maupun.

Every controller therefore owes both an internal and an external audit, with no threshold by size, sector or risk. Audit budget and report retention become a standing compliance line rather than a discretionary one.

What to do about it

Schedule both an internal and an external protection audit and retain the reports as accountability evidence.

Where Europe stands ported from the GDPR GDPR Articles 5, 24, 30

The provision. GDPR Article 5(2) makes the controller responsible for the Article 5(1) principles and requires it to be able to demonstrate compliance with them, a pairing the Regulation itself names accountability.

Against Indonesia. Pasal 47 pairs responsibility with the ability to show it, in the same order as Article 5(2).

Compared at UU Pasal 47, where the full comparison sits.

Penyusunan dan penerapan langkah teknis operasional untuk melindungi Data Pribadi dari gangguan pemrosesan Data Pribadi sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1) huruf a dilakukan berdasarkan tingkat keamanan yang telah ditentukan oleh Pengendali Data Pribadi.
(5)
Pengendali Data Pribadi melakukan penilaian kesesuaian antara penyusunan dan penerapan langkah teknis operasional sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1) huruf a.
(6)
Penyusunan dan penerapan langkah penentuan tingkat keamanan dilaksanakan sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan.
(7)
Lembaga menyusun langkah teknis operasional serta penentuan tingkat keamanan berdasarkan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan.
What changed

RPP Pasal 131(2)(a) required pseudonymisation and encryption together. PP 33/2026 Pasal 123(2)(a) makes them alternatives to each other and to any other technical measure capable of preventing or mitigating the risk of a protection failure.

Analysis

The change sits inside one limb of a list that was already disjunctive. RPP Pasal 131(2) joined its four items with dan/atau, so a controller could always satisfy the provision through item (b), (c) or (d) without deploying cryptography. What item (a) did was fix the content of the cryptographic route by coupling pseudonimisasi and enkripsi with dan.

PP 33/2026 Pasal 123(2)(a) unbundles that pair and adds an open ended third limb, langkah teknis lainnya yang mampu mencegah atau melindungi risiko terjadinya Kegagalan Pelindungan Data Pribadi, so the one place in the chapter that named a specific control now names none. Pasal 123(5) removes the wajib from the conformity assessment that would have tested the choice, which leaves the adequacy of the measure resting on the controller's own judgement.

What to do about it

Document why the chosen technical measure meets Pasal 123(2)(a) if encryption is not deployed.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Article 32

The provision. GDPR Article 32(1) requires the controller and the processor to implement technical and organisational measures appropriate to the risk, judged against the state of the art, the cost of implementation, and the nature, scope, context and purposes of the processing.

Against Indonesia. Both texts calibrate security to risk and UU Pasal 35 huruf b does the work of GDPR Article 32(2), but the calibration inputs and the addressee both differ.

Compared at UU Pasal 35, where the full comparison sits.

What changed

RPP Pasal 87(8) placed a wajib on the controller alone to hand over processing records when the authority asked. PP 33/2026 Pasal 74(9) recasts the same duty as harus and extends it to the processor, while Pasal 74(10) adds a further duty on both to make the records available for audit and supervision.

Analysis

The duty spread across both parties as its deontic marker weakened. PP 33/2026 Pasal 74(9) substitutes harus for wajib and adds dan/atau Prosesor Data Pribadi, so the authority may now demand records directly from a processor rather than only through its controller. Pasal 74(10) is new and converts the obligation from responsive to standing, since records must be available whenever audit or supervision requires them rather than only on request.

Whether harus carries the same sanction exposure as wajib under UU PDP Pasal 57 is unresolved, which makes the extension of the duty the more reliable half of the change.

What to do about it

Hold processing records in a produce-on-demand state and put the same obligation into processor contracts.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Article 30

The provision. GDPR Article 30 requires a written register, not a log.

Against Indonesia. Two differences run here, and the exemption is only the visible one.

What changed

RPP Pasal 173(d) required the party invoking the law enforcement exception before a controller to be a law enforcement officer authorised to execute the statute. PP 33/2026 Pasal 151 carries four criteria and no requester-identity limb.

Analysis

The draft made the identity of the requester a condition of the exception; the enacted text makes it irrelevant. RPP Pasal 173(d) sat between the balancing test and the safeguards limb, whereas PP 33/2026 Pasal 151 runs from necessity through balancing straight to safeguards. The same deletion appears at Pasal 152 for the public interest ground and Pasal 153 for financial supervision, so it is systematic rather than an oversight.

A controller assessing an exception request has lost the one criterion that told it who was entitled to make one.

What to do about it

Verify statutory authority yourself because Pasal 151 no longer requires the requester to hold it.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Article 23

Against Indonesia. GDPR Article 23 assumes two instruments: the Regulation, and a later national law that does the restricting under the GDPR Article 23(2) checklist. Also compared at UU Pasal 50.

PP Pasal 122

What changed

RPP Pasal 129 joined its two consultation grounds with dan, so both had to be satisfied. PP 33/2026 Pasal 122(1) joins them with dan/atau, so either suffices, and recasts limb b from the absence of technical and organisational policy to the absence of langkah teknis operasional.

Analysis

Access to the authority widened by one conjunction. Under RPP Pasal 129 a controller could consult only where the processing caused loss and no mitigating measures existed, whereas PP 33/2026 Pasal 122(1) permits consultation on either ground alone. The verb remains dapat in both instruments, so neither creates the prior consultation duty that a high-risk processing regime would ordinarily carry, and the Lembaga retains no stated obligation to respond.

Pasal 122(2) then sends the remaining detail of the impact assessment regime to a Peraturan Lembaga, which is where any consultation procedure will actually be built.

Consultation is available on either ground now but remains optional and unanswered; do not plan around it.

Analysis

The draft gave camera operators an express route to release footage; the enacted text withdraws it. RPP Article 36 was permissive and open-ended, the phrase tetapi tidak terbatas pada extending it beyond the three named purposes, and nothing in PP 33/2026 replaces it. Article 17(2) operates one step earlier, exempting law enforcement contexts from the signage and non-identification limbs of Article 17(1), which concern installation rather than release.

Any disclosure of footage must now be justified under the processing bases in Article 30(3) and the Chapter IV exemptions, which is a higher evidential burden per request than the draft imposed.

Rebuild footage disclosure procedures on Article 30(3) bases with a documented legal basis recorded for each request.

PP Pasal 59

(2)

  1. a.
    hubungan antara Data Pribadi yang diproses dan tujuan pemrosesan Data Pribadi;
  2. b.

  3. c.

What changed

RPP Pasal 74(2) stated minimisation as an open standard, processing seminimal mungkin while remaining relevant and adequate to the purpose. PP 33/2026 Pasal 59(2) replaces it with three named factors: the relationship between the data and the purpose, the sufficiency of the data for the purpose, and that the data not exceed what is needed.

Analysis

The compliance test changed from a superlative to a structure. RPP Pasal 74(2) asked whether processing was as minimal as possible, which is unfalsifiable in practice, while PP 33/2026 Pasal 59(2) asks three answerable questions that map onto relevance, adequacy and necessity.

Pasal 58 also merges the draft's separate duties into one, requiring processing to be terbatas dan spesifik, sah secara hukum, dan transparan in a single wajib, with Pasal 59 and Pasal 60 supplying the definitions of the first and third limbs. The rewrite gives a controller something to document against and gives the Lembaga three specific questions at inspection.

What to do about it

Record the three Pasal 59(2) factors for each data field rather than asserting minimisation.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Article 5

The provision. GDPR Article 5(1) sets six processing principles: lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; and integrity and confidentiality.

Against Indonesia. UU Pasal 3 is an asas provision in the Indonesian drafting tradition, addressed to how the statute is read; GDPR Article 5 is addressed to the controller and enforced on its own, in the higher fine tier under GDPR Article 83(5)(a). Also compared at UU Pasal 16, UU Pasal 27.

(1)
Prosesor Data Pribadi harus bertanggung jawab atas pemrosesan Data Pribadi dan menunjukkan pertanggungjawaban dalam pemenuhan kewajiban sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan.

  4. d.

What changed

RPP Pasal 163 stated that the processor wajib bertanggung jawab and show accountability under the prevailing legislation, with no itemised content. PP 33/2026 Pasal 141(1) uses harus and Pasal 141(2) adds a four-item minimum covering documentation, responding to the Lembaga, demonstrating compliance and conducting an audit.

Analysis

The draft asserted processor accountability; the enacted text operationalises it while softening the verb. PP 33/2026 Pasal 141(2) gives the processor its own documentation, response and audit duties, mirroring the controller list at Pasal 138(2) but stopping at melakukan audit without specifying internal and external and without the technical and organisational measures limb.

The verb moves from wajib to harus, yet neither instrument attaches administrative sanctions to the article, since RPP Pasal 213(1) omitted Pasal 163 and PP 33/2026 Pasal 184(1) omits Pasal 141, so the four items sit outside the sanction list in both. The duty to respond to information requests from the Lembaga is new for processors, the draft binding them only to carry out the authority's orders under RPP Pasal 164.

What to do about it

Have processors document and audit to the Pasal 141(2) list because those four items are what the Lembaga will request.

Where Europe stands ported from the GDPR GDPR Articles 5, 24, 30

The provision. GDPR Article 5(2) makes the controller responsible for the Article 5(1) principles and requires it to be able to demonstrate compliance with them, a pairing the Regulation itself names accountability.

Against Indonesia. Pasal 47 pairs responsibility with the ability to show it, in the same order as Article 5(2). Also compared at UU Pasal 52.

  5. e.

  6. f.

  10. j.

What changed

RPP Pasal 101 carried four things: the definition of masa retensi at ayat (1), the rule at ayat (2) that a period resting on a legal obligation is set by legislation, the bar at ayat (3) on using data held on that footing for other purposes, and the retention policy document at ayat (4) and ayat (5) with nine minimum contents. PP 33/2026 splits them.

The definition sits at PP Pasal 1 angka 23, differing from the draft only in reading adalah for merupakan. The document sits at PP Pasal 75, without the harus of RPP Pasal 101 ayat (4), and with a tenth item at huruf j requiring dasar hukum pengaturan where the Masa Retensi arises from a legal obligation.

Analysis

The retention period definition was not dropped. PP Pasal 1 angka 23 repeats RPP Pasal 101 ayat (1) almost word for word, adalah for merupakan, so the term is now defined once for the whole regulation instead of inside the retention article, and it reaches every provision that uses it.

What has no counterpart in PP Pasal 75 is RPP Pasal 101 ayat (2) and ayat (3), the rule that retention on a legal obligation is set by legislation and the bar on using data held on that footing for other purposes.

Huruf j picks up part of ayat (2), but as a content item of the policy document rather than a rule of law, and it applies only jika Masa Retensi karena kewajiban hukum. A period justified by pencapaian tujuan pemrosesan alone sits outside huruf j, so the item bites on statutory retention and nothing else.

Two other content items shifted: huruf d now covers jenis dan komponen rather than komponen alone, and huruf e confines deidentifikasi to kepentingan statistik dan penelitian ilmiah, adding the qualifier ilmiah absent from the draft. PP Pasal 75 ayat (1) states the duty in the indicative where the draft used harus.

What to do about it

Read the definition from PP Pasal 1 angka 23, and add a legal basis column to the retention schedule for every period that rests on a statutory obligation, since huruf j reaches those and no others.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Article 30

The provision. GDPR Article 30 requires a written register, not a log.

Against Indonesia. Two differences run here, and the exemption is only the visible one.

Compared at UU Pasal 31, where the full comparison sits.

PP Pasal 15
(1)

(2)

(3)
Prosesor Data Pribadi sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1) harus memastikan Prosesor Data Pribadi lain yang dilibatkan melakukan pemrosesan Data Pribadi sesuai dengan ketentuan dalam Peraturan Pemerintah ini.
(4)

(5)

What changed

The draft obliged a processor with wajib to ensure that any further processor it involves complies with the Regulation. The enacted Article 15(3) states the same duty with harus, while the written consent requirement at Article 15(2) keeps wajib.

Analysis

The duty on a processor to police its sub-processor is downgraded in register. Indonesian legislative drafting separates wajib, which marks an obligation, from harus, which marks a directive, and PP 33/2026 Article 15 now uses both within a single article, wajib for the written consent in paragraph (2) and harus for the assurance duty in paragraph (3).

Article 15(2) appears in the sanctions list at Article 184(1); Article 15(3) does not, as RPP Article 22(3) did not appear in RPP Article 213(1). Assurance over sub-processors therefore rests on the contractual route in Article 15(4) and on the controller's residual liability under Article 15(5) rather than on the duty itself.

What to do about it

Push sub-processor assurance into the processing agreement because Article 15(3) alone will not carry it.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Article 28

The provision. GDPR Article 28(1) lets a controller use only processors that provide sufficient guarantees of appropriate technical and organisational measures.

Against Indonesia. UU Pasal 51 reaches the same allocation of responsibility, then parts company with Article 28 on two mechanisms.

PP Pasal 92
(1)
Pengendali Data Pribadi wajib menghentikan pemrosesan Data Pribadi dalam hal Subjek Data Pribadi menarik kembali persetujuan pemrosesan Data Pribadi.
(2)
Penghentian pemrosesan Data Pribadi sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1) dilakukan paling lambat 3 x 24 (tiga kali dua puluh empat) jam terhitung sejak Pengendali Data Pribadi menerima permintaan penarikan kembali persetujuan pemrosesan Data Pribadi.
(3)

(4)

What changed

Draft Pasal 104(2) excused a controller from stopping processing after a withdrawal of consent if it could show another lawful basis applied. Enacted Pasal 92 contains no such exception and instead adds a verification step and a duty to confirm cessation.

Analysis

The draft's carve-out let a controller answer a withdrawal by re-characterising the processing as contractual necessity or legitimate interests and carrying on. Enacted Pasal 92(1) keeps the obligation to stop, deletes the exception, gates it on verification at Pasal 92(3) and requires the controller to tell the subject that processing has stopped at Pasal 92(4).

Basis switching after a withdrawal therefore has no textual footing, which sits consistently with Pasal 36(2) treating consent evidence as an accountability record and with Pasal 30(2) requiring the basis to be settled before processing begins. A controller relying on consent must choose its basis at the outset rather than after the subject moves.

What to do about it

Fix and record the lawful basis at the point of collection, since you cannot swap out of consent once it is withdrawn.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Article 7

The provision. GDPR Article 7(3) gives the data subject the right to withdraw consent at any time.

Against Indonesia. Under GDPR Article 7(3) withdrawal is a unilateral act: the moment it is made the GDPR Article 6(1)(a) basis falls away, and further processing has no lawful ground unless the controller can stand on another GDPR Article 6(1) basis, which is why GDPR Article 17(1)(b) conditions erasure on there being no other legal ground. Also compared at UU Pasal 40.

Compared at UU Pasal 9, where the full comparison sits.

What changed

The draft imposed a wajib duty to take steps to identify service users and expressly extended it to services directed at children or capable of being accessed by children. PP 33/2026 Pasal 38(1) states a harus duty calibrated to the purpose of processing and deletes the child directed and child accessible trigger.

Analysis

The deleted phrase was the age assurance hook, mirroring the trigger used in the UK Age Appropriate Design Code, and it captured general audience platforms that children reach in practice. Calibrating the duty to the purpose of processing instead lets a controller argue that its purpose does not concern children and therefore requires no identification step, which is circular where the risk arises precisely from unintended child users.

The parental consent duty in Pasal 38(2) keeps wajib, so the substantive obligation survives while the mechanism for knowing when it bites has been weakened.

What to do about it

Keep age assurance on any service children can reach; Pasal 38(1) no longer compels it but Pasal 38(2) still applies.

Where Europe stands ported from the GDPR GDPR Articles 5, 6

The provision. GDPR Article 6(1) makes processing lawful only where one of six bases applies: consent, necessity for a contract or for pre-contractual steps, a legal obligation, vital interests, a task in the public interest or official authority, and legitimate interests.

Against Indonesia. UU Pasal 20 ayat (2) huruf a to f is the six limb list of GDPR Article 6(1)(a) to (f) in the same order, and the transposition shows in the detail. Also compared at UU Pasal 25.

Compared at UU Pasal 20, where the full comparison sits.

Commercial benefit no longer bars the public interest basis

deletedchanges an obligation

RPP Pasal 65
RPP Pasal 65

Pengendali Data Pribadi tidak dapat menggunakan kepentingan umum atau pelayanan publik sebagai dasar pemrosesan Data Pribadi jika pemrosesan dilakukan untuk tujuan pemrosesan yang memiliki dampak atau keuntungan komersil bagi Pengendali Data Pribadi.

Enacted · PP 33/2026
no counterpart

The enacted text carries nothing in its place.

What changed

The draft prohibited use of the public interest or public service basis where the processing carried a commercial impact or benefit for the controller. PP 33/2026 contains no equivalent prohibition anywhere in the lawful bases part.

Analysis

Pasal 65 of the draft was the anti arbitrage rule that stopped a commercially motivated activity being dressed as public service, and it mattered most for state owned enterprises and licensed operators delivering public services on commercial terms. Its removal means the only remaining filter is Pasal 49(2), which asks whether legislation mandates the action, not who profits from it. Mixed motive processing by a concessionaire now passes the enacted test that the draft would have failed.

What to do about it

Commercial upside no longer defeats the public task basis but it should still be disclosed in the Pasal 50 policy document.

Where Europe stands

This finding cites no article of the enacted text, so there is no implementing provision to carry a comparison. The subject is treated in the reading pages.
