Lawful bases and consent

Consent must now be free conscious specific and unambiguous

newchanges an obligation
Draft · 31 August 2023
no counterpart

The draft had no such provision.

Enacted · PP 33/2026
PP Pasal 32
PP Pasal 32
(1)
Pengendali Data Pribadi dapat menggunakan dasar pemrosesan Data Pribadi berupa persetujuan yang sah secara eksplisit.
(2)
Persetujuan yang sah secara eksplisit sebagaimana dimaksud dalam Pasal 30 ayat (3) huruf a harus didapatkan dari Subjek Data Pribadi secara bebas, sadar, spesifik, dan tidak ambigu.
What changed

The draft barred deceptive consent requests and the conditioning of goods or services on consent but never stated what qualities valid consent must have. PP 33/2026 Pasal 32(2) adds a four part test requiring consent to be obtained freely, consciously, specifically and unambiguously.

Analysis

The draft regulated the mechanism, the prior information and the proof of consent but never stated what makes the consent itself valid. Pasal 32(2) supplies that test, so a flow that satisfies the mechanism rules in Pasal 34 can still fail because consent was bundled across purposes or inferred from a pre-ticked box.

The draft's own quality controls were narrower and both survive, since RPP Pasal 49(1) barred any reduction in goods or services where consent was refused, now Pasal 35(1), and RPP Pasal 49(5) barred deceptive or misleading requests, now Pasal 35(3). Read with the proof duty in Pasal 36(1) and its accountability framing in Pasal 36(2), the controller must evidence not only that consent was given but that each of the four qualities was present.

What to do about it

Re-test every consent flow against the four qualities and record which design feature evidences each one.

Where Europe stands ported from the GDPR GDPR Articles 5, 6

The provision. GDPR Article 6(1) makes processing lawful only where one of six bases applies: consent, necessity for a contract or for pre-contractual steps, a legal obligation, vital interests, a task in the public interest or official authority, and legitimate interests.

Against Indonesia. UU Pasal 20 ayat (2) huruf a to f is the six limb list of GDPR Article 6(1)(a) to (f) in the same order, and the transposition shows in the detail. Also compared at UU Pasal 21.

(1)
Pengendali Data Pribadi dapat menggunakan dasar pemrosesan Data Pribadi berupa pemenuhan kewajiban hukum dari Pengendali Data sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan.
(2)
Pemenuhan kewajiban hukum sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1) termasuk:
  1. a.
    perintah dan/atau putusan pengadilan; atau
  2. b.
    perintah keputusan pejabat tata usaha negara yang ditetapkan berdasarkan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan.
What changed

The draft closed the legal obligation basis with an exhaustive dilaksanakan dalam hal list of three sources anchored to the statutory hierarchy. PP 33/2026 Pasal 45(2) opens it with termasuk, keeps two sources and deletes both the hierarchy limb and the draft Pasal 59(3) rule that the obligation need not affect the public interest.

Analysis

Replacing an exhaustive formula with termasuk converts the enumeration into examples, so the two named sources no longer exhaust what can ground the basis. The hierarchy limb is gone from the list, but Pasal 45(1) still requires the obligation to arise sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan, and Pasal 45(2)(b) now requires the administrative decision itself to be established on that footing, so the anchor to legislation survives outside the list.

The clear loss is draft Pasal 59(3), which confirmed that the basis was available for an obligation serving only the subject or the controller with no public interest dimension, and no enacted provision replaces it.

What to do about it

Treat the Pasal 45(2) list as illustrative but record the instrument, its footing in legislation and the specific duty it imposes.

Where Europe stands ported from the GDPR GDPR Articles 5, 6

The provision. GDPR Article 6(1) makes processing lawful only where one of six bases applies: consent, necessity for a contract or for pre-contractual steps, a legal obligation, vital interests, a task in the public interest or official authority, and legitimate interests.

Against Indonesia. UU Pasal 20 ayat (2) huruf a to f is the six limb list of GDPR Article 6(1)(a) to (f) in the same order, and the transposition shows in the detail.

Compared at UU Pasal 20, where the full comparison sits.

PP Pasal 67
(1)

(2)

  1. a.

  2. b.

What changed

The draft declared a non compliant contract void by operation of law. PP 33/2026 Pasal 43(2) instead disqualifies the contract as a lawful basis while leaving the contract itself intact.

Analysis

The phrase batal demi hukum appears nowhere in the enacted text, which removes a private law consequence that a data protection regulation was poorly placed to impose in the first place. The replacement is confined to data protection effect: the commercial bargain survives and only the processing loses its ground, which converts a contract drafting defect into an unlawful processing exposure under the administrative sanction regime.

The trigger also broadens, because Pasal 43(2) attaches to failure on any of the nine content requirements rather than to the single consent limb.

What to do about it

Audit contracts against all nine items in Pasal 43(1); any gap invalidates the basis rather than the agreement.

Against Indonesia. UU Pasal 20 ayat (2) huruf a to f is the six limb list of GDPR Article 6(1)(a) to (f) in the same order, and the transposition shows in the detail. Also compared at UU Pasal 28.

Enacted · PP 33/2026
no counterpart

The enacted text carries nothing in its place.

What changed

The draft obliged the controller to stop legitimate interest processing when the subject objected. PP 33/2026 carries no counterpart; the objection right in Pasal 93 is confined to decisions based solely on automated processing including profiling.

Analysis

The draft paired a self assessed basis with a subject held stop switch, which is the structural safeguard that makes legitimate interests tolerable in the GDPR Article 21 model. The enacted text keeps the basis and removes the switch, leaving only withdrawal of consent in Pasal 92, which by definition does not reach processing grounded on legitimate interests.

Combined with the public body extension in Pasal 55, the result is a self certified basis with no subject initiated exit and no time limit.

What to do about it

Do not promise an objection based stop for legitimate interests; the regulation no longer supplies one.

Where Europe stands

This finding cites no article of the enacted text, so there is no implementing provision to carry a comparison. The subject is treated in the reading pages.

What changed

A flat prohibition on public bodies relying on legitimate interest became a permission, bounded by Pasal 55(2) to purposes outside the public task.

Analysis

RPP Pasal 72 closed legitimate interest to public bodies outright. PP Pasal 55(1) opens it, and Pasal 55(2) confines it to purposes other than performing a public-interest task, public service or the exercise of public authority. GDPR Article 6(1)(f) runs the other way, excluding public authorities acting in the performance of their tasks, so Indonesia now permits the basis in the narrow space the GDPR leaves and the draft had sealed.

What to do about it

For a public body the question is no longer whether legitimate interest is available, but whether the purpose sits outside its public task.

(2)

What changed

The draft required every public body to adopt an internal processing instrument with seven mandatory contents, to publish it for download and to file it with the authority. PP 33/2026 Pasal 50 requires an adequate policy document with two mandatory contents and no publication or filing duty, and it attaches that document to any controller relying on the public task basis under Pasal 49 rather than to Badan Publik as such.

Analysis

The draft package in Pasal 67 was the accountability spine for state processing: it named the data protection officer, disclosed processors, recorded risk and mitigation, and carried a mandatory clause requiring a court determination where processing affected human rights. All of that content disappears, and with it the two transparency duties that made the instrument checkable, easy public download and filing with the authority at the first opportunity.

What survives at Pasal 50(2) is an internal document of two headings, the scope of the task and the purpose of processing, whose preparation is left to a Peraturan Lembaga under Pasal 50(3) that does not yet exist. The addressee moves as well, because Pasal 50(1) binds any controller acting on the Pasal 49 basis, which brings private bodies exercising a statutory task inside a rule the draft aimed at public bodies alone.

What to do about it

Public bodies should keep the draft's seven headings as internal good practice; nothing in the enacted text compels disclosure.

What changed

A duty to document and convey the balancing assessment to the subject became a duty only to document it, disclosed on request under Pasal 56.

Analysis

Under RPP Pasal 71 the controller had to hand the analysis to the subject as a matter of course. PP Pasal 54 requires only that it be documented, and Pasal 56 makes disclosure contingent on the subject asking for an explanation. The burden shifts from a controller who must tell to a subject who must know to ask, which in practice means the assessment is now read by regulators and litigants rather than by the people it concerns.

What to do about it

Write the balancing assessment for an outside reader. It stays private until the moment it does not.

What changed

The draft allowed the public task basis on either of two limbs, a statutory mandate or a directly threatened public interest, joined by dan/atau. PP 33/2026 Pasal 49(2) retains only the statutory mandate limb.

Analysis

The enacted basis is now purely derivative, existing only where legislation commands the controller to act, which makes the mandate instrument the operative source and the regulation a pointer to it. Emergency style processing that the draft would have grounded on a directly threatened public interest must now find either a statute or the vital interests basis in Pasal 46, whose own conditions were cut from the three in RPP Pasal 61 to two.

The statutory mandate condition also now reaches the exercise of authority limb that the draft left unconditioned, since RPP Pasal 64 applied only to kepentingan umum and pelayanan publik while Pasal 49(2) governs all three limbs of ayat (1). How the basis operates in practice is left to a Peraturan Lembaga under Pasal 52.

What to do about it

Cite the specific legislative provision that commands the action; a general public interest rationale no longer qualifies.

What changed

The draft imposed a wajib duty to notify the subject and the subject's parent or guardian after vital interest processing had taken place. PP 33/2026 Pasal 47(1) states the duty in the bare indicative, drops the parent and guardian addressees and fixes no time.

Analysis

The deontic downgrade matters because the administrative sanction regime attaches most cleanly to wajib obligations, so the notice becomes hard to enforce as a discrete breach. Losing the parent and guardian addressees is the sharper practical loss, since vital interest processing frequently concerns an incapacitated or minor subject who cannot receive the notice personally.

The general information duty at PP 33/2026 Pasal 62(1) is still wajib and Pasal 62(2) applies it to every processing basis, but Pasal 62(4) requires that information before processing begins, so it does not substitute for an after the fact notice. Nothing in the enacted text now fixes when the Pasal 47 information must reach the subject.

What to do about it

Notify guardians and set your own deadline for the Pasal 47 notice, because the regulation fixes none.

Where Europe stands ported from the GDPR GDPR Articles 5, 6

The provision. GDPR Article 6(1) makes processing lawful only where one of six bases applies: consent, necessity for a contract or for pre-contractual steps, a legal obligation, vital interests, a task in the public interest or official authority, and legitimate interests.

Against Indonesia. UU Pasal 20 ayat (2) huruf a to f is the six limb list of GDPR Article 6(1)(a) to (f) in the same order, and the transposition shows in the detail.

Compared at UU Pasal 20, where the full comparison sits.

  1. a.

What changed

The draft imposed three cumulative conditions on the vital interests basis, including a low likelihood that the subject would refuse. PP 33/2026 Pasal 46 keeps two and widens the protected class from pihak ketiga lainnya to pihak lainnya.

Analysis

Dropping the third condition removes the only element that asked the controller to predict the subject's own position, which was the draft's proxy for the counterfactual consent test. Replacing third parties with any other party removes the requirement that the endangered person be external to the processing relationship, so a threat to the controller's own interests can now support the basis. Both moves make the basis easier to invoke at precisely the point where the subject cannot be consulted.

What to do about it

Record the threat and the reason consent could not be obtained; likelihood of refusal is no longer a condition to assess.

Consent mechanics downgraded from wajib to harus

(2)

Enacted · PP 33/2026
PP Pasal 31, 34, 37
PP Pasal 31

Pengendali Data Pribadi harus memastikan pemrosesan Data Pribadi tidak bersifat diskriminatif kepada Subjek Data Pribadi.

PP Pasal 34
(1)
Pengendali Data Pribadi harus menyediakan mekanisme perolehan persetujuan Subjek Data Pribadi.
(2)
Mekanisme perolehan persetujuan sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1) dapat disediakan dalam bentuk elektronik maupun nonelektronik.
(3)
Mekanisme perolehan persetujuan sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (2) terhubung dengan Informasi sebagaimana dimaksud dalam Pasal 33.
PP Pasal 37

Pengendali Data Pribadi harus memastikan pemenuhan hak Subjek Data Pribadi untuk menarik persetujuan sewaktu-waktu melalui mekanisme yang disediakan oleh Pengendali Data Pribadi.

What changed

The draft cast the consent mechanism duty in Pasal 46(1), the withdrawal duty in Pasal 47 and the non discrimination duty in Pasal 48(2) as wajib. PP 33/2026 restates all three as harus in Pasal 34(1), Pasal 37 and Pasal 31 respectively.

Analysis

In Indonesian legislative drafting practice wajib marks an obligation whose breach attracts sanction while harus marks a norm of conduct, so the change is one of register. The administrative exposure does not move with it, because RPP Pasal 213(1) never listed Pasal 46 to Pasal 48 among the provisions carrying a sanction and PP 33/2026 Pasal 184(1) does not list Pasal 31, Pasal 34 or Pasal 37 either.

The consent duties that keep wajib are the ones the sanction list does reach, namely the information duty in Pasal 33(1), the proof duty in Pasal 36(1), the parental consent duty in Pasal 38(2) and the disability consent duty in Pasal 39(4), which shows the drafters chose deliberately rather than drifting. Withdrawal remains backed indirectly because Pasal 92(1) makes stopping processing after withdrawal a wajib duty inside that list, with a 3 x 24 hour deadline set by Pasal 92(2).

What to do about it

Rank remediation by the Pasal 184(1) sanction list rather than by the wajib label, because these three duties sit outside the list in both instruments.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Article 7

The provision. GDPR Article 7(3) gives the data subject the right to withdraw consent at any time.

Against Indonesia. Under GDPR Article 7(3) withdrawal is a unilateral act: the moment it is made the GDPR Article 6(1)(a) basis falls away, and further processing has no lawful ground unless the controller can stand on another GDPR Article 6(1) basis, which is why GDPR Article 17(1)(b) conditions erasure on there being no other legal ground. Also compared at UU Pasal 20, UU Pasal 22.

Compared at UU Pasal 9, where the full comparison sits.

  3. c.

What changed

The draft required the contract to guarantee security, resilience, integrity and confidentiality and to disclose any other lawful basis used for processing outside the contract purpose. PP 33/2026 Pasal 43(1) replaces the security guarantee with a general compliance guarantee, adds a guarantee to fulfil subject rights and a statement of rights and controller duties, and drops the other bases disclosure entirely.

Analysis

Losing item h removes the only contractual transparency device for basis stacking, which is the standard route by which service data becomes training or marketing data. The security guarantee survives only in the generalised form of Pasal 43(1)(g), so the specific commitments a counterparty could enforce are gone and the subject is left with the systemic obligations in the security chapter.

The additions at Pasal 43(1)(c) and (h) improve the rights side of the bargain but do nothing for purpose creep. The list is also load bearing in a way the draft's was not, because Pasal 43(2) provides that a contract failing to meet it cannot be used as the basis for processing at all, where draft Pasal 55(3) voided the contract only for want of explicit consent.

What to do about it

Keep an express other bases clause and specific security commitments in contracts even though Pasal 43 no longer requires them.

The provision. GDPR Article 6(1) makes processing lawful only where one of six bases applies: consent, necessity for a contract or for pre-contractual steps, a legal obligation, vital interests, a task in the public interest or official authority, and legitimate interests.

Against Indonesia. UU Pasal 20 ayat (2) huruf a to f is the six limb list of GDPR Article 6(1)(a) to (f) in the same order, and the transposition shows in the detail.

What changed

The draft required parental or guardian verification of a child's request to change data. PP 33/2026 Pasal 38(6) allows the child to make the request and makes fulfilment depend on the controller's assessment of the child's capacity to understand it, with Pasal 38(7) requiring parental consent except for rights relating to processing.

Analysis

The draft placed the gatekeeping decision with the parent; the enacted text places it with the controller, which is a transfer of a protective judgement to the party with the commercial interest in the outcome. The carve out in Pasal 38(7) for rights terkait pemrosesan Data Pribadi is undefined and potentially large, since every subject right in the regulation relates to processing.

Controllers now need a documented capacity test rather than a verification workflow, and no regulation level criteria exist to structure it.

What to do about it

Write a capacity assessment rubric for child requests and record the reasoning on each decision.

Enacted · PP 33/2026
PP Pasal 60
PP Pasal 60
(1)
Transparan sebagaimana dimaksud dalam Pasal 58 dilakukan dengan:
  1. a.
    memastikan Subjek Data Pribadi mengetahui Data Pribadi yang diproses;
  2. b.
    memastikan Subjek Data Pribadi mengetahui cara pemrosesan Data Pribadi; dan
  3. c.
    menyampaikan Informasi dan komunikasi terkait pemrosesan Data Pribadi yang mudah diakses, dipahami, dan menggunakan bahasa yang jelas.
(2)
Pemrosesan Data Pribadi secara transparan sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1) harus dilaksanakan secara jujur dan iktikad baik.
What changed

RPP Pasal 79(2) stated honest and good faith processing as a free-standing wajib on the controller. PP 33/2026 Pasal 60(2) restates it as a harus qualifying transparent processing under ayat (1) rather than processing generally.

Analysis

Good faith stopped being an independent standard and became an adverb attached to transparency. RPP Pasal 79(2) reached all processing, so a controller processing deceptively breached it whether or not the notice was accurate; PP 33/2026 Pasal 60(2) attaches jujur dan iktikad baik to the manner of transparency under Pasal 58, which narrows what the words can be used to test.

The transparency duty itself is unaffected and strengthened, since Pasal 60(1) defines it through three concrete requirements the draft did not have. What is lost is the general fairness hook that a supervisory authority reaches for when conduct is technically disclosed and substantively misleading.

What to do about it

Fairness arguments must now be framed through Pasal 60(1) transparency rather than a general good faith duty.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Articles 4, 5

The provision. GDPR Article 4(2) defines processing as any operation performed on personal data and gives an open list, running from collection and storage through disclosure to erasure, so nothing turns on whether a given activity is named.

Against Indonesia. The eight principles in UU Pasal 16 ayat (2) reach much of GDPR Article 5 by a different arrangement. Also compared at UU Pasal 27.

What changed

The draft applied the marketing disclosure duty to any processing one of whose purposes was the offering of goods or services. PP 33/2026 Pasal 35(2) applies it only where that processing rests on explicit valid consent.

Analysis

The disclosure package covers the recipients, the form of the offer and the withdrawal and complaint route, which is the practical control on data sharing for marketing. Confining it to consent based processing leaves direct marketing conducted on the legitimate interests basis under Pasal 53 with no equivalent duty, and Pasal 55 now opens that basis to public bodies as well.

The general information duty in Pasal 62 applies across all bases but does not require third party recipients or an offer specific withdrawal route.

What to do about it

Marketing run on legitimate interests escapes Pasal 35(2); disclose recipients anyway to stay defensible under Pasal 62.

    perjanjian yang akan disepakati oleh Subjek Data Pribadi dan Pengendali Data Pribadi digunakan sebagai dasar untuk melaksanakan hak dan kewajiban Subjek Data Pribadi dan Pengendali Data Pribadi.
(2)
Dalam hal perjanjian telah disepakati, perjanjian dapat digunakan sebagai dasar pemrosesan Data Pribadi sesuai dengan ketentuan sebagaimana dimaksud dalam Pasal 40 dan Pasal 41.
PP Pasal 44

Pengendali Data Pribadi tidak dapat memuat atau mencantumkan klausul perjanjian yang mengalihkan tanggung jawab kepada Subjek Data Pribadi sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan.

What changed

The draft required only that a request exist and that the parties agree they would sign a contract. PP 33/2026 Pasal 42(1)(a) requires the request to be written or recorded.

Analysis

The pre contract limb of Pasal 30(3)(b) is the basis that covers quotations, applications and onboarding, where the subject has asked for something but nothing is yet signed. Pasal 42(1)(a) imposes an evidential form on that request, which converts an oral enquiry into an insufficient trigger unless the controller captures it. The corresponding relaxation is that the draft's requirement of agreement to sign is replaced in Pasal 42(1)(b) by an intention to be bound, which is easier to satisfy.

What to do about it

Log or record inbound enquiries at the point of contact if pre contract processing will follow.

Where Europe stands ported from the GDPR GDPR Articles 5, 6

The provision. GDPR Article 6(1) makes processing lawful only where one of six bases applies: consent, necessity for a contract or for pre-contractual steps, a legal obligation, vital interests, a task in the public interest or official authority, and legitimate interests.

Against Indonesia. UU Pasal 20 ayat (2) huruf a to f is the six limb list of GDPR Article 6(1)(a) to (f) in the same order, and the transposition shows in the detail. Also compared at UU Pasal 23.

Compared at UU Pasal 20, where the full comparison sits.

What changed

The draft required notice immediately after processing had begun and carried its exception inside the same clause. PP 33/2026 Pasal 51(2) requires notice when processing starts and moves the exception to Pasal 51(3).

Analysis

The timing moves earlier, from a point after processing to the moment it commences, which brings the public task basis closer to the general rule in Pasal 62(4) that information is given before processing begins without matching it.

The exception in Pasal 51(3) is now expressed by reference to disruption of kepentingan umum or pelayanan publik rather than the draft's broader pelindungan kepentingan publik, and the deferred notice still falls due when the purpose is met. The duty itself is stated in the bare indicative in Pasal 51(1) rather than as wajib, so the enforceable hook remains Pasal 62.

What to do about it

Build public task notices into the start of processing and record any Pasal 51(3) deferral with its reason.

Controller no longer has to prove its grounds for refusal

narrowedchanges an obligation
Draft · 31 August 2023
RPP Pasal 107
RPP Pasal 107
(1)
Pengendali Data Pribadi dapat menolak keberatan apabila:
  1. a.
    dapat membuktikan tidak terjadinya dampak hukum dan/atau dampak signifikan; dan
  2. b.
    dapat membuktikan akurasi sistem yang sangat baik dan memiliki mitigasi sistem untuk menghindari dampak bagi Subjek Data Pribadi.
(2)
Penolakan keberatan oleh Pengendali Data Pribadi tidak menghilangkan hak Subjek Data Pribadi untuk menarik kembali persetujuan pemrosesan Data Pribadi yang telah diberikan sebelumnya.
Enacted · PP 33/2026
PP Pasal 95
PP Pasal 95
(1)
Pengendali Data Pribadi dapat menolak keberatan dalam hal:
  1. a.
    tidak terdapat akibat hukum dan/atau dampak signifikan pada Subjek Data Pribadi; dan
  2. b.
    Pengendali Data Pribadi memiliki akurasi sistem yang sangat baik dan sistem mitigasi untuk menghindari dampak bagi Subjek Data Pribadi.
(2)
Penolakan keberatan oleh Pengendali Data Pribadi tidak menghilangkan hak Subjek Data Pribadi untuk menarik kembali persetujuan pemrosesan Data Pribadi yang telah diberikan sebelumnya.
(3)
Pengendali Data Pribadi harus memberitahukan penolakan sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1) kepada Subjek Data Pribadi.
What changed

Draft Pasal 107(1) let a controller refuse an objection only where it dapat membuktikan the absence of impact and the accuracy of its system. Enacted Pasal 95(1) removes the proof language and states the same two limbs as facts.

Analysis

The draft placed the evidential burden on the controller, which matters because the subject cannot see inside the model. Enacted Pasal 95(1) recasts limb (a) as tidak terdapat akibat hukum dan/atau dampak signifikan and limb (b) as the controller memiliki akurasi sistem yang sangat baik dan sistem mitigasi, so the conditions are asserted rather than demonstrated.

Pasal 26 then lets the controller determine the conditions of fulfilment and refusal where RPP Pasal 27(b) had required it only to understand them, and neither provision requires the accuracy evidence to be disclosed. Pasal 95(3) requires only that the refusal be communicated. The subject is left contesting a system they cannot inspect, with the impact assessment under Pasal 120 the only document likely to record the accuracy claim.

What to do about it

Keep the accuracy and mitigation evidence in the impact assessment file, since that is where a supervisor will look for it.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Articles 21, 22

The provision. GDPR Article 22(1) says the data subject shall not be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects them.

Against Indonesia. The trigger wording in UU Pasal 10 ayat (1) tracks Article 22(1) closely, down to profiling and the legal-effect-or-significant-impact threshold, so the qualifying clause reads as a lift.

Compared at UU Pasal 10, where the full comparison sits.

(2)

Enacted · PP 33/2026
PP Pasal 78
PP Pasal 78
(1)
Berdasarkan permohonan salinan Data Pribadi sebagaimana dimaksud dalam Pasal 76 ayat (1), Pengendali Data Pribadi harus menyampaikan salinan Data Pribadi pemohon pada kesempatan pertama.
(2)
Dalam melaksanakan pemenuhan permohonan salinan sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1), Pengendali Data Pribadi juga melakukan konfirmasi serta penyampaian jangka waktu yang diperlukan dalam penyediaan salinan Data Pribadi kepada Subjek Data Pribadi paling lambat 3 x 24 (tiga kali dua puluh empat) jam sejak permohonan diterima dan terverifikasi.
(3)
Dalam hal salinan Data Pribadi yang dimohonkan tidak dapat disediakan, Pengendali Data Pribadi menyampaikan kepada pemohon disertai dengan alasannya.
What changed

Draft Pasal 90(2) ran the 3 x 24 hour confirmation clock for a copy request from permohonan diterima. Enacted Pasal 78(2) runs it from permohonan diterima dan terverifikasi.

Analysis

The draft started the clock on receipt, which made verification under RPP Pasal 42 a task the controller had to complete inside the window. Enacted Pasal 78(2) inserts dan terverifikasi, so the window opens only once the controller is satisfied of identity, and Pasal 100(2) uses the same construction for a refusal of restriction.

The other rights articles reach the same result by a second route, keeping the 3 x 24 hour clock running from receipt at Pasal 71(1), Pasal 77(1), Pasal 92(2) and Pasal 99(1) while making performance conditional on verification at Pasal 71(3), Pasal 77(2), Pasal 92(3) and Pasal 99(3). Because Pasal 25 asks only for a proportionate verification mechanism and no article caps how long it may take, the front end of every one of these deadlines is unbounded.

What to do about it

Put an internal service level on identity verification, because the regulation no longer bounds it.

Where Europe stands aligned GDPR Article 15

The provision. GDPR Article 15(1) gives the data subject confirmation of whether processing is happening, access to the data itself, and eight named items of information: purposes, categories of data, recipients or categories of recipients, retention period, the rights to rectify, erase, restrict and object, the right to lodge a complaint, the source where the data was not collected from the subject, and the existence and logic of automated decision-making.

Against Indonesia. UU Pasal 7 pairs akses with salinan, the same two-part structure as GDPR Article 15(1) and GDPR Article 15(3), but it transposes none of the content into the right itself. Also compared at UU Pasal 32.

Compared at UU Pasal 7, where the full comparison sits.

Enacted · PP 33/2026
PP Pasal 64
PP Pasal 64

Dalam hal Data Pribadi didapatkan secara tidak langsung dari Subjek Data Pribadi, Pengendali Data Pribadi melaksanakan kewajiban penyampaian Informasi sebagaimana dimaksud dalam Pasal 62 ayat (1) paling lambat 30 (tiga puluh) Hari setelah Data Pribadi dikumpulkan atau diperoleh.

What changed

Draft Pasal 77(2) required notice within 30 calendar days, written hari. Enacted Pasal 64 requires it within 30 Hari, and Pasal 1 of the enacted text defines Hari adalah hari kerja.

Analysis

The capital letter is the whole change. The draft used lower case hari and carried no definition of the term, so the ordinary calendar day reading applied. Enacted Pasal 1 introduces the defined term and Pasal 64 uses it, converting a 30 day deadline into roughly six calendar weeks once weekends and Indonesian public holidays are counted.

Pasal 64 also widens the trigger to data dikumpulkan atau diperoleh, so data received from a broker rather than collected starts the same longer clock, and the subject waits materially longer to learn that a controller holds their data at all.

What to do about it

Recalculate every indirect collection notice schedule on working days, and check any other deadline written with a capital Hari.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Articles 12, 13, 14

The provision. GDPR Article 13 requires the controller to hand over a fixed list of information at the moment data is collected from the data subject: identity and contact details, the data protection officer, purposes and legal basis, any legitimate interests relied on, recipients and transfers under GDPR Article 13(1), and then under GDPR Article 13(2) the retention period, the data subject rights, the right to complain, whether provision is statutory or contractual, and any automated decision-making.

Against Indonesia. UU Pasal 5 names four heads, identity, dasar kepentingan hukum, tujuan, and akuntabilitas of the party seeking the data.

Compared at UU Pasal 5, where the full comparison sits.

(3)

  1. a.
    akses terhadap Data Pribadi yang diproses beserta rekam jejak pemrosesan Data Pribadi sesuai dengan jangka waktu penyimpanan Data Pribadi;
  2. b.

  3. c.
    akses perubahan Data Pribadi.
(4)

  1. a.
    membahayakan keamanan, kesehatan fisik, atau kesehatan mental Subjek Data Pribadi dan/atau orang lain;
  2. b.
    berdampak pada pengungkapan Data Pribadi milik orang lain; dan/atau
  3. c.
    bertentangan dengan kepentingan pertahanan dan keamanan nasional.
What changed

RPP Pasal 83(5) obliged the controller to refuse a correction request on three closed grounds: danger to safety or physical or mental health, disclosure of another person's data, and conflict with national defence and security. PP 33/2026 Pasal 71(5) states only that the controller may refuse, with no grounds attached; the three grounds survive at Pasal 77(4) but bear on requests for access to change data rather than on correction itself.

Analysis

A closed list of compulsory refusals became an open discretion. RPP Pasal 83(5) made refusal both mandatory and exhaustively defined, so a controller refusing outside those grounds was in breach; PP 33/2026 Pasal 71(5) supplies dapat menolak with no criteria, and the only discipline left is Pasal 71(7), which requires reasons to be given in accordance with legislation.

The three grounds now sit in Pasal 77(4) attached to akses perubahan, which is a different request under a different bagian. The result is that correction, the remedy UU PDP Pasal 6 grants outright, is the one right in this chapter whose refusal is governed by no stated test.

What to do about it

Bind the refusal discretion internally to the Pasal 77(4) grounds and record reasons on every refusal.

Where Europe stands aligned GDPR Articles 16, 19

The provision. GDPR Article 16 gives the data subject the right to obtain rectification of inaccurate personal data without undue delay, and to have incomplete data completed, including by a supplementary statement, having regard to the purposes of the processing.

Against Indonesia. UU Pasal 6 reaches the same two acts as GDPR Article 16, correction of inaccuracy and completion of what is incomplete, but it does not track the article's shape: the limbs run in the reverse order, memperbarui is added as a third act, and the purpose qualifier closes the whole right where GDPR Article 16 attaches it only to the completion limb. Also compared at UU Pasal 7, UU Pasal 30, UU Pasal 32.

Compared at UU Pasal 6, where the full comparison sits.

  2. b.

Enacted · PP 33/2026
PP Pasal 106
PP Pasal 106
(1)
Permintaan ganti rugi atas pelanggaran pemrosesan Data Pribadi diajukan Subjek Data Pribadi kepada Pengendali Data Pribadi.
(2)
Dalam pengajuan permintaan ganti rugi sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1), Subjek Data Pribadi menyampaikan paling sedikit mengenai:
  1. a.
    identitas Subjek Data Pribadi;
  2. b.
    data, Informasi, dan/atau dokumen yang dijadikan bukti oleh Subjek Data Pribadi untuk mengajukan permintaan ganti rugi; dan
  3. c.
    hubungan hukum antara Subjek Data Pribadi dan Pengendali Data Pribadi terkait pemrosesan Data Pribadi.
What changed

Draft Pasal 117(a) required proof of a breach that had an impact on the subject tanpa harus membuktikan kerugian yang diderita, while Pasal 117(b) to (d) asked for supporting evidence of the amount and of the processing. Enacted Pasal 106(2) keeps only a general duty to supply the evidence relied on and the legal relationship with the controller, and says nothing about relief from proving loss.

Analysis

The draft relieved the subject of proving loss as a condition of bringing the claim at Pasal 117(a), while Pasal 117(b) still asked for evidence of the amount claimed and Pasal 119 left the valuation to the chosen forum or the judge.

Enacted Pasal 106(2) drops that relief and requires the submission to contain the subject's identity, the data, information or documents relied on as evidence, and the legal relationship with the controller, so the ordinary burden returns in full. Read with Pasal 108(1), which makes the controller the first assessor of its own liability, the whole evidential load sits with the subject before any independent eye reaches the file.

Subjects rarely hold the processing records that would prove loss, and Pasal 74 keeps those records with the controller.

What to do about it

Anchor a claim in the controller's own processing records and obtain them through an access request before claiming.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Articles 79, 82

The provision. GDPR Article 82(1) gives any person who has suffered material or non-material damage from an infringement a right to compensation from the controller or processor.

Against Indonesia. GDPR Article 82 is a self-standing cause of action and the Court has filled in its contours.

Compared at UU Pasal 12, where the full comparison sits.

PP Pasal 64

Dalam hal Data Pribadi didapatkan secara tidak langsung dari Subjek Data Pribadi, Pengendali Data Pribadi melaksanakan kewajiban penyampaian Informasi sebagaimana dimaksud dalam Pasal 62 ayat (1) paling lambat 30 (tiga puluh) Hari setelah Data Pribadi dikumpulkan atau diperoleh.

What changed

Draft Pasal 77(1) required the information to be given before personal data was collected or obtained directly from the subject. Enacted Pasal 62(4) requires it before processing, and the enacted text has no direct collection article at all.

Analysis

Collection is itself an act of processing, so the enacted wording does not in law license later notice; what it removes is the express rule for the direct case. Enacted Pasal 62(4) sets the duty to begin sebelum pemrosesan Data Pribadi, while Pasal 64 keeps the draft's thirty day deadline for data obtained indirectly, so the chapter still names the indirect case and leaves the direct one to the general rule alone.

The drafting also drops RPP Pasal 76(4), which required information both before and during processing, and replaces it with the standing availability requirement in Pasal 62(3). A controller that treats collection as a step preceding processing has room to argue for notice after the fact, and nothing in the chapter closes that reading.

What to do about it

Serve the notice at the point of collection regardless, because the enacted wording invites an argument you do not want to have with a supervisor.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Articles 12, 13, 14

The provision. GDPR Article 13 requires the controller to hand over a fixed list of information at the moment data is collected from the data subject: identity and contact details, the data protection officer, purposes and legal basis, any legitimate interests relied on, recipients and transfers under GDPR Article 13(1), and then under GDPR Article 13(2) the retention period, the data subject rights, the right to complain, whether provision is statutory or contractual, and any automated decision-making.

Against Indonesia. UU Pasal 5 names four heads, identity, dasar kepentingan hukum, tujuan, and akuntabilitas of the party seeking the data.

Compared at UU Pasal 5, where the full comparison sits.

PP Pasal 111
(1)

(2)
Subjek Data Pribadi berhak menggunakan dan mengirimkan Data Pribadi tentang dirinya ke Pengendali Data Pribadi lainnya, sepanjang sistem yang digunakan dapat saling berkomunikasi secara aman sesuai dengan prinsip Pelindungan Data Pribadi.

PP Pasal 113

Ketentuan lebih lanjut mengenai mekanisme pelaksanaan hak mendapatkan dan menggunakan portabilitas dan interoperabilitas diatur dalam Peraturan Lembaga.

What changed

Draft Pasal 122 set five criteria defining which data a portability request could reach. Enacted Pasal 113 drops them and defers the mechanism to a Peraturan Lembaga.

Analysis

The draft criteria did real work: the data had to relate to the subject, be stored and processed electronically, have been supplied by the subject, and be data processed up to the moment the request was received, with a residual power for the Lembaga to add more.

Enacted Pasal 111(3) retains only the two gating conditions of lawful basis and automated processing, so nothing defines the perimeter of the exported data set. The most consequential loss is draft Pasal 122(c), the limit to data the subject supplied, which excluded observed and inferred data and is the boundary most likely to be litigated.

Pasal 112 keeps the competition law qualifier, so the enacted text still limits how far a controller must go without saying what it must hand over.

What to do about it

Scope portability exports to subject-supplied data and document the reasoning until the Peraturan Lembaga issues.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Article 20

The provision. GDPR Article 20(1) lets the subject receive the personal data he or she provided to a controller, in a structured, commonly used and machine-readable format, and transmit it to another controller without hindrance.

Against Indonesia. The format wording in UU Pasal 13 ayat (1) is the part that tracks GDPR Article 20(1); the gates are not in the statute.

Compared at UU Pasal 13, where the full comparison sits.

  2. b.

  3. c.
    bertentangan dengan kepentingan pertahanan dan keamanan nasional.
What changed

Draft Pasal 83(5) required the controller to refuse a rectification request on three stated grounds. Enacted Pasal 71(5) provides that the controller dapat menolak, with no grounds stated at all.

Analysis

The draft's three grounds, danger to health or safety, disclosure of another person's data, and national defence and security, worked as both shield and ceiling: outside them refusal was not available. Enacted Pasal 71(5) replaces the closed list with a bare discretion and keeps only the duty in Pasal 71(7) to give reasons.

The same three grounds survive in the enacted text but only for access to change data at Pasal 77(4), so identical facts yield a mandatory refusal on the access route and an unbounded discretionary one on the rectification route.

Pasal 26 now lets the controller determine the conditions for granting or refusing a rights request, where the draft's Pasal 27 huruf b required it only to understand those conditions as fixed by legislation, so the boundary of a lawful rectification refusal sits in the controller's own policy.

What to do about it

Adopt the Pasal 77(4) grounds as your internal rectification refusal test so refusals stay defensible.

Where Europe stands aligned GDPR Articles 16, 19

The provision. GDPR Article 16 gives the data subject the right to obtain rectification of inaccurate personal data without undue delay, and to have incomplete data completed, including by a supplementary statement, having regard to the purposes of the processing.

Against Indonesia. UU Pasal 6 reaches the same two acts as GDPR Article 16, correction of inaccuracy and completion of what is incomplete, but it does not track the article's shape: the limbs run in the reverse order, memperbarui is added as a third act, and the purpose qualifier closes the whole right where GDPR Article 16 attaches it only to the completion limb. Also compared at UU Pasal 7, UU Pasal 30, UU Pasal 32.

Compared at UU Pasal 6, where the full comparison sits.

(2)

What changed

Draft Pasal 120 sent a refused or unagreed compensation claim to the Lembaga PDP to reach agreement on the form and amount. Enacted Pasal 108(3) sends it to a gugatan under the general law, and the draft's eight valuation factors in Pasal 119(2) are dropped.

Analysis

The draft supplied both a forum and a valuation apparatus: Pasal 119(2) listed the controller's economic gain from the breach, the duration and frequency, its assets and its remedial efforts among the factors fixing quantum, and Pasal 119(1) named who could apply them. None of that survives. Enacted Pasal 108 leaves the controller to assess the claim and answer it, and on refusal or deadlock the subject sues.

The Lembaga has not vanished from the system, since Pasal 201 lets a party report a dispute and Chapter X provides facilitation and mediation, but the compensation article no longer routes claims there or gives the authority any role in fixing the sum.

What to do about it

Treat the Pasal 201 reporting route as optional facilitation and budget for litigation on quantum.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Articles 79, 82

The provision. GDPR Article 82(1) gives any person who has suffered material or non-material damage from an infringement a right to compensation from the controller or processor.

Against Indonesia. GDPR Article 82 is a self-standing cause of action and the Court has filled in its contours.

PP Pasal 66

Ketentuan lebih lanjut mengenai permintaan dan penyampain Informasi diatur dalam Peraturan Lembaga.

What changed

Draft Pasal 76(2) set a 16 item minimum content list for the information given to subjects. Enacted Pasal 62 keeps only the seven subject headings of draft Pasal 76(1) and drops the list, with Pasal 66 deferring the detail to a Peraturan Lembaga.

Analysis

The draft list was the operative specification of a privacy notice: controller and processor identity, the data protection officer contact, the legal basis, the periods for use, storage and destruction, the consent and withdrawal mechanism, the access and copy mechanism, the objection mechanism and the security measures.

Enacted Pasal 62(1) retains the seven headings and Pasal 62(3) requires delivery through a sarana pemberitahuan Pelindungan Data Pribadi that stays available throughout processing, but nothing now states what the notice must say. Pasal 66 sends the content to a Peraturan Lembaga that has not issued. Until it does, compliance with Pasal 62 is testable only against seven abstract headings, which leaves a supervisor no benchmark for an inadequate notice.

What to do about it

Keep drafting notices to the draft's 16 item list until the Peraturan Lembaga promised by Pasal 66 issues.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Articles 12, 13, 14

The provision. GDPR Article 13 requires the controller to hand over a fixed list of information at the moment data is collected from the data subject: identity and contact details, the data protection officer, purposes and legal basis, any legitimate interests relied on, recipients and transfers under GDPR Article 13(1), and then under GDPR Article 13(2) the retention period, the data subject rights, the right to complain, whether provision is statutory or contractual, and any automated decision-making.

Against Indonesia. UU Pasal 5 names four heads, identity, dasar kepentingan hukum, tujuan, and akuntabilitas of the party seeking the data.

Compared at UU Pasal 5, where the full comparison sits.

What changed

RPP Pasal 76(2) prescribed a sixteen-item minimum content schedule for the information given to data subjects, running from controller identity and data protection officer contact through source, basis, types, use, storage and destruction periods, consent withdrawal mechanism, access and objection mechanisms and security measures. PP 33/2026 Pasal 62 retains only the seven headline categories in ayat (1) and carries no minimum content schedule at all.

Analysis

The draft fixed the contents of the privacy notice; the enacted text fixes only its headings. RPP Pasal 76(2) functioned as a drafting template a controller could audit itself against, whereas PP 33/2026 Pasal 62(3) substitutes a delivery standard, requiring the seven categories to sit in an accessible pemberitahuan Pelindungan Data Pribadi that remains available throughout processing.

Retention survives as a headline category at Pasal 62(1)(d), but the item level detail does not, so nothing in the enacted text now requires the notice to state when data will be destroyed, how consent is withdrawn, or how access and objection are exercised. Pasal 66 leaves that detail to a Peraturan Lembaga, so notice adequacy is judged against seven abstractions until one is issued.

What to do about it

Retain the RPP Pasal 76(2) schedule as the internal notice template; the enacted text no longer supplies one.

PP Pasal 107

Pengendali Data Pribadi harus memiliki mekanisme dan kebijakan penanganan permintaan ganti rugi.

What changed

Draft Pasal 118(5)(d) required the compensation policy to state that a claim would be answered or refused within 3 x 24 hours. Enacted Pasal 107 requires only that the controller have a mechanism and policy, and sets no deadline.

Analysis

The draft prescribed the policy in detail: a document published in Indonesian through the privacy notice under Pasal 118(4), covering the claim procedure, the types of compensation available, a statement that claims beyond what may be requested of the controller may be refused, the 3 x 24 hour answer, and the processor's data protection officer contact where a processor was involved.

Enacted Pasal 107 reduces all of it to a single sentence. Pasal 108(2) requires an answer but fixes no time for it, so the only limit on delay is whatever the controller writes for itself. A subject facing an unanswered claim has no point at which delay itself becomes a breach, and must move to the litigation route in Pasal 108(3) to get anywhere.

What to do about it

Set and publish your own answer window for compensation claims, because the regulation now sets none.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Articles 79, 82

The provision. GDPR Article 82(1) gives any person who has suffered material or non-material damage from an infringement a right to compensation from the controller or processor.

Against Indonesia. GDPR Article 82 is a self-standing cause of action and the Court has filled in its contours.

Compared at UU Pasal 12, where the full comparison sits.

What changed

Draft Pasal 95(2) made the duty to erase unlawfully obtained or processed data exercisable only berdasarkan putusan pengadilan. Enacted Pasal 82(2) supplies three alternative triggers, including an administrative sanction of erasure imposed by the Lembaga.

Analysis

Conditioning the duty on a court judgment made the draft's Pasal 95(1)(d) close to inoperable, since a subject would have to litigate to unlock an erasure the regulation already required. Enacted Pasal 82(2) breaks the condition into unlawfulness under the applicable legislation, an administrative sanction of erasure by the Lembaga, and a court judgment that has become final.

The first limb is the consequential one, because it requires no external determination: a controller that concludes its own acquisition was unlawful must erase. The third limb tightens the litigation route by requiring kekuatan hukum tetap rather than any judgment.

What to do about it

Add an unlawful acquisition test to data intake review, because a self-assessment now triggers a mandatory erasure.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Articles 17, 18, 21

The provision. GDPR Article 17(1) gives a right to erasure on six exhaustive grounds, among them that the data is no longer necessary, that consent is withdrawn with no other basis available, that the subject objects under Article 21 and no overriding legitimate grounds exist, and that processing was unlawful.

Against Indonesia. UU Pasal 8 states one right spanning three acts, mengakhiri pemrosesan, menghapus and memusnahkan, with no grounds and no exceptions on the face of the article. Also compared at UU Pasal 43.

Compared at UU Pasal 8, where the full comparison sits.

What changed

Draft Pasal 94(3) barred a subject from seeking erasure if they had previously withdrawn consent. Enacted Pasal 83 bars it only where the withdrawal has already been followed by an erasure actually carried out under Pasal 82(1)(b).

Analysis

The draft's bar attached to the act of withdrawing, so a subject who withdrew consent and then met inaction had spent the request route without receiving anything, even though RPP Pasal 95(1)(b) obliged the controller to erase on withdrawal in any event. Enacted Pasal 83 attaches the bar to performance, biting only once the controller has completed the erasure that withdrawal triggers under Pasal 82(1)(b).

The change restores the request in the common case where a controller stops processing but retains the data. It also makes the controller's own erasure record the evidence that the bar applies, which ties the point back to the recording duty in Pasal 74.

What to do about it

Log the erasure that follows a withdrawal, because that record is what defeats a later erasure request.

What changed

Draft Pasal 88(3) allowed the copy given to a subject to include the processing trail. Enacted Pasal 76(2) deletes that paragraph and rewrites the third party exclusion as a limit on what may be given.

Analysis

The draft framed the third party point descriptively at Pasal 88(2) and then extended the copy to the rekam jejak pemrosesan at Pasal 88(3). Enacted Pasal 76(2) recasts it as hanya diberikan untuk Data Pribadi yang tidak berdampak bagi pengungkapan Data Pribadi orang lain and drops the processing trail from the copy right entirely.

The trail survives on the access side at Pasal 77(3)(a), so a subject may inspect it but has no stated entitlement to receive it. That split matters, because the portable evidential form of a rights request is the copy and not the inspection, and Pasal 106(2) now makes the subject responsible for evidencing a compensation claim.

What to do about it

Expect subjects to ask for the trail under access and decide now whether you will supply it in copy form.

Where Europe stands aligned GDPR Article 15

The provision. GDPR Article 15(1) gives the data subject confirmation of whether processing is happening, access to the data itself, and eight named items of information: purposes, categories of data, recipients or categories of recipients, retention period, the rights to rectify, erase, restrict and object, the right to lodge a complaint, the source where the data was not collected from the subject, and the existence and logic of automated decision-making.

Against Indonesia. UU Pasal 7 pairs akses with salinan, the same two-part structure as GDPR Article 15(1) and GDPR Article 15(3), but it transposes none of the content into the right itself. Also compared at UU Pasal 32.

Setelah Pengendali Data Pribadi berhasil melakukan pembaruan dan/atau perbaikan Data Pribadi, Pengendali Data Pribadi harus menyampaikan Data Pribadi baru atau yang telah diperbaiki kepada pihak lain yang menerima Data Pribadi tersebut dari Pengendali Data Pribadi, termasuk Prosesor Data Pribadi yang memproses Data Pribadi tersebut.
(2)
Penyampaian Data Pribadi oleh Pengendali Data Pribadi kepada pihak lain sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1) dikecualikan dalam hal penyampaian keberhasilan dianggap tidak memungkinkan atau melibatkan upaya yang tidak seimbang dari Pengendali Data Pribadi.
Enacted · PP 33/2026
PP Pasal 72
PP Pasal 72
(1)
Dalam hal terdapat Pengendali Data Pribadi lain dan/atau Prosesor Data Pribadi, kewajiban pembaruan dan/atau perbaikan Data Pribadi sebagaimana dimaksud dalam Pasal 71 ayat (1) termasuk penyampaian pembaruan dan/atau perbaikan Data Pribadi kepada Pengendali Data Pribadi lain dan/atau Prosesor Data Pribadi.
(2)
Penyampaian Data Pribadi oleh Pengendali Data Pribadi kepada Pengendali Data Pribadi lain sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1) dikecualikan dalam hal penyampaian keberhasilan dianggap tidak memungkinkan atau melibatkan upaya yang tidak seimbang dari Pengendali Data Pribadi.
What changed

RPP Pasal 86(1) required corrected data to be pushed to any pihak lain that had received it from the controller, processors included. PP 33/2026 Pasal 72(1) confines the push to Pengendali Data Pribadi lain and Prosesor Data Pribadi, and folds it into the wajib in Pasal 71(1).

Analysis

The class of recipients contracted while the deadline tightened. RPP Pasal 86(1) reached every downstream recipient under a free standing harus, whereas PP 33/2026 Pasal 72(1) reaches only other controllers and processors and does so as part of the Pasal 71(1) obligation, which carries the 3 x 24 jam limit.

Recipients who are neither controllers nor processors of that data, such as one off disclosure targets under a statutory request, now fall outside the propagation duty. The excuse narrowed with it: Pasal 72(2) confines the impossibility and disproportionate effort exception to transmission to another controller, where RPP Pasal 86(2) covered every pihak lain. Propagation to a processor is therefore unqualified on the face of the enacted text.

What to do about it

Map recipients by role. Controllers and processors attract the 3 x 24 jam duty, and only the controller leg carries the disproportionate effort exception.

Where Europe stands aligned GDPR Articles 16, 19

The provision. GDPR Article 16 gives the data subject the right to obtain rectification of inaccurate personal data without undue delay, and to have incomplete data completed, including by a supplementary statement, having regard to the purposes of the processing.

Against Indonesia. UU Pasal 6 reaches the same two acts as GDPR Article 16, correction of inaccuracy and completion of what is incomplete, but it does not track the article's shape: the limbs run in the reverse order, memperbarui is added as a third act, and the purpose qualifier closes the whole right where GDPR Article 16 attaches it only to the completion limb. Also compared at UU Pasal 30.

Compared at UU Pasal 6, where the full comparison sits.

(2)

  1. a.

  2. b.

  3. c.

(4)

  1. a.

  2. b.
    berdampak pada pengungkapan Data Pribadi milik orang lain; dan/atau
  3. c.
    bertentangan dengan kepentingan pertahanan dan keamanan nasional.
What changed

RPP Pasal 83(1) framed the correction right as exercised through a facility provided by the controller, either self-service or by written request. PP 33/2026 Pasal 70 removes the facility and the two exercise routes, and qualifies the right by the purpose of processing.

Analysis

The draft told a controller to build something; the enacted text tells it what the right is limited by. RPP Pasal 83(1) implied an operational obligation to provide a sarana and named self-service as an acceptable route, whereas PP 33/2026 Pasal 70 is silent on how a request is made and writes sesuai dengan tujuan pemrosesan Data Pribadi into the right itself.

The draft used those same words only at Pasal 83(2), as the measure against which the controller verified a request, so the purpose test has moved from the verification step to the definition of the right. It now sits alongside the unstructured discretion at Pasal 71(5), where draft Pasal 83(5) had listed three mandatory refusal grounds, which leaves correction the right with the weakest procedural scaffolding in the chapter.

What to do about it

Provide a documented correction channel voluntarily; the enacted text no longer requires one.

Where Europe stands aligned GDPR Articles 16, 19

The provision. GDPR Article 16 gives the data subject the right to obtain rectification of inaccurate personal data without undue delay, and to have incomplete data completed, including by a supplementary statement, having regard to the purposes of the processing.

Against Indonesia. UU Pasal 6 reaches the same two acts as GDPR Article 16, correction of inaccuracy and completion of what is incomplete, but it does not track the article's shape: the limbs run in the reverse order, memperbarui is added as a third act, and the purpose qualifier closes the whole right where GDPR Article 16 attaches it only to the completion limb. PP Pasal 103
(1)

(2)

What changed

Draft Pasal 38(2) obliged a controller processing electronically to provide an electronic rights channel. Enacted Pasal 21(2) instead states that where the controller processes electronically, the request is submitted electronically.

Analysis

The draft placed the burden on the controller: electronic processing triggered a duty to build an electronic channel. Enacted Pasal 21(2) recasts the same fact pattern as a rule about how the subject submits, leaving the duty language only in Pasal 21(1), which requires a channel yang mudah diakses without tying the medium to the processing medium.

The enacted text compensates at Pasal 21(3), which requires the outcome to be communicated through the medium the subject used or another easily accessible one, a rule the draft carried only for restriction at Pasal 114(3). Controllers gain latitude on the intake and lose it on the reply.

What to do about it

Keep the electronic intake channel, and reply through the same channel the subject used.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Articles 18, 19

The provision. GDPR Article 18(1) gives a right to restriction of processing on four closed grounds: the accuracy of the data is contested, for a period enabling the controller to verify it; the processing is unlawful but the subject asks for restriction instead of erasure; the controller no longer needs the data but the subject needs them for legal claims; or a GDPR Article 21(1) objection is pending verification.

Against Indonesia. GDPR Article 18 is an interim measure in two of its four grounds, not in all four. Also compared at UU Pasal 14, UU Pasal 41.

Compared at UU Pasal 11, where the full comparison sits.

Subject rights

Exoneration ban reworded and re-scoped to the privacy notice

duty changed
Draft · 31 August 2023
RPP Pasal 78
RPP Pasal 78

Pengendali Data Pribadi dilarang memberlakukan klasula eksonerasi dalam hal persetujuan terhadap perubahan yang dilakukan oleh Pengendali Data Pribadi terkait legalitas, tujuan, jenis dan relevansi, jangka waktu dan rincian informasi yang dikumpulkan.

Enacted · PP 33/2026
PP Pasal 65
PP Pasal 65

Pengendali Data Pribadi tidak dapat mencantumkan klausul eksonerasi dalam pemberitahuan Pelindungan Data Pribadi sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan.

What changed

RPP Pasal 78 used dilarang and targeted exoneration clauses in consent to changes of legality, purpose, type and relevance, period and details collected. PP 33/2026 Pasal 65 uses tidak dapat, drops the enumerated change categories, and re-scopes the ban to exoneration clauses in the pemberitahuan Pelindungan Data Pribadi, subject to other legislation.

Analysis

A specific prohibition became a general one and lost its trigger.

RPP Pasal 78 was aimed at the practice of using a consent flow for a change of purpose or retention period to disclaim liability, which is why it enumerated the five change categories; PP 33/2026 Pasal 65 covers exoneration clauses anywhere in the privacy notice but says nothing about consent to changes, and its closing sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan subordinates the ban to whatever other legislation provides on such clauses.

Whether tidak dapat carries the same weight as dilarang is untested. A clause disclaiming liability that sits in terms of service rather than the notice is now outside Pasal 65 on its face.

What to do about it

Audit the privacy notice specifically for liability disclaimers and keep the RPP Pasal 78 change scenarios in view.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Articles 12, 13, 14

The provision. GDPR Article 13 requires the controller to hand over a fixed list of information at the moment data is collected from the data subject: identity and contact details, the data protection officer, purposes and legal basis, any legitimate interests relied on, recipients and transfers under GDPR Article 13(1), and then under GDPR Article 13(2) the retention period, the data subject rights, the right to complain, whether provision is statutory or contractual, and any automated decision-making.

Against Indonesia. UU Pasal 5 names four heads, identity, dasar kepentingan hukum, tujuan, and akuntabilitas of the party seeking the data. Also compared at UU Pasal 23.

Compared at UU Pasal 5, where the full comparison sits.

Recorded request stops being optional and becomes the route

duty changed
Draft · 31 August 2023
RPP Pasal 37
RPP Pasal 37

Pelaksanaan hak Subjek Data Pribadi dapat diajukan melalui permohonan tercatat yang disampaikan secara elektronik atau nonelektronik kepada Pengendali Data Pribadi sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang - undangan.

Enacted · PP 33/2026
PP Pasal 20
PP Pasal 20

Pelaksanaan hak Subjek Data Pribadi diajukan melalui permohonan tercatat yang disampaikan secara elektronik atau nonelektronik kepada Pengendali Data Pribadi sesuai dengan ketentuan peraturan perundang-undangan.

What changed

Draft Pasal 37 provided that rights dapat diajukan through a recorded request. Enacted Pasal 20 deletes dapat, so a recorded request is the form in which a rights request is made.

Analysis

The draft treated the recorded request as one available route, which left room for an informal request over a counter or a helpline to count. Enacted Pasal 20 removes the permissive verb and states that the exercise of rights is made through a recorded request, electronic or non-electronic, to the controller.

Read with Pasal 22, which fixes the moment a recorded request is received, recordability becomes the practical trigger for the 3 x 24 hour clocks that run from receipt, such as the access clock in Pasal 77(1). A request that leaves no record now starts nothing.

What to do about it

Route every rights request into a logged intake channel and timestamp it, because an unrecorded request does not start the clock.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Article 12

The provision. GDPR Article 12 governs how rights are exercised and answered.

Against Indonesia. Two things separate these.

Compared at UU Pasal 14, where the full comparison sits.

Enacted · PP 33/2026
no counterpart

The enacted text carries nothing in its place.

What changed

RPP Pasal 124(5) exempted the controller from notifying where the protection failure did not result in disclosure of personal data. PP 33/2026 carries no equivalent; Pasal 114 states the 3 x 24 jam duty with no exception clause.

Analysis

The draft's only off-ramp from breach notification has gone. RPP Pasal 124(5) meant that an availability or integrity incident with no disclosure component never reached the subject or the authority, whereas PP 33/2026 Pasal 114(1) now attaches the 3 x 24 jam duty to any Kegagalan Pelindungan Data Pribadi as defined in Pasal 1, which covers unlawful destruction, loss and alteration alongside disclosure.

Ransomware that encrypts without exfiltration, a mis-set retention job that destroys records, and a botched migration now all notify. Controllers calibrated to the draft will under-report, and the volume implication for the Lembaga is substantial.

What to do about it

Rewrite the breach triage rule; no-disclosure incidents are now notifiable within 3 x 24 jam.

Where Europe stands

This finding cites no article of the enacted text, so there is no implementing provision to carry a comparison. The subject is treated in the reading pages.

PP Pasal 114
(1)
Dalam hal terjadi Kegagalan Pelindungan Data Pribadi, Pengendali Data Pribadi wajib menyampaikan pemberitahuan secara tertulis paling lambat 3 x 24 (tiga kali dua puluh empat) jam kepada:

(2)

(3)

    Data Pribadi yang terungkap;
  2. b.

  3. c.
    upaya penanganan dan pemulihan atas terungkapnya Data Pribadi oleh Pengendali Data Pribadi.

PP Pasal 115
(1)
Pengendali Data Pribadi wajib memberitahukan kepada masyarakat mengenai Kegagalan Pelindungan Data Pribadi dalam hal:
  1. a.
    Kegagalan Pelindungan Data Pribadi mengganggu pelayanan publik; dan/atau
  2. b.

What changed

RPP Pasal 124(3)(c) required the notification to state the impact of the protection failure alongside the handling and recovery steps. PP 33/2026 Pasal 114(3)(c) keeps the handling and recovery steps and deletes dampak, leaving impact out of the mandatory content.

Analysis

The subject is told what the controller did and no longer what it means for them. RPP Pasal 124(3)(c) paired dampak with upaya penanganan, so the notice had to disclose consequence as well as response; PP 33/2026 Pasal 114(3) reduces the mandatory content to the data exposed, when and how it was exposed, and the remediation, with Pasal 114(4) adding the PPDP or contact point.

Impact survives only in the internal documentation at Pasal 116(1)(c), which goes to the Lembaga and not to the subject. A person receiving a Pasal 114 notice cannot judge from it whether to freeze credit, change credentials or do nothing.

What to do about it

State impact in the notice anyway; the enacted minimum does not equal a defensible notice.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Articles 32, 33, 34

The provision. GDPR Article 33(1) requires notification to the supervisory authority without undue delay and where feasible within 72 hours of the controller becoming aware of a breach, unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to rights and freedoms.

Against Indonesia. The clock is the difference that gets missed, and it is a difference about the start, not the length.

Compared at UU Pasal 46, where the full comparison sits.

PP Pasal 115
(1)
Pengendali Data Pribadi wajib memberitahukan kepada masyarakat mengenai Kegagalan Pelindungan Data Pribadi dalam hal:
  1. a.
    Kegagalan Pelindungan Data Pribadi mengganggu pelayanan publik; dan/atau
  2. b.
    Kegagalan Pelindungan Data Pribadi berdampak serius terhadap kepentingan masyarakat.

What changed

RPP Pasal 124(4) required public notification on three triggers, the third being that the controller could not be sure subjects would receive direct notice. PP 33/2026 Pasal 115(1) retains only the public service and serious public interest triggers and deletes the third.

Analysis

Public notification is now a public interest measure rather than a response to individual notice failing. RPP Pasal 124(4)(c) covered the case where contact details are stale or the subject population is unidentifiable, which is the ordinary situation in a scraped or legacy dataset breach; PP 33/2026 Pasal 115(1) leaves that case with no route at all, since the Pasal 114(1) duty to notify each subject remains but becomes impossible to discharge.

Pasal 115(2) adds that public notification runs through electronic and non-electronic media, so the mechanism exists and only the trigger is missing. Controllers who cannot reach their subjects are left with a duty they cannot perform and a public notice the enacted text does not require.

What to do about it

Where subjects are unreachable notify publicly and record why individual notice under Pasal 114 failed.

Against Indonesia. The clock is the difference that gets missed, and it is a difference about the start, not the length.

PP Pasal 117

(2)

  1. a.

  2. b.

  4. d.

What changed

RPP Pasal 126 obliged the controller by wajib to adopt and implement a breach prevention and handling policy. PP 33/2026 Pasal 117(1) states the same in the plain indicative and adds that the policy applies di internal Pengendali Data Pribadi.

Analysis

The incident response policy lost its enforceable marker and gained a boundary. PP 33/2026 Pasal 117(1) drops wajib in the same way as Pasal 116, and the added words yang berlaku di internal confine the policy to the controller's own organisation, which sits awkwardly with Pasal 118 placing a reporting duty on the processor and with Pasal 126(1) retaining wajib for supervising every party under the controller's control.

The four minimum contents at Pasal 117(2) survive from RPP Pasal 126, including role allocation, the analysis and escalation mechanism, documentation and reporting, and periodic review. The policy remains the practical prerequisite for meeting the 3 x 24 jam clock at Pasal 114(1) whatever its deontic status.

What to do about it

Keep the incident response policy and extend it to processors by contract since Pasal 117 stops at the perimeter.

PP Pasal 116
(1)
Pengendali Data Pribadi menyusun dokumentasi atas terjadinya Kegagalan Pelindungan Data Pribadi paling sedikit memuat:
  1. a.
    Data Pribadi yang dilindungi;
  2. b.
    deskripsi Kegagalan Pelindungan Data Pribadi;
  3. c.
    dampak atau akibat Kegagalan Pelindungan Data Pribadi terhadap Subjek Data Pribadi dan Pengendali Data Pribadi;
  4. d.

  5. e.

(2)

What changed

Draft Pasal 125 used wajib twice, to compose the documentation and to send it to the authority. Enacted Pasal 116 drops the word in both places and shortens the required contents from eight items to five. Pasal 116 does not appear in the sanction list at Pasal 184(1).

Analysis

The notification duty itself did not soften: Pasal 114 keeps the 3x24 hour clock to both the subject and the Lembaga and remains sanction-backed under Pasal 184(1). What softened is the evidentiary layer beneath it. Dropping wajib and leaving Pasal 116 out of the Pasal 184(1) list means the documentation that would prove a notification was timely and complete is now the least enforceable part of the breach regime.

The contents shrank as well, losing the cause of the failure, its chronology and the conclusion on whether personal data was in fact disclosed, which are the three items an examiner would use to test the timing of the notification.

What to do about it

Keep producing incident documentation regardless. It is what you will be asked for at examination.

Against Indonesia. The clock is the difference that gets missed, and it is a difference about the start, not the length.

(3)

(4)

What changed

The draft said further specific data dapat ditentukan by a ministry or agency after coordinating with the authority. The enacted Pasal 6(2) states that it ditentukan by the ministry or agency and moves coordination to Pasal 6(3), where it accompanies the determination rather than preceding it. The enacted text also deletes the three designation criteria in RPP Pasal 7(2), keeping only the bare greater impact test at Pasal 6(4).

Analysis

The draft expressed sectoral expansion of the specific data category as a permission exercisable after coordination; the enacted text expresses it as the ministry's own determination. PP Pasal 6(2) drops dapat, and PP Pasal 6(3) requires coordination with the Lembaga in the course of the determination rather than before it, which removes the sequencing RPP Pasal 7(3) imposed.

The criteria that disciplined such a designation, namely discriminatory treatment, material or immaterial loss, or other unlawful impact under RPP Pasal 7(2), are gone, and PP Pasal 6(4) retains only the untested dampak lebih besar formula. A controller in a regulated sector should expect the specific data category to expand by sectoral instrument, with no enumerated yardstick against which the designation can be tested.

What to do about it

Track sectoral regulators as well as the Lembaga for additions to the specific personal data category.

Where Europe stands diverges GDPR Articles 9, 10

The provision. GDPR Article 9(1) prohibits processing of a closed list of special categories: racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, trade union membership, genetic data, biometric data processed for the purpose of uniquely identifying a person, health data, and data concerning sex life or sexual orientation.

Against Indonesia. The largest difference is structural and it is easy to miss while the two lists are being compared.

Compared at UU Pasal 4, where the full comparison sits.

PP Pasal 8, 70
PP Pasal 8

Pemrosesan Data Pribadi meliputi:

  1. a.
    pemerolehan dan pengumpulan;
  2. b.
    pengolahan dan penganalisisan;
  3. c.
    penyimpanan;
  4. d.
    perbaikan dan pembaruan;
  5. e.
    penampilan, pengumuman, transfer, penyebarluasan, atau pengungkapan; dan/atau
  6. f.
    penghapusan atau pemusnahan.
PP Pasal 70

Subjek Data Pribadi berhak melengkapi, memperbarui, dan/atau memperbaiki kesalahan dan/atau ketidakakuratan Data Pribadi tentang dirinya sesuai dengan tujuan pemrosesan Data Pribadi.

What changed

RPP Pasal 10 to Pasal 15 attached a Pengendali Data Pribadi harus checklist to each of the six processing stages listed in RPP Pasal 9. PP 33/2026 keeps the enumeration at Pasal 8 and attaches no checklist to it. One item survives in changed form.

RPP Pasal 13 huruf a put memfasilitasi Subjek Data Pribadi untuk melengkapi, memperbarui, dan/atau memperbaiki kesalahan dan/atau ketidakakuratan Data Pribadi on the Pengendali Data Pribadi as a duty, and PP Pasal 70 states that same conduct as a right of the Subjek Data Pribadi over data tentang dirinya, qualified by sesuai dengan tujuan pemrosesan Data Pribadi.

Analysis

The draft regulated the lifecycle stage by stage. The enacted text keeps the stages as a list at Pasal 8 and attaches no duty to any of them. That is a narrowing, not a clean deletion. Perbaikan dan pembaruan reappears at PP Pasal 70, addressed to the Subjek Data Pribadi as a right rather than to the Pengendali Data Pribadi as a duty.

Both texts run on the subject acting, so what changes is who the provision addresses and the two added limits, tentang dirinya and sesuai dengan tujuan pemrosesan Data Pribadi. Whether a controller must give effect to that right is not stated by Pasal 70 and is not settled by anything compared here.

The rest of RPP Pasal 13 has no counterpart at Pasal 70, neither verifikasi Data Pribadi dari Subjek Data Pribadi at huruf b nor the processing principles at huruf c. RPP Pasal 14 huruf b is a different case.

PP Pasal 174 shares the phrase transfer Data Pribadi ke luar wilayah hukum Negara Republik Indonesia but governs a different object, deferring pelaksanaan persetujuan to a Peraturan Lembaga, so it does not carry the compliance duty forward. Two storage items from the draft are gone. RPP Pasal 12 huruf d angka 2 and angka 3 named salinan cadangan terhadap Data Pribadi and enkripsi dan/atau penyamaran data of those copies.

Neither is in Pasal 8, and neither has an equivalent in the articles set against it here.

What to do about it

Do not read the missing checklist as relief. Rebuild it internally, and treat PP Pasal 70 as the enacted route for perbaikan dan pembaruan Data Pribadi.

Where Europe stands aligned GDPR Articles 16, 19

The provision. GDPR Article 16 gives the data subject the right to obtain rectification of inaccurate personal data without undue delay, and to have incomplete data completed, including by a supplementary statement, having regard to the purposes of the processing.

Against Indonesia. UU Pasal 6 reaches the same two acts as GDPR Article 16, correction of inaccuracy and completion of what is incomplete, but it does not track the article's shape: the limbs run in the reverse order, memperbarui is added as a third act, and the purpose qualifier closes the whole right where GDPR Article 16 attaches it only to the completion limb. Also compared at UU Pasal 16, UU Pasal 30.

Compared at UU Pasal 6, where the full comparison sits.

Scope and definitions

The rule making a data requester a controller is deleted
